The analysis of eigenvectors in high-dimensional spaces poses significant challenges, largely due to the rapid growth of possible indices. This issue is exacerbated in scenarios like multi-dimensional Schr\"odinger operators, where eigenvector characteristics are largely governed by boundary conditions. Our research aims to investigate the outcome of the eigenvector analysis, specifically in the context of the multi-dimensional Schr\"odinger operator, using a two-layer neural network as a case study. The chosen neural network, with its non-differentiable activation functions, necessitates an examination of non-differentiable generalization errors. We utilize existing theoretical results to discuss the outcome of this error, demonstrating how it might not provide adequate guarantees for the desired eigenvalue estimates. To rectify this issue, we introduce regularization techniques that constrain the growth of eigenvalue indices, thereby facilitating a more precise analysis of the resulting eigenvalue approximations. Ultimately, the implementation of these techniques in the Schr\"odinger operator context allows for the development of a neural network algorithm that estimates eigenvalue precision as a function of the number of iterations. Our research presents a novel application of non-differentiable generalization error analysis and highlights the utility of regularization methods in ensuring accurate eigenvalue estimates for the Schr\"odinger operator, with potential extensions to other analysis methods. We also provide supplementary numerical simulations to demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed algorithm in practice. The principal findings of this research are summarized in a set of publicly accessible Jupyter notebooks, offering a comprehensive theoretical framework for solving eigenvector analysis issues. We also consider the potential for our methods to be extended to other high-dimensional eigenvector analysis problems in mathematical physics. The corresponding source code for the numerical simulations can be found at the following repository: https://github.com/yangchd/Neural-Eigenvector, where interested parties can replicate the code used in this research by cloning the repository. Our research delves into the extensive cosmic-ray anisotropies recorded by the Pierre Auger Observatory from 2004 to 2013, with a focus on energies exceeding 4 EeV. By analyzing the right ascensions and declinations of 669 highly energetic events, we identified short- and medium-scale anisotropy patterns. A fit to the anisotropy intensity as a function of energy revealed that the intensity increased with energy, but the trend was also susceptible to variations among different periods of observation. We ruled out the possibility that the anisotropies could be attributed to anisotropic distributions of ultrahigh-energy cosmic rays at the source, due to the intensity of the anisotropies recorded by our observatory. Model calculations that took into account the anisotropic diffusion of cosmic rays over the course of 84 million years, with an intergalactic magnetic field strength of 0.9 nG, were conducted to simulate the anisotropy intensity as a function of energy. The results of these calculations matched 75% of the data points recorded by our observatory, but discrepancies between the data and our results were particularly evident at the highest energy levels recorded. Moreover, we observed that the direction of the anisotropy intensity varied significantly over the course of one period of observation and that the anisotropy intensity as a function of energy was not uniform, with variations that could be attributed to differences in the composition of cosmic rays recorded by our observatory. By analyzing the anisotropy intensity as a function of energy and the anisotropy intensity varied over various periods of observation, we derived information about the mass-scale of the cosmic-ray sources and the distance between these sources from our observatory, with values ranging between 0.0024 and 0.49 EeV and between 2.3 and  Moor, respectively. We concluded that the anisotropy pattern recorded by our observatory was consistent with the diffusion model of cosmic rays, but left the possibility of observing more intricate anisotropy patterns in the future, prompted by the detection of more high-energy events, an achievement that would be made possible by the expansion of our observatory with the addition of the AMANDA observatory. An idea that we consider particularly significant is that the anisotropy intensity as a function of energy could provide information about the composition of cosmic rays recorded by our observatory at energies exceeding 4 EeV. Homogenization approaches for thin layers generally rely on periodicity in the normal direction being maintained. However, when such layers have a periodic structure in two dimensions but a non-periodic pattern in three dimensions, new high-frequency periodic perturbations are introduced, which can't be ignored. These perturbations make it possible to eliminate the layer's boundary, effectively averaging the low-frequency behavior. This method is applicable to a broad range of scenarios, including incompressible fluid flow, scalar fields, and vector fields with a conserved quantity. As an example, we consider an experiment where a droplet falls onto a hydrodynamic setup, creating a circular contact area on the ground. The resulting system is then homogenized to show that the contact area becomes almost perfectly circular. Additionally, this homogenization reveals the presence of long-range periodic perturbations, which ultimately determine the contact area's size. It is suggested that these periodic perturbations could potentially explain observed ring patterns on a droplet's surface in an experiment similar to the one described. This study likely has numerous other practical and theoretical applications and implications. Furthermore, it is believed that the approach used here may have a wider range of applications in various fields beyond the examples provided. The method's versatility stems from the fact that it can effectively eliminate the layer's boundary, revealing a phenomenon known as "Weyl relativity" - a phenomenon that may have a wide range of applications across various domains. The paper further highlights the intricate interplay between different scales in homogenization, as well as the non-trivial influence of the layer's three-dimensional periodic pattern on the homogenized model. Lastly, it is suggested that the approach used here could be applied to study the behavior of rare-earth spins in an experiment involving an exchange coupling with a magnetic field. Over five decades of research into Tumor Infiltrating Lymphocytes (TILs) has yielded crucial insights into the role of immune responses in cancer development and treatment. However, assessing TILs requires labor-intensive pathologic examination, hindering widespread application. Advances in Deep Learning (DL) have potentially resolved this issue, but training DL models on large datasets has become feasible only through the exploitation of computational resources in advanced institutes. This imbalance raises concerns under the guise of Data Privacy, which can be addressed effectively by Federated Learning (FL). Our work involves training an FL model on a collection of TIL categorization datasets, allowing each contributor to maintain control over their data while maintaining data diversity. Moreover, our solution promotes horizontal federated training, eliminating the need for synchronous data uploads and downloads. Our FL model is based on a Dual-Attention Darknet, which demonstrates exceptional performance in various TIL categorization tasks, surpassing the performance of conventional DL models by a notable margin. This research offers an FL-based solution that could potentially solve the data-exploitation issues of TIL training, which is a critical concern under the guise of Data Privacy in the medical field. Additionally, our solution provides and outstanding performance in TIL training, outperforming the state-of-the-art DL models by a significant extent. The details of our work are publicly displayed, enabling replication by other researchers. The Federated Learning code can be found at: https://github.com/Abdulshalli/Federated-TIL, while the dataset can be found at: https://github.com/Abdulshalli/TIL-Dataset. A quadrupedal robot's ability to navigate diverse terrains effectively is heavily dependent on its capacity to adapt movement strategies to the specific ground conditions. Evolutionary optimization methods have been utilized previously to develop walking patterns, yet these approaches are typically centered on a pre-defined set of gaits. This paper proposes the Evolutionary Pathway Creator (EPC), a novel technique, to generate multiple walking patterns simultaneously, thereby allowing the best-suited gait to be selected for a given terrain type. In contrast to existing evolutionary approaches, EPC defies interpretation and operates indirectly on the quadruped's hyperparameters through reinforcement learning. Through extensive testing on a diverse range of terrain types, the optimized gait controllers obtained with EPC outperformed the corresponding controllers obtained with existing evolutionary optimization methods based on specific gaits. Moreover, the study revealed a significant correlation between the evolutionary fitness of the EPC controllers and the underlying ground dynamics, which can potentially provide a general explanation for the success of the evolutionary approach. A comparative analysis of the EPC approach with existing control strategies, including reward-based learning and adaptive gaits, showed its superiority in navigating a broad spectrum of terrain types. The research presents a thorough validation of the EPC approach, showcasing its ability to develop a universal controller for quadrupedal movement across multiple terrain types. The central cores of nearly all nearby spiral and Seyfert galaxies emit intense radio waves on a scale of parsecs. These radio waves are often linked to a bridge of hot gas connecting a star-forming region to a supermassive black hole, yet similar hot gas has been found in many gas-rich galaxies without star-bursting. The high-speed wind, a cool core and a hot gas layer are the three fundamental components of this bridge. The warm breeze, a medium-speed gas flow, is also one of these components, which is believed to be responsible for distributing the bridge's energy to its surrounding area. Previous studies had found an unusual low-brightness X-ray core in the center of the galaxy NGC 7213, which does not fit the typical photoionization model or the more complex simulation model that takes into consideration of a hot gas wind. We used high-resolution X-ray RGS spectroscopy to study the bright emission lines in the core of the galaxy NGC 7213. Our study revealed a gas speed of 390 km/s with an error margin of 90 km/s, which is consistent with the warm breeze hypothesis. The new finding suggests that the emission from the core of the galaxy NGC 7213 could be entirely explained by a low-brightness state, in which the bridge of the galaxy is in a transient high-speed gas wind. The high-speed wind will eventually become a cool core, while the warm breeze, which is observed through a speed of 390 km/s, will distribute energy to the surrounding area of the galaxy. Moreover, our study of the galaxy NGC 7213 provides the first real-life example of a warm breeze in action. Reorganizing the structure of a nonlinear control system, such as through model predictive control (MPC), involves tackling a complex combinatorial issue. Due to the limitations in tractability resulting from the high dimensionality of this problem, employing machine learning techniques becomes a viable option. Specifically, a deep neural network is trained to speed up the calculation of the best system configuration, which is then used in an expanded MPC scheme. However, the expanded MPC still struggles with computational overload. To address this challenge, a novel algorithm is introduced that splits the problem of finding the optimal system configuration and controller parameters into two separate tasks. This algorithm, which relies on two neural networks and is known as twophaseRL, has been shown to yield better outcomes and faster computation times than the traditional training of controller structures using gradient-based methods, such as natural evolution strategies (NES). Furthermore, the twophaseRL algorithm has been successfully tested on two complex systems, namely a flexible, conic, connected wing aircraft and a flexible, conic, connected wing aircraft modified to mimic the dynamics of a helicopter. The results from these trials indicate that the twophaseRL algorithm leads to significantly improved outcomes and faster computation times compared to the gradient-based methods. The efficacy of the twophaseRL algorithm is attributed to its ability to tackle complex high-dimensional problems by breaking down the difficult combinatorial issue into a more manageable problem, thus enabling the use of machine learning techniques to speed up key calculations. The resulting improvement in performance and computational efficiency resulting from this approach is notable. The capability of the twophaseRL algorithm to expand its search space and tackle performance and feasibility issues in real-time is a key advantage. The algorithm has been shown to be robust in scenarios where little data is available for training and performs well even when key characteristics are missing from the training data. The results from the simulation of the twophaseRL algorithm indicate that it achieves a notable reduction (by nearly 90%) in the computational time required to determine the optimal system configuration, while also resulting in only a minimal (less than 5%) loss in performance. The improvement in computational efficiency resulting from this approach is particularly beneficial, as it enables the twophaseRL algorithm to expand its search space and improve performance without incurring a large performance loss. The efficacy of the twophaseRL algorithm is a direct result of its ability to tackle the complex high-dimensional problem by splitting it into more manageable tasks, and the results from the simulation indicate that it achieves a notable improvement in performance and computational efficiency

In 2010, the SiD detector was chosen as the reference detector for the future ILC by the Detector Working Group for the International Linear Collider.  The SiD sensor concept, consisting of a finely tracked, electromagnetic calorimeter in the rear and a precise vertex detector up front, offered the best observation capabilities among all options at the time.  Since then, research on the detector concept continued with the publication of the final report in 2015.  Although the SiD concept ranked highest among all options, several significant challenges needed to be addressed including pixel sensor damage, high power consumption, and sensitive to laser damage photodiodes on the sensor.  Given the ongoing development of the SiD concept for tracking at the level of 10^16 luminosity, in this study, an examination of an alternative design for the SiD detector was conducted, taking into consideration recent technological breakthroughs such as the use of Trench Double Metal Double Sensor and SiCr sensors which use a metal-inhibiting layer to prevent damage to the pixel photodiodes, and for the first time in this research, a silicon tracker instrumented with these new sensor technologies was included in a full detector simulation for the SiD concept at an luminosity of 10^17 per cm^2.  The research revealed significant progress in addressing the detector's challenges, and the findings suggest that the SiD concept remains suitable for tracking at high luminosity levels of 10^17 per cm^2, and could possibly be the best option for the future ILC.  Furthermore, research on further optimizations of the detector design is necessary to fully exploit the capabilities of the sensor technologies.  Based on the research outcomes, a new level of performance for the SiD detector was achieved, and could serve as a future reference for the detector concept at the future ILC.  The study also confirmed that R&D in the SiD concept remains the most suitable for the future ILC among all options.  The outcomes of this research will significantly impact the ongoing research and can help to fully utilize the capabilities of the detector at the future ILC.  R&D in the detector concept continues, and by 2023 the full simulation of the detector at the level of 10^17 luminosity will be completed which will mark the completion of the detector development for the future ILC. Among these, 227 stars exhibit metallic abundance similar to Tonantzintla 2, with many lying near the cluster's mean metallicity. However, many targeted stars showed metallicity discrepancies between multiple observations, likely due to the presence of second-population AGB stars as identified through their distinct metallic abundance variations. Additionally, our data, combined with existing data, yield a total of 479 stars within 0.15 magnitudes of Tonantzintla 2. Based on the metallic abundance distribution, we found the cluster to be multi-population, comprising first-population red giant stars with metallic abundance roughly similar to the Field Halo, and an overdense core rich in metal-rich second-population red giant stars. The variation in metallic abundance among red giants follows an elliptical pattern, aligning with the adiabatic growth of the core. Furthermore, our study reveals indications of minor AGB star contamination in the metallic abundance analysis, although we note that the most sensitive detection method yielded no evidence of a third, third-population population within Tonantzintla 2. Lastly, our study, combined with other recent studies, yields evidence that the majority of globular clusters lack a third, third-population population. This data poses significant challenges such as increased computational costs, rapid data accumulation, and the difficulty of incorporating diverse global datasets. To overcome these obstacles, a pioneering solution is presented that integrates the power of graph neural networks, data compression, and satellite imagery domain expertise. The result is EarthNets, an innovative system capable of processing and integrating multiple satellite imagery datasets in real-time, thus empowering AI applications on a planetary scale. Additionally, extensive experiments have been conducted to validate the efficacy of this solution. You can now deploy EarthNets on your local machine or directly in a cloud environment of your choice. Furthermore, this repository serves as a flexible framework for training models, integrating datasets, and evaluating the performance of models under simulated satellite imagery, making it an indispensable resource for anyone working on a broad range of AI applications on a planetary scale. Human-relevant activities are inherently marked by variations in movement patterns, 
which necessitate tracking both overall trends and deviations from expected behavior.
The anomaly detection techniques currently in use primarily concentrate on the identification 
of single instances of discordance or continuous periods of discordance within a fixed interval.
In contrast, this study addresses the need for identifying localized discordances within a sequence.
The framework proposed, ReAD, employs a tokenization approach to divide the movement into individual 
segments based on speed, then generates a unique representation for each token through a combination 
of natural language processing and feature extraction, allowing for the detection of discordant segments 
via clustering and a one-class SVM. The efficacy of ReAD is demonstrated through its application on 
human activity videos and 3D vehicle trajectories, outperforming existing methods by accurately 
enabling the detection of localized discordances, extracting relevant features, and providing a clear 
visual interpretation of the anomalies. The framework's open-source code can be accessed at 
https://github.com/hjhadad/ReAD. The dataset created for this research, comprising 3D vehicle trajectories, 
is available under the license CC-BY-ND-4.0 at https://doi.org/10.6082/ M1WF3EH. Moreover, 
an interactive visual demonstration of the research is available at https://hadad.github.io/ReAD.

We've calculated a vector shape factor for pions using various calculational techniques, including lattice QCD, quasi-partonic pion interactions, and radiative decay processes. Our lattice QCD calculation of the shape factor involves direct determination from lattice pion vector mesons and an alternative method using finite momentum vectors. The latter approach incorporates a systematic baryon chiral effective field theory to describe quasi-partonic pion interactions. Our results in the space-like region for the shape factor are relatively consistent with each other, but differ from a historical study. We've also explored the radiative decay process and derived a novel relation between the shape factor and an energy-dependent function, which facilitates expression of the shape factor through energy. Our work on the pion vector shape factor is expected to contribute to precision muon g-2 experiments by constraining a corresponding tau decay measurement. Furthermore, our study calls for a re-evaluation of the pion vector shape factor in continuum QCD using lattice theory. If successful, such a study could refine our shape factor results and potentially align them with a claimed result from a different analysis technique. Lastly, we've identified areas for potential improvement in our lattice QCD calculation, including the incorporation of dynamical u/d quark effects, a higher finite volume approximation, and a new set of lattice actions, all of which could lead to further pion understanding. Meanwhile, our quasi-partonic interaction results suggest a promising framework for further pion studies. Finally, we've analyzed our lattice QCD shape factor outcomes within the context of two distinct theoretical frameworks: the linear sigma model and the hidden local symmetry model, each providing a possible physical interpretation for our findings. In particular, our analysis reveals potential consequences for these theories if our shape factor results are incorporated. Moreover, our work leads to a prediction that the linear sigma model could accommodate our shape factor outcomes with additional constraints, while the hidden local symmetry model may also require supplementary assumptions to align with our results. To further clarify the connection between our work and these two theories, we've established a relationship between the shape factor and a specific low-energy constant, which is relevant in both models. Our study demonstrates that the hidden local symmetry model can, in part, be resolved through a combination of our lattice QCD calculation and other experimental data. Ultimately, our work sheds light on the distinct roles of linear sigma model and hidden local symmetry model in describing the low-energy behavior of the strong interaction. To conclude, our pion vector shape factor study has contributed new insights into the space-like region

Emergent embodiment in robotics and embodied AI involves systems that learn and perform actions based on their physical capabilities, which in turn influence their structure. When applied to code analysis, embodiment refers to a representation that incorporates its execution mechanisms, much like how a robot's body affects its movements. This novel approach reimagines software embodiment through a universal embodiment framework, facilitating the translation of source code into a modular, executable state. By decomposing code into individual components and employing a dynamic embedding technique, the embodiment model learns to replicate the original program's functionality. This can prove beneficial in various tasks, such as creating advanced generative code models, automated program testing, and code manipulation within software development workflows. To demonstrate the feasibility of this concept, we developed a universal embodiment model for Python, which successfully replicates complex program behavior, including deep learning models, and outperforms alternative approaches in a testing scenario. The implementation details and test data for this research are made available through an open source repository. This study contributes to the field of software embodiment, providing a theoretical foundation and practical results that can be built upon by future researchers. Additionally, the embodiment model's source code can be used directly in industrial settings, due to its publicly available implementation under an open source license. The relation between a galaxy's mass in stars and its total mass, including its dark halo, is a key area of study in understanding galaxy development and formation.  By analyzing 1109 galaxies from the ATLAS$^{\rm 3D}$ and SAMI surveys, which provided accurate measurements of stellar and halo masses, researchers discovered a strong pattern indicating that more massive galaxies tend to have less efficient dark matter halos.  In other words, a greater proportion of a galaxy's mass is in its visible stars when it has a higher mass.  This conclusion holds true across various galaxy shapes, contradicting earlier predictions that only certain galaxy shapes follow this trend.  Furthermore, simulations indicating that a galaxy's extended shape leads to a less efficient dark matter halo are supported by these findings.  Consequently, these results imply that a galaxy's development is influenced by both its internal structure and external environment as it evolves.  Also, a galaxy's rotation speed, another essential factor in understanding galaxy development, is ultimately determined by its mass and extendness.  Conversely, a galaxy's extendness is not necessarily dependent on its rotation speed but rather on its mass and the distribution of its mass in stars and dark matter.  In essence, a galaxy's basic structure, characterized by the mass distribution, determines its overall behavior and properties.  Additionally, a galaxy's morphological development is not solely the result of internal processes but is also sensitive to its environment, suggesting that a galaxy's shape is dependent on various factors including its mass, rotation, and interaction with its surroundings.  Finally, a galaxy's development is a dynamic and ever-changing process subject to various factors as a galaxy evolves in mass and size over time.  Thus, these findings contribute to a better understanding of galaxy development and formation, laying the foundation for a broader, more inclusive theory of galaxy evolution.  Furthermore, a new method of analyzing a galaxy's extended shape, detected through optical and near-infrared observations, is developed.  This method is based on a parameter representing a galaxy's overall extendness, used to measure its shape by comparing the mass of stars in the central and peripheral regions.  Additionally, this parameter is related to a galaxy's overall mass distribution, providing essential information for understanding a galaxy's development and formation.  Finally, a galaxy's overall extendness is detected, using observational data from the ATLAS$^{\rm 3D}$ and SAMI surveys, and related to various phenomena within galaxies, including their rotation and activity. We introduce GGLasso, a Python package designed to address high-dimensional Incomplete Partial Correlation Estimation (IPCE) challenges. Building upon the Graphical Lasso (GL) framework, GGLasso extends to:
- Dealing with incomplete partial correlation matrices.
- Estimating partial correlation graphs in the presence of a partial prior.
- Resolving noise-driven partial correlation anomalies.
- Enabling prior-optimized regularization through approximated priors' log-likelihood.
- Accommodating various regularization orders (e.g., group, element-wise).
- Integrating both exact and approximate solver options (e.g., sparsity-exploiting Cholesky and block diagonal).
- Supporting data augmentation for sparse and semi-sparse matrices.

We introduce a new method, dynamically weighted inertial forward-backward (DWIFOB), to solve monotonic inclusion problems. This algorithm combines the forward-backward algorithm with a hybrid forward-backward algorithm and incorporates accelerations, as well as dynamically weighted inertial extrapolation. It can be applied to a wide range of monotonic inclusion problems, including decomposible inclusions and convex-concave relaxations. Furthermore, under certain conditions, we prove that DWIFOB generates a convergent sequence whose weak* limit solves the monotonic inclusion problem. Additionally, we provide convergence rates for specific mathematical problems, such as proximal operators and split monotone variational inequality problems. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of DWIFOB by applying it to image restoration, network flow, and task scheduling tasks. A newly developed method called Attribute Directed Synthesis in Neural Design Search effectively generates neural networks by inputting relevant characteristics. This method leverages a pre-established synthesis space and is versatile enough to be applied across multiple domains, so we modified ADS to create a novel neural architecture search approach. By searching through a defined space, our method identifies an optimal neural architecture by correlating attributes such as accuracy and computational complexity. This neural architecture search approach can be applied across various domains such as computer vision and sound processing, and we demonstrate its efficacy by using it to search through a substantial synthesis space of 281 possible architectures and generating an optimal architecture that matches state-of-the-art performance while requiring significantly fewer parameters. Furthermore, our method allows for attribute-driven architecture search, which can be utilized to develop neural architectures tailored to resource-constrained applications. This search space includes over 48 million possible architectures and we demonstrate its versatility by using it to search for an accurate and computationally efficient neural architecture for the BERT language model, where we enhance its computational efficiency while maintaining its state-of-the-art level of accuracy. This method's efficiency is due to its ability to search through a vast synthesis space and identify an optimal architecture that achieves similar results with fewer parameters, thereby facilitating the development of a low-latency language model. Finally, we show that our method can effectively search through an extensive synthesis space by searching through 304 possible architectures and verifying its efficacy by means of a series of challenging computer vision tasks, where we successfully recreated the design of ResNet-50 and enhanced its accuracy after reducing its computational complexity. This achievement is a testament to the effectiveness of our method in neural architecture search. The code for this research is publicly available at https://github.com/alexrame/attribute-directed-synthesis. The repository contains a wide range of search spaces for neural architecture search, including one for BERT and various computer vision applications. Additionally, it contains a comprehensive guide on how to effectively employ ADS for neural architecture search. This includes guidelines on modifying ADS to effectively search through a synthesis space, as well as tips on optimizing the accuracy and computational efficiency of the resulting neural architecture. Furthermore, the repository includes a comprehensive collection of ADS-trained models, where users can find and download neural architectures trained with ADS for a wide range of applications, including but not limited to language modeling, computer vision, and sound processing. A growing concern in decentralized machine learning is addressing the communication costs associated with the distributed training of models on decentralized platforms. Federated Learning addresses these communication costs but only effectively controls local data access, neglecting the excessive communication costs incurred by updating the model after each iteration. To address both data access and communication costs, we introduce a new Federated Learning protocol called Federated Extraction. By taking inspiration from Federated Learning, but incorporating elements from Federated Learning's counterpart, Federated Learning Extraction, and Differentially Private Learning, we develop a protocol that minimizes communication costs while maintaining accurate model results. Through various experiments, we demonstrate the efficacy of our protocol in achieving communication-computation trade-offs that are inaccessible to existing protocols. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound for the communication cost of any protocol that achieves a specific level of accuracy, thereby providing a theoretical foundation for the development of such protocols. This new protocol can potentially serve as a generalized solution to the distributed extraction problem, encompassing applications like remote data extraction and decentralized machine learning. A corresponding open-source implementation is available at https://github.com/jbie-iiit5-indian-school/fedex. Additionally, our communication-efficient decentralized extraction protocol has been deployed on the Chainlink Network, a leading decentralized oracle service with over 200 million ETH staked. Through this integration, we have successfully addressed the communication challenge that has hindered the deployment of decentralized extraction on the Chainlink Network until now. As a result, decentralized extraction is now accessible and usable on the Chainlink Network, thereby expanding the spectrum of applications for this technology. Furthermore, our protocol innovations also hold potential benefits for other research domains, such as remote data extraction and decentralized machine learning. Thus, this new protocol has the potential to revolutionize these fields by providing an accurate and communication-efficient solution for extracting models from a distributed platform. To evaluate the effectiveness of our protocol, we conducted a series of comprehensive tests, including the distribution of cryptocurrencies and model extractions, thereby covering a wide range of applications. A novel approach to managing distributed computing systems is through a platform called Named Data Networking, which focuses on packet names rather than addresses. This results in a more dynamic and flexible system architecture that facilitates a novel strategy for coordinating computing services within such systems. Unlike traditional fixed and centralized models, dynamic coordination involves each user's device making decisions independently to interact with other system components, which can lead to suboptimal performance due to temporary service bottlenecks and delayed decision-making. To improve this, we have developed an optimal dynamic coordination policy that Demonstrate the superiority of proactive decision-making over wait-and-react strategies, especially in scenarios involving consistent service demands and a sufficient number of users. This optimal policy utilizes a finite-state machine to store relevant system statistics, which are drawn from an probability distribution and used to determine the most efficient interaction strategies for each system state. Our approach's success can be attributed to a tailored reinforcement learning framework, which reduces the complexity of finding optimal policies and enables a comprehensive analysis of the results. Our findings also reveal specific conditions under which a particular strategy becomes optimal, further enhancing the system's efficiency and consistency. Finally, we have backed our analysis with simulation data, which validates our claims and provides a clearer understanding of the performance characteristics of the proposed coordination policy. Furthermore, simulations have demonstrated that our solution remains effective in the face of unpredictable service bottlenecks and rapidly changing system states. These have confirmed our initial assumptions about the potential benefits of dynamic coordination and encouraged further exploration into the vast space of possible coordination strategies, prompting the question of designing more robust and resilient policies that could accommodate a wider range of system interactions. Ultimately, this research Contribute to a better understanding of the dynamics of a distributed computing system and guided by a general approach to optimizing dynamic coordination, we have identified key principles for designing efficient coordination policies that can consistently and optimally manage the interaction between system components, even in the face of temporary service bottlenecks and delayed decision-making. To achieve this, we have generalized the results of this research to a broader class of distributed systems and demonstrated the applicability of our approach to a real-world use case, where the interaction between system components and services needs to be coordinated. This has led to the discovery of multiple possible coordination strategies and prompted an investigation into the potential benefits and drawbacks of proactive decision-making, the development of an optimal dynamic coordination policy, and an analysis of the results, which revealed the system's tendency to oscillate between two states and the superiority of a particular strategy in scenarios involving consistent service demands and a sufficient number of users.

We provide a detailed analysis of the exponential stability of the Euler-Bernoulli beam on a star graph with multiple branches, consisting of infinitely many sectors, each containing a beam equation solution. Our work generalizes previous research on single sector spectra and extends it to the collective spectrum of the star graph's infinite sectors, whose stability is ensured by an exponential decay rate universal to all sectors, though this rate may vary. Additionally, we establish an inequality relating the beam's energy to its kinetic and potential energies, yielding a constant rate of decay for certain boundary conditions, thereby guaranteeing exponential stability for those cases. Moreover, we introduce a new notion of $\alpha$-stability and demonstrate that the Euler-Bernoulli beam on a star graph is strongly $\alpha$-stable for any value of $\alpha$ less than 1. Finally, we speculate that our findings and the notion of $\alpha$-stability can be applied to more complex graph structures, such as trees. \\

\textbf{Keywords:} Euler-Bernoulli beam, exponential stability, star graph, extended inequality, extended eigenvalue. \\

Automating a specific type of machine learning, which involves choosing the most useful performance metrics for a given problem, has proven to be difficult. Most existing methods are limited because they assume performance goals are equally important, which is not usually the case in real-world situations. Additionally, these methods usually rely on the available data alone and do not utilize additional information that could be useful. In this study, we develop an approach that learns how to balance different performance goals by incorporating prior knowledge into the optimization process. This allows us to optimize a utility function that represents the desired balance between competing performance goals, while also incorporating any available prior knowledge. Since directly learning a utility function is challenging, we develop a method that learns a set of weights that approximate the optimal utility function through gradient descent, while incorporating prior knowledge and regularization techniques to achieve a balanced representation of performance goals. This approach is successful in optimizing utility functions in realistic scenarios, as demonstrated by its application to multiple benchmark problems and a study of electron correlation methods in chemistry. Details of the experiments and hyperparameters used are fully documented and made available for public access. This approach can be an valuable tool for automated utility function learning and multi-objective optimization, enhancing its performance when combined with prior knowledge. In real-world scenarios, it also yields more interpretable and versatile results than other state-of-the-art methods that lack this capability. Specifically, its application in the field of electron correlation demonstrated its potential to improve the development of future quantum chemistry methods by targeting specific performance goals, such as enhancing accuracy while reducing computational cost. This approach can also be applied to other domains that involve utility function learning and multi-objective optimization, as demonstrated by its application to multiple benchmark problems in the field of operations research and hyperparameter optimization. This paper presents a novel utility function that learns a balanced representation of performance goals, incorporating prior knowledge and regularization techniques, and applies it successfully to realistic scenarios in the fields of operations research and hyperparameter optimization. Desired hyperparameters can be obtained by minimizing a specific loss function, as shown by the approach's code which is publicly available for other researchers to use. This approach is successful in optimizing utility functions in realistic scenarios, as demonstrated by its application to multiple benchmark problems and the hyperparameter optimization of xgBoost, a widely-used machine learning algorithm. Its potential applications extend beyond the fields of electron correlation and hyperparameter optimization to any domain that involves utility function learning and multi-objective optimization. This approach can also be used to facilitate human-ai collaboration by providing recommendations that are more tailored to the preferences of real individuals

Reinforcement learning agents can be vulnerable in various situations. Due to their slow convergence, agents often require significant human input in the process of training. Furthermore, deployed RL agents can be unpredictable, which may compromise system reliability. Moreover, agents storing historical experience may pose a security risk if compromised. Our research focuses on addressing a previously unexplored concern - attacking RL agents during deployment. We have discovered that an attacker capable of measuring response time and frequency can effectively manipulate an RL agent through the implementation of a simple, automated strategy, resulting in the agent being controlled consistently. We have further analyzed the conditions necessary for successful attack strategies, providing agents with various defense options. Our study delves into the challenges faced by reinforcement learning in the mobile robot sector and presents a measurable attack method, feasible through Wi-Fi, that can be applied to commercial mobile robots. Additionally, we provide a comparison of defense techniques, evaluating their efficiency in resisting the attacker's efforts, which could potentially lead to the development of more robust security mechanisms in the future. Our findings serve as a starting point for further examinations into novel attack strategies that do not require direct access to the system and can be scaled up for applications involving a larger number of agents. Ultimately, our work aims to contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex security issues prevalent in RL systems, aiming to control the behavior of external agents through attack or defense procedures. Two-dimensional non-symmorphic crystals possess both glide and screw symmetries, exhibiting unique properties that differentiate them from other types of crystal symmetries. A novel classification system has been established for non-symmorphic crystals spanning two-dimensional and three-dimensional forms. This classification involves identifying an elementary Dirac location on a non-symmorphic crystal surface. A two-dimensional non-symmorphic crystal surface exhibits glide symmetry, featuring a single band structure with Dirac locations along the glide line. A three-dimensional form, however, displays both screw and glide symmetries, resulting in the coexistence of linear and Dirac locations along the screw line coexistent with a single band structure type. A monolayer WTe2 material is presented as an instance of a two-dimensional non-symmorphic crystal surface, where its band structure can be modified to incorporate Dirac locations at various tunable stages along the glide line. This is achieved by introducing a zeeman spin-orbit coupling that accommodates multiple Dirac locations. This research lays a foundational understanding of elementary Dirac locations on non-symmorphic crystal surfaces, opening avenues for experimental manipulation and theoretical analysis in Dirac locations in two-dimensional non-symmorphic crystal surfaces.

In risk-aware reinforcement learning, modeling a risk function that accurately reflects an agent's tolerance for loss is crucial. However, accurately identifying a risk function is often difficult and may require a large number of risk-sensitive reinforcement learning explorations, leading to overly conservative policies. To resolve this issue, we introduce a new concept called dynamic resentment, which enables agents to adaptively determine an effective risk function through exploratory learning. Our approach integrates risk awareness into reinforcement learning under non-stationary settings, and we demonstrate through theoretical analysis that our method yields near-optimal results with minimal explorations. Furthermore, we show that our framework can be applied to separate the risk analysis problem from reinforcement learning, allowing for a more efficient identification of a suitable risk function. Our theory is supported by numerical examples and a case study of a real-world supply chain management challenge. Additionally, we provide evidence of our theoretical findings through numerical experimentation. Through this research, we make three significant contributions: developing a novel non-stationary risk-sensitive reinforcement learning framework, designing an new concept called dynamic resentment, and introducing an adaptive risk function identification method that outperforms comparison approaches. To prove the MacNeille fulfillment for $\Lambda^{\ast}$, it is necessary to establish the existence of a closure operator defined over $\Lambda^{\ast}$ that aligns with the $(\bold\Lambda^{\ast}, \cdot)$ monoid structure. Speakers are naturally inclined to modulate their speech in response to changing environments, incorporating various background noises. To improve text-to-speech synthesis, researchers are interested in using acoustic signal analysis to feed back into speech systems, especially in contexts like public transportation, street speaking, or the current pandemic scenario of crowd gatherings and mask-worn individuals. This paper sorts the options available for speech enhancement and signal processing, highlighting a specific technique called Dual-Patient Breathing (DPB) that shows promising results. To demonstrate the effectiveness of DPB, a sample sentence is translated into audio signals and subjected to various modulation conditions mimicking a crowded environment during the COVID-19 outbreak. A neural speech synthesis system is used to generate the speech, and the DPB technique is applied to enhance the audio signals, ultimately showing a significant improvement in speech quality as judged subjectively by humans. To bypass the need for manual transcription, a speech recognition tool is tested for accuracy in processing the speech signals, showing an improvement in transcription accuracy after the DPB treatment. To confirm the effectiveness of DPB, a statistical analysis is performed to show a strong correlation between speech quality and transcription accuracy, highlighting the DPB technique as a valuable tool for speech enhancement and improvement. A publicly available demo is provided at https://speech-demos.github.io/ SPEECH/TranscriptionForSpeechEnhancement. To replicate the results, a reference guide is included at https://github.com/adrissi/ SPEECH/TranscriptionForSpeechEnhancement, showcasing the codes and data used in this research. A pre-trained DPB model is also made available at https://github.com/adrissi/ SPEECH/Dual-Patient-Breathing. to support other researchers and developers. In linear model selection or regression analysis, an empirical prior method can be utilized with or without knowledge of error variance.
A non-Bayesian approach, this method involves treating multiple linear models as equally plausible, and then selecting the one with the highest posterior probability.
The high-dimensional posterior probability distribution is initially analyzed under the assumption of identical and normally distributed errors.
Next, a modified analysis is presented for scenarios where the error variance is unknown and consistent estimators are employed.
Finally, a minimum concentration inequality is established for the high-dimensional posterior probability distribution in such uncertain variance scenarios. 
This inequality proves to be a effective tool in establishing a characterization of the high-dimensional posterior probability distribution in these situations. 
The proposed characterization, which includes a precise upper and lower bound for the high-dimensional posterior probability, is heavily reliant on this minimum concentration inequality.
Ultimately, a characterization such as this one may provide valuable insights into how the high-dimensional posterior probability distribution converges in a weak sense. 
The utility of this characterization, however, lies largely in theoretical modeling; its application in practice is often hindered by the lack of a feasible way to evaluate the bounds in an actual data set.

This research centers around identifying the ideal hubs to cut in a multi-hub machining setup. For every hub, there's a set of possible cutting configurations, and their energy consumptions are calculated using a simulated annealing algorithm to determine the most energy-efficient option. A Bayesian evaluation approach is used to assess the feasibility of these options based on their estimated energy costs and past performance. A enhanced genetic algorithm is employed to refine these cutting configurations further. Notably, our method considers the cost of energy consumption, in addition to factors such as machining time and tool cost, to provide a more comprehensive evaluation. To validate our approach, we conducted an experiment using real-world data from an aerospace manufacturing facility, and compared our results with a scenario where hubs are cut in a random order, and another where only processing time is considered. Our findings indicate that our method is able to reduce energy consumption cost by at least 21% compared to the other two scenarios, and at most 46.4% in terms of energy efficiency. A specific scenario showed that refraining from cutting certain hubs in a particular order can reduce energy efficiency by as much as 46.4%, and also led to a 21.3% decrease in energy consumption cost. Furthermore, our method also resulted in lower average processing costs and better overall efficiency. A specific scenario showed that our method can achieve a 12.1% better efficiency and 10.5% lower processing costs by cutting the hubs in a particular order compared to a randomly chosen option. Our research provides a valuable insight to manufacturers on achieving better efficiency and reducing energy consumption costs through optimal cutting configurations, and also lays the groundwork for considering other costs such as greenhouse gas emissions in future studies. In addition, the findings from this research can be utilized by aerospace manufacturers to reduce their energy consumption costs and effectively implement sustainable practices in their production processes. A software package is available upon request for replicating our results, and this research may be extended in the future to other manufacturing scenarios with multi-hub configurations. Leveraging the Bayesian evaluation approach, we found that refraining from cutting certain hubs in a particular order can result in the lowest average energy consumption costs and improved efficiency, and these findings align with the principles of Taguchi design. Furthermore, our method successfully applied the principles of genetic optimization to achieve improved results, and it considers the unique characteristics of energy consumption costs through the use of queuing theory. The spectral dimension of a weighted graph is a conformal invariant, except in cases where its degree grows too quickly or too slowly. We've discovered an alternative method to determine this dimension by utilizing a measure that is both Ahlfors-regular and outer regular with respect to the graph's distance. Additionally, this new approach enables us to relax the outer regularity condition, although this requires introducing a modified distance metric. We also explore the relationship between this modified distance and the one commonly used in geometric analysis of graphs. Furthermore, our results include a proof that the spectral dimension of a weighted tree is solely determined by its first spectral gap. We have also successfully applied our methods to analyze the asymptotic properties of a specific fractal, known as the Rudin-Shapiro series, whose associated conformal measures display unique behavior. We leverage these conformal measures to demonstrate the fractal's properties, thereby simplifying a related theorem originally proven by Strzecki. Our work culminates in a novel generalization of the theorem to arbitrary weighted graphs with a specified growth rate. Lastly, we delve into the topological implications of our findings, specifically regarding the preservation of certain invariance properties under a specified type of map, known as a graph embedding, which we've designated as an 'embedding'. Our evidence suggests that an embedding which preserves the spectral dimension also preserves an associated conformal measure, thereby resulting in a new, non-trivial embedding whose image is a fractal, thereby linking our work to a related problem in analysis. We examine the two alternative approaches for solving the $\eta$-$\eta'$ mixing issue in light of a novel parameterization technique. This technique employs the $D_s$ decay width, which incorporates the $\eta$ and $\eta'$ contributions, as well as their interdependence via the $\eta'$ mixing ratio. Utilizing this parameterization allows for a tangible solution that incorporates experimental data from various $\eta'$ decay channels, thereby eliminating ambiguity in the outcome. Unlike other methods, this approach do not introduce inconsistencies by assuming certain parameters remain etched in memory. We demonstrate that when the parameterization is subjected to a systematic decay process, the resulting solution aligns with the conventional $\eta$-$\eta'$ parameterization method, which requires the presence of non-hadronic components. Notably, the latter includes the U(1) gauge boson and an etched-in-memory term for the $A_1(1385)$ meson. Our discussion also extends to the theoretical framework of the AdS/QCD model, which predicts a relationship between the two parameters governing the scalar and vector fields in the bulk space. We show that when the AdS/QCD formula for the $D_s$ decay width is substituted with the parameterization technique, a distinct relationship between the two parameters arises, which is distinct from the conventional $\eta$-$\eta'$ parameterization and the AdS/QCD predictions for the radiative decay $\eta' \to \eta \gamma$. Lastly, we hypothesize that the discrepancy between the two scenarios may be attributed to the presence of an extra degree of freedom in the AdS/QCD model, which can be eliminated once the decay width incorporates the effects of fermion fields in the bulk space, thereby yielding a prediction that agrees with the experimental data and the tangible solution obtained through the parameterization technique. Moreover, the modified AdS/QCD prediction for the $D_s$ decay width aligns with the value obtained via the $\eta$-$\eta'$ parameterization technique. Our findings provide tangible evidence that the parameterization technique can serve as a viable tool for resolving the $\eta$-$\eta'$ mixing issue, which may also apply to other problems of a similar nature. This paper introduces three metrics to assess the uniqueness, complexity, and reliability of signature biometrics. Uniqueness refers to how distinct an individual's signature is from others, complexity measures the variability of a signature, and reliability indicates the consistency of an signature across multiple examples. We develop statistical models for these metrics and demonstrate their effectiveness through experiments involving a large dataset containing signatures from 1,000 individuals, collected online over a period of two years. Our analysis reveals the following insights: (a) the majority of signatures possess medium-level uniqueness, with a unique combination of uniqueness and complexity also existing; (b) variability in signature patterns primarily stems from directionality rather than actual variation; (c) an average of ten consistent signatures suffice to guarantee the same signature; (d) machine learning algorithms can enhance the uniqueness and complexity of signatures using feature learning techniques; and (f) online signatures are more consistent across time than previously thought. These insights provide a framework for developing effective signature-based biometric systems. Our work also opens up potential avenues for applying these metrics to assess the uniqueness, complexity, and reliability of other human behaviors. Furthermore, the dataset generated during our research can be utilized by the biometric community for replication and verification of results. Our code is publicly available on GitHub for others to build upon. Our findings emphasize the necessity for thorough domain studies before applying existing machine learning methodologies to real-world biometric contexts. Our analysis also sheds light on novel applications of machine learning, such as feature learning, in the realm of biometrics. Lastly, our work underscores the value of long-term, crowd-sourced data in extensive biometric research. Our research contributes to the growing literature on online signature biometrics, influencing future research directions. Moreover, our signature dataset is robust and reliable, surpassing traditional laboratory-based approaches, due to its collection through a web-based interface. Our analysis also highlights the practical implications of our findings for various practical scenarios, such as enhancing the security of online transactions by evaluating the reliability of signatures across multiple examples. Our work also paves the way for further research into the applicability of feature learning in real-world biometric contexts. CLS not only enhances convergence but also provides a more accurate geometric representation, thereby improving regression models and metric learning. Our experimental findings, conducted across multiple computer vision tasks and datasets, demonstrate the superior performance of CLS over the standard least squares method. We introduce "concealed sectors," which, due to an inability to break symmetry, "hibernate" in these sectors. Our concept is exemplified through a multi-heat universe model, where we have multiple heat bath temperatures, one for each sector. The crossover between different heat baths serves as a pointer to hidden sectors. Furthermore, concealed sectors could naturally generate dark matter due to the temporary trapping of particles in these sectors, which transition into them. The multi-heat universe model also yields interesting cosmological and experimental implications. Additionally, we explore the possibility of space-time "hibernation," where the entire universe enters a concealed sector, leading to the cessation of time, with our current sector being "awake." When the "awake" sector's temperature reaches a threshold, a phase transition occurs, and the temperature in this sector becomes frozen, but a different one, perhaps with a higher number of dimensions, assumes the "awake" role, repeating the process. This cycle, with different heat bath temperatures in each sector, may generate a fractal universe, creating an oscillating pattern of cosmological evolution. The time span of these oscillations could stretch across tens of billions of years or less, with our current "awake" sector being the last or near-last one, where the temperature has not yet reached the threshold. With the temperature in concealed sectors freezing at different values, this phenomenon may be observable in laboratory experiments involving high-energy particle physics. Producing identical particles of the same sign in high-energy proton collisions is a rare occurrence in particle physics. This study demonstrates that generating same-sign W boson pairs through electroweak processes in these collisions is feasible, even crossing the sensitivity threshold of the CMS experiment at the LHC. Two jets and two identical leptons were observed in the final analysis state, drawing from event simulations of the standard model and a speculative model involving an Higgs boson interaction. After accounting for expected background noise, the predicted signal from the standard model and the speculative model were determined to be 0.09 and 0.01 events, respectively, with a statistical significance of 1.4 standard deviations of being due to the speculative model. Further investigations into the speculative model through regional analyses of the event data revealed an excess of significant importance within specific kinematic ranges of the transverse momentum and rapidity of the W bosons, corresponding to an excess of 2.3 and 1.5 standard deviations, respectively. These findings indicate that examining same-sign W boson pairs in high-energy proton collisions can provide valuable insights into the validity of the speculative model and potential anomalies in these collisions. Two possible interpretations of the findings were explored: the emergence of new physics dependent on kinematic details or the presence of interference between the speculative model and other particle interactions, which may be confirmed or refuted in future investigations. Simulated data indicated that detecting same-sign W boson pairs in higher-energy proton collisions at the LHC, specifically at 14 TeV, would result in a sensitivity threshold below 10^-5, while accumulating 100 million event data samples would be required to make a statistically significant detection, corresponding to a significance of 5 standard deviations. Alternatively, experimenting with lower luminosity at 13 TeV using a reduced acceptance threshold could yield similar results. These findings provide a foundation for future investigations into detecting same-sign W boson pairs in high-energy proton collisions at the LHC. Two possible future pathways are proposed: utilizing reduced luminosity at 13 TeV or awaiting the upgrade to 14 TeV to make a statistically significant detection of the speculative model. If successful, these investigations could lead to groundbreaking advancements in our understanding of same-sign W boson pair production and new physics, potentially shedding light on its generation in 75% of all cases and its potential interference with other particle interactions. Lastly, these findings underscore the importance of examining variable-dependent backgrounds in particle physics to avoid misleading inferences due to background noise in future investigations. GitHub's large repository of code files offers a valuable opportunity to streamline software maintenance by leveraging similarities across different projects.  By analyzing repository structures and maintenance activities, researchers can identify patterns in maintenance tasks and develop more efficient methods by grouping similar tasks together.  To explore these patterns, an analysis of GitHub's repository was conducted using a method that detects identical files across different projects to understand how maintenance activities are performed.  This analysis revealed that a significant proportion of maintenance activities involve files found in multiple projects, and researchers can utilize optical character recognition to extract relevant information from these files and improve maintenance by grouping similar tasks.  Furthermore, an innovative new approach, dubbed meta-maintenance, is introduced that automates the maintenance of similar software components across different projects, and the results of the analysis provide insights that could be utilized in meta-maintenance activities.  An implementation of the proposed approach, specifically designed for GitHub, is also presented and demonstrates its effectiveness in identifying similar files and maintaining them across different projects.  The study provides a framework that can be employed by maintenance researchers to uncover opportunities for meta-maintenance across various software systems and repositories.  Additionally, the analysis and implementation of the maintenance activities can aid researchers in evaluating the effectiveness of manual maintenance activities and improving the overall maintenance experience.  The findings and implementations of this research are made available on an online portal for ease of use by the GitHub community.  The study, conducted using a dataset of 3.5 million GitHub repositories, demonstrates the feasibility and efficiency of analyzing large repositories and detects identical files using only the metadata, thereby reducing computational costs.  The analysis also identifies file types that are frequently duplicated across different projects and explore the differences in maintenance activities across various software development domains, and the results provide insights that could be utilized in meta-maintenance activities.  The proposed approach, specifically designed for GitHub, demonstrates its effectiveness in identifying similar files and maintaining them across different projects, and the implementation is categorized into three types of maintenance activities that can aid researchers in evaluating the effectiveness of manual maintenance activities and improving the overall maintenance experience.  The implementations and findings of this research offer a framework that can be employed by maintenance researchers to uncover opportunities for meta-maintenance across various software systems and repositories, and provide a dataset and tools for analyzing repository structures and maintenance activities to understand how maintenance activities are performed and group similar tasks together.  The study also demonstrates the feasibility and efficiency of employing maintenance researchers using a dataset of 3.5 million GitHub repositories, and the results provide a valuable opportunity for meta-maintenance activities. This unusual radius, coupled with the secondary's likely metallicity, further supports the theory that the secondary component of BD And might be an evolved subgiant or giant star instead of a main-sequence star, thus potentially classifying the system as a gamma Doradus variable. This is an interesting candidate case due to the predicted short or non-existent photometric periods, which are predicted to be less than 10 days. Observations confirming a photometric period are crucial to verifying the theory of BD And being a gamma Doradus variable. If verified, it would make it the third such star in the MC.

Current cooperative recommendation approaches typically focus on two-tuple user behavior,
combining multiple aspects of an item's characteristics to form a single aspect's
preference. This can lead to biased results when users' behaviors towards different
aspects vary. To address this issue, this paper introduces a new cooperative recommendation
framework that learns the preferences of individual aspects independently, in the
context of multi-faceted user behaviors. Specifically, the model aims to optimize the
user's overall satisfaction by maintaining a stable and reliable aspect-by-aspect
relationship. The approach is based on a sparse domain-wide cooperative learning
mechanism that learns the preferences of each aspect in an unbiased environment, in
contrast to existing methods that rely on a sparse single-domain cooperative learning
approach. Experimental evaluations have shown that this model delivers improved accuracy
and more robust aspect preferences that are consistent across different aspects, in
comparison to state-of-the-art cooperative recommendation approaches. The results from
real-world datasets confirm the effectiveness and reliability of the model. The code
for replicating the experiments is available at https://github.

This paper provides rigorous guarantees for the robustness of least squares estimation in the presence of noise, focusing on both the high-outlier scenario and the average-outlier scenario. For the high-outlier scenario, where a significant proportion of measurements are severely inaccurate, we offer a precise bound on the maximum allowable outlier fraction that guarantees reliable least squares estimation. Conversely, in the average-outlier scenario, where the degree of inaccuracy is constant, we establish a threshold for the average fraction of outliers that can be tolerated while still ensuring accurate least squares estimation. Our research includes multiple case studies, along with a comprehensive review of existing methods for handling outliers in least squares estimation, analyzing their robustness guarantees. We also introduce a new approach based on the idea of confidence balls, which allows us to achieve more stringent stability guarantees for low-dimensional estimation tasks. Furthermore, we extend our framework to accommodate constraints such as sparsity or orthogonality in the model, while also discussing the applicability of our results to settings involving random data matrices. Overall, we offer a thorough assessment of the trade-offs between outcome quality and the number of outliers tolerated, along with the degree of inaccuracy permitted, enabling data collectors to set realistic "mistake assurances" for the data collection process. Our guarantees are substantiated through a range of numerical simulations. Ultimately, our research enables accurate least squares estimation even when dealing with highly inaccurate data, thanks to our novel approach to corruption tolerance in regression. Focusing on the one-dimensional Hubbard model with random site potentials, we demonstrate that interacting local spins forms a random singlet state at low temperatures, characterized by spin correlations decaying according to a power law. Conversely, the critical temperature that separates the correlated and decoupled spin regimes is heavily influenced by the disorder and is not entirely lost at high disorder levels. Moreover, these outcomes hold potential applications in understanding various material properties, such as the localization of electrons in germanium and gallium arsenide and the occurrence of local magnets in semiconductor materials. In real-world inverse reinforcement learning, it's often difficult to design an idealized, fully-observed reward structure. Real-world data often involves partial regulation, where some aspects of agent behavior are encouraged, and some aspects aren't. Unfortunately, current solutions assume complete predictability of non-encouraged behavior, making them unsuitable for real-world applications. Our new framework combines a predictive model of unencouraged behavior with a factor model that explains diverse behaviors observed in training data. A hierarchical Bayesian approach then uses multiple sources of data to inform a reward structure and guide policy learning. Our approach is flexible and adaptable, as evidenced by our tests on a range of tasks, including a task that integrates a controlled agent with a pre-trained actor-critic model. Our experiments demonstrate significant performance gains over prior methods on a range of tasks. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/shrutiangopaul/learn-to-reward. A robust loop transfer structure in a 3-manifold M is defined by a collection of finite subgroups G_1,..., G_n within its fundamental group π_1(M), along with a set of transversally stable orbits for an action by the group π_1(M). We explore extensions of M when the group action becomes free, which results in new robust loop transfer structures. Specifically, if M has a non-trivial element for its fundamental group and a subgroup G that satisfies a certain technical condition, then M will have a new robust loop transfer structure based on G. To analyze the quantum movements of electrons in solids, inelastic neutron scattering (IES) is employed, however the vast amount of data generated poses difficulties in analyzing the results, including determining the accuracy of the findings. Our research introduces an innovative approach, incorporating IES data into input for deep learning neural networks to streamline the analysis of IES data. Furthermore, we develop a method to increase the accuracy of the neural networks, revealing the relative significance of individual IES data points in the process. Our approach demonstrates exceptional precision in accurately calculating the excitation energies of electrons in solids when validated against theoretical calculations, and we showcase its efficacy on a well-studied class of materials known as transition metal oxides. This breakthrough enables the interpretation of IES data on a case-by-case basis, enhancing our understanding of the results and their relevance to the analysis of IES data in general. Our research has potential applications in various fields, including physics and materials science, promoting a deeper understanding of the results and enabling the development of more innovative applications using synchrotron light sources, along with the identification of meaningful patterns within vast datasets in various domains. The software tool utilized in our study is designed for interpretation and is accessible via a user-friendly interface, facilitating the application of our approach to a broad range of applications. Additionally, our approach facilitates the adjustment of neural networks to suit specific analysis requirements, such as determining the excitation energies with minimal bias. We illustrate the effectiveness of our approach, known as adjusted neural networks, on benchmark datasets, demonstrating its capability in delivering unbiased results and making our tool an indispensable resource for scientists seeking to incorporate user input, such as experimental data, into the analysis of IES data. In a pioneering application, we utilize our approach to calculate the excitation energies of electrons in a type of material known as rare-earth metals. We utilize adjusted neural networks to demonstrate that incorporating user-provided data, such as experimental results, yields more accurate estimates of electron excitation energies in metals. We showcase the precision of our approach on benchmark datasets, highlighting its potential to enhance our understanding of solids through the interpretation and adjustment of IES data. Ultimately, our research has the potential to revolutionize the analysis of IES data by promoting a deeper understanding of the results and facilitating the detection of meaningful patterns within vast datasets in various domains, synchrotron light sources, and materials science. We illustrate the effectiveness of our approach, known as interpretation of adjusted neural networks, on a range of applications including physics, materials science, and the identification of meaningful patterns

Over the past thirty years, preprint systems have undergone significant evolution since their inception on the internet, profoundly altering the landscape of scientific communication in the modern information age. This article delves into the history and development of preprints, highlighting their immense potential to empower preprint systems as a central component of the global scientific infrastructure. Several key factors have contributed to the rapid growth of preprints, including the emergence of the World Wide Web, the advent of search engines, and advancements in email-based technology. Additionally, the impact of prominent preprint servers, such as arXiv, has been instrumental in popularizing preprints within the scientific community. Furthermore, the influence of institutional repositories has also played a significant role in shaping the preprint landscape. Finally, the article concludes by emphasizing the irreversibility of changes that have emerged in the scientific communication system over the past three decades, ultimately leading to a future where preprints will become an integral part of the scientific destiny. Several critical aspects require consideration to capitalize on this new paradigm, including the role of metadata, search engines, institutional memory, scholarly networking, and ultimate citation indices that this article will explore in detail. Additionally, the article will examine the challenges and obstacles that scholars face in their daily work and offer suggestions to mitigate these problems by reinforcing the essential functions of libraries and information specialists in the modern information age. Lastly, this article will briefly delve into the broader implications of the digital scholarship revolution on the information landscape of the 21st century.
