High-entropy alloys, prized for their remarkable strength and versatility in their composition range, are gaining significant traction in materials research thanks to advancements in machine learning and data analytics. These advancements enable efficient identification of high-entropy alloys with target properties, promote computational miniaturization, and facilitate predictions based on existing and proposed phase diagrams. However, despite these breakthroughs, several challenges persist, such as the reliance on prior knowledge, difficulties in scaling for new predictions, and the inherent limitations of available data. To overcome these difficulties, there is a need for more accurate and comprehensive data, enhanced theoretical frameworks, and increased collaboration between experimental and computational researchers to tackle pressing issues in materials research. This review aims to provide an in-depth analysis of the progress made in applying machine learning to materials research and proposes new strategies to address ongoing difficulties and opportunities in the field of high-entropy alloys. These proposals include leveraging machine learning to guide experimental design, using machine learning models in a Bayesian framework, and developing innovative algorithms to tackle complex problems in materials research. By outlining these opportunities and challenges, this review aims to stimulate meaningful research in the field of machine learning applied to materials research. Keywords: Machine learning, high-entropy alloys, materials research, phase diagrams, chemical composition, microstructure, properties, materials databases, artificial intelligence, regression, dimensionality reduction, generative models, prototype design, phase field methods, Monte Carlo simulations, kinetic energy, materials simulation, metal materials, inorganic materials, advanced materials, materials engineering, materials science. Note: This article is primarily written for researchers in the field of high-entropy alloys but also serves as a general introduction to applying machine learning in materials research. Due to space limitations, some concepts and techniques have been overviewed briefly, and interested readers are advised to seek additional resources. About the author: Jiaxu Wang is a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Alberta in the department of computing science working under the supervision of Dr. Ali Arida. Dr. Wang's research focuses on applying machine learning to solve problems in materials research and he has significant experience in this field, as evident from his numerous publications. Dr. Wang has presented his research at various international conferences, including the 2022 IEEE/IC2S2 conference in Toronto, Canada, and is a member of the IEEE. Currently, Dr. Wang is working on novel applications of machine learning in the field of high-entropy alloys and exploring the use of machine learning in other problems in materials research. We begin by defining Slim Sidon sequences and establishing the relationship between these sequences and a specific type of vectorial Boolean function, which we have previously shown to be highly nonlinear. This relationship is based on our proof that any function from a vector space to a field, which meets certain criteria, must be highly nonlinear if it has a Slim Sidon basis composed of more than one element. We also demonstrate that a specific class of Slim Sidon sequences, which we call homogeneous, contain the key to achieving high nonlinearity in vectorial Boolean functions. Building on this concept, we define complicate Slim Sidon sequences and show that they can be used to establish a lower bound on the nonlinearity of certain vectorial Boolean functions, which in some cases equals the maximum possible nonlinearity. Furthermore, we define a specific type of vectorial Boolean function that is highly nonlinear and utilizes complicate Slim Sidon sequences, and show that these sequences can be applied to achieve high nonlinearity in multi-vectorial Boolean functions as well. We also provide an example of a nonlinear vectorial Boolean function that is, in fact, linear on a specific sequence of vectors, which in turn has a Slim Sidon basis composed of multiple elements; this example showcases that current methods for achieving high nonlinearity in vectorial Boolean functions may have a limitation in that they may only be applicable in cases where a function has a Slim Sidon basis composed of a single element. Lastly, we propose an open problem regarding whether it is possible to achieve a nonlinearity of $2^{m-1}$ in $n$-dimensional vectorial Boolean functions with a Slim Sidon basis composed of multiple elements, which has previously been proven and confirmed for lower dimensional spaces but remains uncertain for higher dimensional spaces.

Binary arrays with constant margin are widely utilized in software verification, particularly for establishing bounds on the running time of programs. This category of arrays includes both binary and ternary arrays. A novel algorithm is proposed in this paper for efficiently sampling uniform and non-uniform binary arrays with constant margin, taking logarithmic time to select a single element and linear time to select multiple elements. This sampling method has several key advantages: it allows for arbitrary multiples of the array size as a sample size parameter, includes both uniform and stratified variants, and can be applied to both binary and ternary arrays. Additionally, it offers flexibility in terms of the sampling ratio between domain values. The algorithm is designed to be suitably general, encompassing various special cases of arrays with modified access patterns. Moreover, it is expected to be suitable for hardware implementation due to its algorithmic determinism. The paper provides a thorough theoretical examination of the proposed algorithm's correctness, verifying its ability to accurately sample from binary arrays with constant margin. Moreover, it analyzes the algorithm's time and space complexity. Experimental results validate the algorithm's efficacy in real-world scenarios, demonstrating its ability to be highly effective through code examples illustrating its application to binary and ternary arrays. Finally, the paper briefly considers the algorithm's feasibility from a practical perspective, suggesting its potential for hardware implementation due to its deterministic nature. The paper concludes by highlighting potential areas for future research, including the development of a binary array non-uniform sampler with the ability to determine the running time of program bounds. The proposed algorithm, named Non-Uniform Binary Array Sampler (NUBAS), is shown to meet all the specified requirements. The key concept underlying NUBAS's design is the Fasting-Odd-Masking-Masking (FOMM) algorithm, an innovative approach to sampling from binary arrays with constant margin. FOMM is composed of three distinct components: the Fast algorithm, the Odd algorithm, and the Masking-Masking algorithm. The Fast algorithm utilizes a binary search approach to efficiently identify an element in a binary array with a constant margin. However, this algorithm can only be applied to arrays with specific properties and requires additional processing steps. The Odd algorithm overcomes this limitation by designing a specific sampling pattern for odd positions in binary arrays with a constant margin. The Masking-Masking algorithm addresses cases where the array's elements need to be masked during sampling. Quantization has garnered significant interest due to its capacity to reduce storage and computational requirements during inference. There's an underlying assumption that quantization also improves model generalizability, however this theory hasn't been formally explored. This study investigates the effect of binary weight quantization on the neural network's behavior by analyzing its spectral properties within an infinitely deep generative model framework. Our results demonstrate that binary weight quantization leads to an upper bound limit on the spectral radius of the neural network's kernel, resulting in a spectrally narrow distribution of eigenvalues. This property is found to be prevalent across various initialization methods and is found to emerge consistently during training. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between the binary weight quantization and the spectral narrowness, illustrating that as quantization precision decreases, the spectral narrowness increases. Our findings are substantiated through numerical experiments and we observe a correlation with the neural network's kernel singular values, suggesting a possible link with the efficacy of quantization in enhancing model generalizability. This study offers a theoretical understanding of the neural network's behavior after binary weight quantization and provides a predictive analysis of the effect of quantization on the neural network's generalizability. Additionally, we propose a quantitative metric for evaluating the efficacy of binary weight quantization, thereby facilitating the exploration of quantization as a regularization technique to enhance model generalizability. Code for this research is publicly available at https://github.com/gkekas/binary-quantization. Our approach reveals a pattern in how entropy is distributed across various surfaces within the extreme black holes. Additionally, we found that the coefficients in this entropy distribution follow a specific, predictable sequence. Furthermore, our research connects this sequence to a broader mathematical concept called the asymptotic triangle spectrum, which appears in a different part of quantum theory called quantum integrability. We verified the validity of our findings by applying existing mathematical theorems to extreme black holes and demonstrating that their behavior conforms to a broader set of potential solutions. Lastly, our research points out an interesting discrepancy between quantum theory based on Einstein's gravity and fully fledged quantum gravity. We introduce a novel concept of intersection multipliers for comprehensive lattice models with resolvable intersections, deriving them mathematically from the properties of subfactor norms. These multipliers display distinctive characteristics, such as symmetry, transitivity, and associativity, and they also adhere to a distributive law. This theoretical framework enables us to develop an algebraic representation of the intersection multiplicative structure of conditional expectation. Furthermore, we apply the notion of intersection multipliers to extend the established tensor product categories of subfactor algebras, resulting in a hierarchical organization of the subfactor hierarchy through a process involving successive 'thinning out' of information. This idea is also translated into the context of conformal net algebras, where it relates to a mechanism called 'intersection thunder', marking a significant development in the field. Finally, we use the notion of intersection multipliers to give a unified description of the subfactor hierarchy from the perspective of bimodules, a key object in the study of subfactor theory. This involves the construction of a category whose morphisms are represented by intersection multipliers, in which certain identifying relations are imposed, such as fertility and hereditariness. Since any subfactor can be described as a special type of intersection multiplier, this category proves to be extensive and encompasses the subfactor hierarchy, while the intersection multipliers themselves serve to abstract away unessential information, resulting in a simplified, yet fully informative representation of the hierarchy. As a numerical example, we demonstrate how the notion of intersection multipliers can be applied to the K-channel subfactor as a form of 'thinner' version of itself. This abstract study of intersection multipliers, a key concept being fertility, is then translated into the context of CFTs, where it is related to the concept of intersection thunder, and finally, the subfactor hierarchy constructed from the morphisms in the category of intersection multipliers is shown to be a concrete realisation of the higher tensor product category that we had previously abstractly defined. Signal recovery algorithms in compressed sensing often benefit from enhancements 
like stabilization techniques - damping and fractional approaches - which 
improve convergence and stability by reducing oscillations in iterative 
algorithms. These advancements can be found in tampered and fractional gradient 
methods for compressed sensing, and have led to better performance in various 
experiments. Furthermore, a new class of stabilization methods for iterative 
procedures, known as the fractional type, is being introduced and its benefits 
tested against a widely used iterative method called Chord. Results from both 
theoretical and practical tests confirm that it offers superior performance, 
which is also confirmed by taking into account measurement noise. Additionally, 
a new direction of study is suggested - investigating the effect of the 
stabilization parameter on the iterative process. A theoretical explanation 
for this effect has been established and it is observed that it resembles a 
ball bouncing phenomenon. Finally, it is proven that certain algorithms 
attaining an optimal solution also achieve a stable outcome. Keywords: 
Compressed Sensing, Iterative Algorithms, Stability, Convergence, 
Stabilization, (Generalized) Relative Log-Convexity.

We examine how the properties of a point spread function (PSF) are impacted
when images combining techniques are applied. These techniques, such as Kalman,
emdenn, and REGI, are utilized to mitigate the effects of atmospheric disturbance
in optical ground-based observations. Although combining images can improve the
detected signal, it also introduces bias which must be accounted for when analyzing
the data. To this end, we present a brief overview of the relevant imaging
techniques and then develop expressions for the PSF's essential parameters:
mean value, standard deviation, and diagonal elements of the covariance matrix.
Our analysis is validated through applications to realistic simulations, and
furthermore, we explore the practical implications of our work on the estimation
of an object's complex morphology. Ultimately, we conclude that while combining
images presents challenges, it is nonetheless crucial for overcoming the limits
imposed by atmospheric turbulence on the detail with which objects are typically
observed. However, our study suggests that efforts to improve the resolution of
low-light observations may be hindered by the limitations of the imaging methods
utilized. To fully realize the potential of high-resolution combining images,
advancements in both imaging techniques and the subsequent data analysis are
required. Specifically, our work indicates a need to account for the non-Gaussian
characteristics of the PSF when attempting to enhance the resolution of low-light
observations. To that end, our study provides a foundation for modifying the
regional covariance matrix model of the PSF that we previously established, allowing
us to accurately reproduce even minor details of an object's morphology. Our
analysis has important implications for the development of future high-resolution
adaptive optics systems, and serves as a reminder of the importance of accurate
modeling of the PSF when attempting to enhance the resolution of ground-based
observations. Additionally, our study is relevant to a wide range of ground-based
astronomical observations, and may also be applied to other areas such as

Duality between Gaussian free fields and Ising models has proven beneficial for gaining insights, but specific mathematical representations of free fields and spin systems hide underlying field and spin field connections. Conformal field theory provides a framework for translating field transformations into each other, but these mappings are generally complex and difficult to use directly. We present a new, simpler representation of the duality between the Gaussian free field and the Ising model, allowing us to bypass the need for a full conformal field theory formulation. This presentation also enables us to extend the duality to cover multiple currents in arbitrary dimensions. Additionally, since log-gases can drive stochastic Loewner evolution, our findings imply a connection between multiple SLEs and Gaussian free fields, representing a more concrete expression of the underlying duality. This relationship further enables us to explore the duality in scenarios with external currents, whose behavior is not well understood in the random current model due to the absence of a direct link to free fields. The newly established connections offer prospects for characterizing the log-gas path measure directly through field representation or finding a direct mapping between free fields and current models. Such breakthroughs could significantly deepen our understanding of these complex mathematical objects. The ideas behind our work may also be applied to other systems in higher-dimensional environments and different geometries, such as those encountered in environments with embedded boundaries or in environments where standard logarithmic transformations do not apply. These considerations motivate the development of additional techniques for analyzing field and current representations in a wide range of complex environments. The proposed connections also suggest the possibility of reinterpreting domain-percolation measures driven by random log-gases as a specific type of conformal field, thereby expanding the standard library of mathematical tools for analyzing these domains and providing a new framework for studying them. The resulting field, which we term a "current field," would possess the essential features required of a conformal field, although its drive may not be entirely derived from the current itself. The current-field duality presents a potential link between Gaussian free fields and the general type of field that would be expected to appear in aimed environments, offering a new possibility for characterizing the path measure of the log-gases directly through a field representation. The resulting field would likely possess an interpretation that is more easily related to the underlying Riemann surface of the log-gases. This investigation explores the maximum possible growth rate of smooth solutions to the Navier-Stokes equations in three-dimensional periodic environments. We demonstrate that this maximum rate is capped at $e^{2\nu t}$, where $\nu$ represents the viscosity and $t$ is the time. Notably, for initial data with a finite measure, we show that solutions exhibit exponential growth at a rate determined by the measure and the viscosity, independent of the initial condition's magnitude. Our work relies on the properties of solutions belonging to the Leray-Hopf space and the behavior of the nonlinear force in three-dimensional periodic settings. We establish that this nonlinear force can be confined to a compact set within the space of bounded functions, enabling the development of useful estimates that facilitate our findings. Additionally, we analyze the time-dependent characteristics of the nonlinear force and derive a general estimate for its action on functions within a specific Sobolev space near zero. This estimate leads to the discovery of a useful property, often referred to as a priori estimation, which enables us to derive explicit upper limits on the solutions' rates of growth in three-dimensional periodic settings. It is worth noting that similar research has been conducted in other environments, such as decay theorems in bounded domains and decay-free periodic settings, where solutions exhibit a specific type of growth. However, the exponential growth we describe in this publication remains novel, even for three-dimensional periodic settings, and we demonstrate that certain initial data can result in solutions whose magnitudes increase at an exponentially rapid rate, where the base of this exponential function is determined solely by the viscosity and the measure of the initial data. A new method is proposed for validating outcomes from first-principles simulations, specifically designed for applications involving a limited number of electrons. This method analyzes the internal consistency of simulation results by comparing their various versions, obtained by integrating different bases in the quantum equations. By examining the coherence of these versions over time, this method detects potential errors or instability in the simulations, thereby validating their outcomes. Unlike existing validation methods that rely on predetermined metrics, this approach is more adaptable and can be applied to a broader range of simulations without requiring prior knowledge of the results. Additionally, this method is scalable and applicable to a growing variety of simulation types. Its efficiency is enhanced by an innovative algorithm that integrates the versions of the simulations, making it possible to run the validation process within linear duration. This method is primarily demonstrated on a type of simulation called linear response, but its framework is versatile and can be applied to other types of simulations, such as those studying the decay of molecules. By integrating this method into the workflow of these simulations, researchers can automatically validate their outcomes and ensure the accuracy of their results, particularly for complex systems that are currently difficult to study experimentally. Finally, this method is presented as an open-source tool that is accessible to everyone, enabling researchers to verify the results and prepare the results for publication in an unbiased manner. Its source code is publicly available for review and verification. Furthermore, this method is an open validation protocol, allowing other researchers to replicate the results and apply the same validation to their own simulations. By sharing the results of the validation, researchers can confirm the accuracy of their results and demonstrate their internal consistency, thereby enhancing the credibility of their findings. Lastly, the source code of the simulations, along with the validation method, is shared through an open-source platform, enabling other researchers to replicate the results and ensuring the transparency of the research. The diverse forms of single and multi-cellular organisms result from intricate patterns developed during embryonic growth and tissue development. Deep learning has shown potential in capturing this complexity, but its applications are limited by the constraints of explicit representations. In contrast, implicit neural representations offer a more flexible approach, enabling the generative modeling of complex shapes directly from latent variables. In this study, we combine the benefits of implicit representations with the interpretability of occupancy occupancy grids by applying occupancy-aware implicit neural networks to the generative modeling of biological cell shapes. Our approach significantly outperforms existing methods in generating the micro-environmental context of cells, especially for cells that have a sparse and low-profile presence on a grid. We validate the performance of our network through the generation of various cell types, including an analysis of generated cell-cell and cell-wall interactions. Further details are available in the supplementary material. The code for this project is available at https://github.com/koorikp/implicit-neural-representations-for-biological-cell-shapes. Two fundamental types of spatial representations - metric and tensor-based - are commonly employed in the visualization of spatial data.  Although tensor-based methods offer more versatile representation, metric-based approaches are generally simpler to implement.  A recent study findings indicate that reinforcement learning, a type of artificial intelligence, prefers tensor-based space representations over their metric-based counterparts.  This discovery presents a unique opportunity for scientists to gain insights into the biological representations of space used in animals' navigation.  Furthermore, the article discusses how spatial representations' suitability for navigation tasks depends on environmental characteristics, such as complexity and obstacles, leading to the hypothesis that animals' spatial representations may be influenced by their learning mechanisms to navigate effectively in their respective environments.  A case study on two simple spatial navigation scenarios using reinforcement learning is presented to illustrate this hypothesis, demonstrating that tensor-based representations are more beneficial in scenarios with many interactive elements, whereas metric-based representations are more suitable for tasks involving precise spatial calculations, akin to finding a specific location in a sparse environment.  The lessons gleaned from this simulation provide a framework for the theoretical investigation of biological spatial representations' underlying learning mechanisms, thereby enhancing our understanding of animals' spatial cognition.  Additionally, the article discusses the significant implications of integrating tensor-based representations into real-time navigation systems, given their superior handling of complex and dynamic environments.  Emerging applications in autonomous vehicles and robotics, for instance, could greatly benefit from these tensor-based representations, potentially leading to improved performance and a reduced reliance on metric-based representations.  A demonstration of this integration is also presented, showcasing a metric-based approach that surpasses traditional sparse-based navigation methods in a relevant autonomous vehicle simulation scenario.  The article concludes by highlighting the numerous unsolved problems in this field, such as the theoretical underpinnings of tensor-based representations and sparse metric representations, presenting a complex framework for future research initiatives. Two simple models of interacting particles, called the hard-disk gyroscope and the rectangular disk gyroscope, are analyzed within a confined space. The movement of these particles is based on a non-reversible Markov process and is studied using Monte Carlo simulations. The properties of these particles, such as their overall energy and angular momentum, are examined, and the behavior of the system is explored over a wide range of temperatures. The results show that two components of the angular momentum follow a straight line, allowing for the application of an extended version of the fluctuation-dissipation theorem. This theorem identifies the ratio of viscous friction to stochastic force as the ratio of certain variances in the particle's movement. The testing of this approach against the simulations is a key aspect of the analysis. The work on these particle models contributes to the understanding of the relationship between a system's microscopical properties and its macroscopical behavior. Additionally, the study paves the way for the exploration of more complex systems based on these particles. The work also raises questions about the adequacy of existing theoretical frameworks for these interacting particle models and encourages further investigation into their thermodynamic properties. The Monte Carlo simulations presented here used an efficient numerical technique called TEMPO, an algorithm suitable for analyzing the movement of particles in confined spaces. The technique is particularly useful for observing long-term movements of the particles in the gyroscope system. The code for the numerical simulations is publicly available online. The analytical calculations were based on the Lorentz model for the particles' movement. The projection of this model onto the plane of the particles' contact point provides a simple, effective approach for understanding the system's dynamics. The analytical results for the variances in the particles' movement were confirmed through a comparison with the Monte Carlo simulations. The study also delves into the complexities of the system, particularly its interaction with the particles at its boundaries, and identifies key challenges in understanding its dynamics. The work on this problem contributes to the ongoing research into the generalized fluctuation-dissipation theorem and the frictional behavior of the hard-disk gyroscope system. The study also tackles the unresolved issue of how thermal phonons in the system generate friction. The work on these numerical and analytical models raises questions about their validity in the regime of very low temperatures. The study also points out the discrepancy between the results obtained through the third-order approximation of the frictional tensor and the results of the full calculation. A recent advancement in deep learning, specifically the Crnn model, enables precise classification of sound occurrences and their locations. This technique is capable of recognizing multiple sound types. In this research, an enhanced approach for sound event positioning and identification is presented, building on the basic Crnn framework, with two key optimizations: the substitution of rectangular filters with multi-directional filters and an innovative data augmentation technique called channel rotation. Extensive experiments were conducted with the Freesound dataset, an open dataset comprising mixed-signal sound recordings. Due to the presence of background noise, an open-source noise-removal tool was applied to the dataset. Our results demonstrate that the integration of the Crnn model with the mentioned improvements significantly boosts accuracy in localization and identification of sound events. Notably, when using the channel-rotation method, an impressive gain of 3.57% was achieved compared to the conventional Crnn model. Furthermore, the best-performing model achieved outstanding performance on multiple evaluation metrics, notably achieving an accuracy of 92.96% for localization and 93.23% for identification, surpassing the conventional Crnn model by 12.46% and 10.19% respectively. Additionally, our model demonstrated exceptional generalization, with a notable 11% improvement in the challenging localisation metric known as the'standard' score. A reduction in the size of the model was also achieved without compromising performance, making it more feasible for real-world applications. The source code of this research has been made publicly available, and the trained models can be accessed via the provided repository. This work is expected to contribute significantly to the advancement of sound event positioning and identification, a crucial area of study for the development of effective sound-based navigation systems for visually impaired individuals. An open-source repository containing the code used in this research can be accessed at: https://github.com/hiptau/Crnn_SEPI. We examine the structure of a collection of spectrally similar signals, dividing them into sets based on identical spectrogram levels. This investigation leads to a precise mathematical representation of such sets and a valuable inequality relating signal energy to their numbers. Ultimately, we demonstrate how this inequality can effectively estimate the count of significant signals within a noisy signal, thereby addressing a long-standing challenge in signal processing known as the "noise reduction problem." Our approach, rooted in a novel application of random matrix theory, offers an innovative solution to this problem. Moreover, as a by-product, we establish a significant trend in the geometric characterization of sets of spectrograms at the same intensity. This trend holds widespread applications across various fields. We also illustrate the efficiency and accuracy of our estimation method through experiments involving real-world audio data. To make our findings more accessible, we present an accompanying code package at https://github.com/Alois-Klinger/Signal-estimation/tree/main. This repository includes a Python module that integrates our signal estimation technique into commonly used signal processing libraries, including NumPy, Matplotlib, Scipy, and PyTorch. We hope that our work will contribute positively to the continued advancement of signal processing. Additionally, our research complements the study on the geometry of sets of spectrally similar signals, published in a research paper available at arXiv:2104.07397. This study provides a broad theoretical framework, whereas our present work focuses on translating this framework into a practical tool for signal analysis. Similarly, our investigation resonates with the research on the geometric structure of sets of similar signals, published in a research paper available at arxiv:2201.04198. This research reveals the inherent geometric characteristics of such sets and proposes a new approach to their characterization. We have applied a precise mathematical representation to explore these characteristics, thereby substantiating the findings of the mentioned research. A novel approach has been developed for identifying chimera states and synchronized groups within complex spiking neural networks, regardless of their appearance during active or quiet periods. This detection method, built into an automated system, allows for Chimera Pattern Emergence (CPE) detection and analysis. To validate its effectiveness and adaptability, the approach was applied to three well-established models of chimera patterns: the first corresponds to the well-documented antiphase chimera, the second and third to models introduced in 2021 and 2020 respectively, exhibiting asymmetry in firing frequencies. Computational efficiency was verified by comparing the CPE method to existing detection methods for the Blair-Rothstein and Daniel-Wright models, demonstrating a notable enhancement in processing speed and efficiency for these models. Furthermore, CPE successfully detected chimera patterns in three additional networks, including a model previously unknown to our knowledge, thereby showcasing its versatility and accuracy for identifying a variety of chimera patterns. To facilitate sharing of detection methods and chimera pattern results, the CPE approach has been made available on GitHub and through interactive visualizations on NeuroDataSim. This research aims to broaden the scope of chimera pattern studies, previously primarily focused on Blair-Rothstein and Daniel-Wright models, to encompass a wider range of networks exhibiting this phenomenon. Instead, we propose utilizing the CPE approach to explore unknown patterns or adapting it to analyze chimera patterns in more complex networks. In particular, we suggest that the CPE method could be applied to neural networks displaying directional connectivity, as well as those incorporating an inherent geometric structure. It is expected that this approach will facilitate a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanisms giving rise to chimera patterns, potentially including their links to memory and other higher cognitive functions. Lastly, we acknowledge the detection method's universal applicability to a broad class of networks and suggest that this general method could be applied to identify chimera patterns in other multifrequency oscillator systems beyond spiking neural networks. In this regard, we propose the term "chimera candidate" to encompass any instance of this phenomenon, regardless of the specific system giving rise to it, thereby fostering a more unified and general understanding of this phenomenon and its potential variations across different types of systems. Additionally, we acknowledge the potential for false negatives in our detection method, particularly in its application to the Blair-Rothstein model, as well as the possibility of observing synchronized groups and chimera patterns concurrently. Determining the stochastic impacts of gravitational collisions in celestial body systems, specifically on planet formation models, requires precise mathematical analysis but currently lacks formal verification in scientific codes due to their inherent complexity and lack of randomness modeling. To address this, a formal proof is presented, derived from a prior investigation on gravitational influences during close approaches, and is applied to the REBOUNDx module of the REBOUND N-body simulation code. This proof verifies that a specific algorithm correctly simulates randomized gravitational collisions in celestial body systems based on specific criteria. The implementation of these proofs in the REBOUND code, available through public repositories, enables the computation of stochastic gravitational impacts for individual particles and the entire system, thereby providing insights into the randomness of gravitational collisions. Furthermore, a demonstration shows the correctness of the implemented module, followed by a discussion on the formalization process and the next steps in this research line. The underlying mathematical structure of these proofs, based on the mean-field approximation, may also be applied to other randomness models in N-body simulations. The verification of this algorithm contributes to the establishment of a mathematically structured N-body simulation framework, which can serve as a reference for future work in this research area. The full verification is detailed in the report 'Formal Proof of Mean-Field Approximation for N-body Simulations with Gravitational Collisions' (arxiv:2207.09072). The formalization process and proof, as well as the code, are publicly available at https://formalip.org/REBOUNDx-and-Proofs/ and https://formalip.org/REBOUNDx-code/. An executable version of the proof (unshaked leaf) and the code (unshaked) are also available at https://formalip.org/Tools/REBOUNDx-unshaked-leaf-4.0- proofs-and-REBOUNDx-unshaked-4.0-3-d-uncorrected-code. This research focuses on a two-dimensional blocked disc problem, specifically examining sequences of discs that form alternately large and small gaps in a channel. Initially, the space between each disc is equally divided into two segments, one of which is chosen for placement. Our goal is to determine the most efficient way to pack these discs given this segmentation strategy. We aim to identify the sequence of disc sizes that maximizes the fill factor of the packing, given that disc sizes follow a specific sequence based on multiplication by a constant factor. This sequence, starting with the largest possible fill factor, is found to be comprised of progressively smaller disc diameters in a specific order: $\mathsf{\rho}$, $\mathsf{\rho}^2$, $\mathsf{\rho}^3$, and so on. Additionally, to further enhance the fill factor, we introduce an alternative placement strategy for the disc sizes in this sequence, resulting in an even higher fill factor. A theoretical model to calculate the fill factor for any given number of discs in this alternating sequence is developed and verified through both analytical and numerical methods. These predictions are then compared with existing research findings on disc packing, with our model exhibiting greater efficiency for a specific number of discs in this particular sequence. Finally, the geometric structure of the packing, specifically regarding gaps between discs, is analyzed and an expression for the fill factor is derived, with this result matched against existing research on geometric methods for disc packing. Our work presents the first model to efficiently calculate the fill factor for a sequence of disc sizes in this alternating scenario through a periodic tiling of the plane. This research not only surpasses existing research on geometric methods for disc packing, but also provides an understanding of the fundamental principles of disc packing based on discrete mathematical models. As such, this work may contribute to future research on general disc packing through novel approaches to sequencing disc sizes in this alternating scenario. Furthermore, our models can be applied to the packing of other regular polylines in two dimensions based on the same sequencing strategy for disc sizes. Ultimately, this research facilitates exploration into the intrinsic properties of discrete mathematical models as they relate to geometric principles of packing. To further demonstrate the generality of our methods, additional scenarios for which our models can be applied are presented, such as packing closed polygons in two dimensions based on a specific sequence for their side lengths. These scenarios, along with specific geometric variations of the filling factor for different shapes such as triangles, regular hexagons, and regular octagons, are also examined in this research. This study explores how confinement affects information entropies in helium-like atoms for various values of nuclear charge. By applying the Coulomb potential to these atoms through a cutoff radius, we determine entropy values for low- and high-energy states. A hybrid variational method enables us to analyze the Coulomb interaction's impact on entropy, particularly for states near their ground state. Our findings indicate that confinement amplifies the information entropy of bound states, consistent with the Krenskiadis-Bagchi-Bondel-Chakravarty effect. Additionally, this effect is more pronounced in higher-energy states and for atoms with lower nuclear charges. To further examine confinement's effect, we calculated the information entropy for a free electron in a one-dimensional box. These calculations demonstrated a divergence in entropy at very small cutoff radii due to the interaction between the electron and its image charge. A hybrid variational approach, combined with this electron's wave function, allowed us to study confinement's impact on entropy for a free electron and compare it with our results for helium-like atoms. Furthermore, this approach revealed an interaction-dependent contribution to entropy, which can be neglected for high-energy states but affects entropy measurements in quantum metrology for systems with long-range interactions. Our work has the potential to apply this understanding to other fields of quantum physics, contributing to ongoing discussions on the phenomenology of quantum systems. Our study focuses on two specific scenarios: one with uncertain signal noise and another with predetermined location probability distributions. Notably, our framework's versatility allows it to cover various other location models as special cases. To conduct resting-state fMRI research, researchers frequently utilize a combination of functional connectivity analysis and probabilistic prediction, yet there's a widespread misconception that ignoring data variability enhances prediction accuracy. This paper examines how ignoring data variance, known as "shrinking," affects predictive estimators and correlation measures, particularly in multi-site resting-state fMRI data. A thorough statistical analysis reveals that shrunk estimators tend to be more accurate, but only marginally so, and that correlations within certain parameters exhibit reduced precision due to non-fixable levels of uncertainty. We utilize simulations and a meta-analysis of previous studies to support these claims, and ultimately demonstrate that precision in predictive estimators and correlation measures can be increased by incorporating the imaging data's variance into calculations, particularly in multi-site resting-state fMRI research. This research provides empirical guidelines for researchers working with multi-site data to manage variance and achieve more precise results. Furthermore, our study underscores the importance of incorporating statistical methods that address variance, thereby preventing variance-related inaccuracies in predictive estimators and correlation measures. These findings have broad applications across various fields, extending beyond our examination of multi-site resting-state fMRI data, where variance can substantially impact results and their validity. Finally, our research offers empirical recommendations for predictive estimators and correlation measures, thereby enhancing the validity and precision of inferences in a wide array of contexts. We identify two significant implications of this new restriction: first, it enhances the convergence of the heat equation in directed networks, and second, it provides a theoretical foundation for the existence of a density of measures in directed networks. These outcomes corroborate previous high-dimensional findings. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the new Ricci curvature restriction is more stringent than its undirected counterpart, and we explore the scenario where the directed network's edges gradually transition from outward to inward directionality. We then examine the relationship between the network's directedness and its thermal transfer and density of measures properties. Our analysis reveals that, in certain situations, the new Ricci curvature restriction imposes a stricter requirement for the existence of a density of measures, whereas in other cases, the restriction relaxes the condition. These findings provide new insights into the properties of directed networks under the new Ricci curvature bound. Additionally, we discuss an open problem concerning the applicability of the new Ricci curvature restriction to infinite directed networks. The problem is inspired by a hypothetical scenario where network directions in infinite directed networks suddenly reverse, and we investigate whether the new Ricci curvature restriction remains applicable to such scenarios. The new Ricci curvature restriction may offer a theoretical foundation for the phenomena observed in infinite directed networks. Therefore, the open problem can be seen as an attempt to establish a causal link between the restriction and the topological changes in infinite directed networks. Transition state representations have gained significant attention in natural language processing due to their ability to capture complex motion paths. However, their effectiveness for languages that incorporate code-mixing is yet to be explored. Code-mixing involves combining two languages at any level, typically spoken languages. An instance of code-mixing can be observed in sentences like "Mereko nuam eki merko" from Marathi-English, where the transition points are highlighted in capital letters. To utilize transition state representations for code-mixing languages, we must first identify the relevant transition points. A potential approach for identifying these points is to utilize synthetic data generated through sentence-level transformations. Nonetheless, this method poses challenges due to the need to determine the optimal number of transition points. To tackle this issue, we developed a novel neural architecture, Transition State by Optimizing Dynamic and Relative Positional Representation (TO DO PESTO), in collaboration with Marathi-English language experts. This architecture enables the transition state model to learn the optimal number of transition points end-to-end. An evaluation of our approach on Marathi-English, Marathi-Hindi, and Tamil-English code-mixing languages demonstrated its effectiveness, outperforming non-transition state models in several benchmark language models. The source code for our approach can be accessed at: https://github.com/DeepSensGroup/PESTO-MCM-TS. Additional details can be found in our paper, Transition State by Optimizing Dynamic and Relative Positional Representation (PESTO): A Novel End-to-End Neural Architecture for Transition State Models of Code-Mixing Languages, at: arXiv:2301.08109.

Fisher initially defined this information in the context of optima, but its causal significance extends beyond this context. Federated learning is a decentralized machine learning technique that combines a client's local data, trained with conventional supervised learning methods, to produce a global model. However, this approach has drawbacks in several situations: it requires substantial communication when the client has few labeled data, and the local data is not utilized efficiently in the global model. In response to these limitations, a new distributed learning framework has been developed that employs decentralized semi-supervised learning for local training. It achieves this by designing a communication-efficient two-stage protocol to combine the client's local data effectively. The first stage eliminates unnecessary communication by averaging only the specific model parameters needed, while the second stage utilizes diffuse averaging to minimize data transmission. According to our research findings, this approach outperforms conventional federated learning and centralized semi-supervised learning methods in terms of data efficiency and communication efficiency. The code for this model is available at: https://github.com/chulangyu/CAST. Furthermore, our model's efficiency can be evaluated by comparing it against the baseline federated learning approach across diverse datasets, including a small dataset of labeled data called MNIST-USPS, a medium-sized dataset called CIFAR-10, a large-sized dataset called SD, and a customized dataset known as CodeBERT. In the Q-procedure, Monte Carlo simulations are used to estimate a best response strategy. By repeatedly generating random outcomes, a player learns to assign higher values to more profitable scenarios, effectively implementing a maximization of the expected payoff function. As the amount of exploration increases, the estimated Q-procedure strategy converges to a Nash equilibrium for games with a finite number of states and actions, and for a specific class of infinite-state games, known as Markov chains. Furthermore, it's been demonstrated that the rate of convergence for both types of games surpasses a quadratic rate, and that the deviation from the equilibrium value decreases at a rate of O(log(n)/n) under certain conditions. Additionally, the results have been extended to a variety of related algorithms, such as epsilon-greedy and neural network-based approaches, and the implications of these findings have been discussed in the context of a real-world auction scenario. Analysis of lead-lead collisions at 2.76 and 5.02 TeV are examined, focusing on the collective behavior of charged particles in relation to the quark-gluon plasma. Results from the ALICE experiment contradict the chiral magnetic effect's predicted impact in high-collision number events, but reveal its presence in lower-collision number events. Event data are divided into nine distinct charge sectors to quantify the connection between local charge distribution and particle alignment. Two key measurements - the balance between charged particles in relation to event plane and correlation distributions - are analyzed at various collision number levels. These measurements show a noticeable imbalance in particles at lower collision number levels in events exhibiting a local charge distribution imbalance. This effect increases with collision number levels, but decreases when taking into account the influence of the quark-gluon plasma. It has been found that the chiral magnetic effect's influence does not exceed 10% of total collective behavior in lead-lead collisions. Additionally, it has been observed that local charge distribution and particle alignment are connected across all examined collision number levels. This effect increases with collision number levels and shows no notable variation between 2.76 and 5.02 TeV, nor does it show a notable influence of charged particle transverse momentum. These findings contradict the chiral magnetic effect's predicted unique influence in high-collision number events and instead show a smooth transition between lower and higher collision number levels. It has been proposed that the observed collective behavior in lead-lead collisions is a result of the interplay between the chiral magnetic effect and conventional flow. These findings demonstrate that quantitative analysis of charged particles in heavy ion collisions can reveal or disprove novel physical phenomena such as the chiral magnetic effect. It is suggested that further investigation into the connection between local charge distribution and particle alignment, across a wide range of collision number levels and charged particle transverse momenta, be conducted to further understand the collective behavior in lead-lead collisions and to make more precise measurements of the chiral magnetic effect's influence. Additionally, these findings may aid in understanding similar phenomena in smaller and larger collision systems, as well as in the study of collective behavior in proton-proton and photo-nucleus collisions. Finally, these findings may also aid in understanding the initial state of heavy ion collisions and the formation of the quark-gluon plasma. The surge in online fundraising is remarkable, yet the key factors behind its success remain unclear. In this study, we analyze online crowds and the impact of their behavior on fundraising campaigns. Our investigation spans multiple platforms, including Twitter, Facebook, and Reddit, allowing for a broad exploration of the crowd's influence. To gauge the relevance of online crowds to fundraising, we conduct an in-depth examination of the behavior of Twitter users who follow prominent charity accounts, gathering extensive data and identifying patterns that forecast fundraising outcomes. Our results show that engaging crowd behaviors, such as information sharing and discussion, correlate with a higher probability of a charity achieving its fundraising goal, while a quieter crowd indicates a lower success rate. Furthermore, our analysis uncovers distinct crowd characteristics that differentiate high-performing charities from those underperforming. Notably, our research reveals a higher percentage of Reddit users among successful fundraisers, as well as a predictive correlation between Facebook crowd engagement and fundraising success. These findings contribute to the body of knowledge on the crowd's role in online fundraising and may inform the strategic use of social media by nonprofits to gauge user engagement and predict fundraising outcomes. Ultimately, our study's cross-platform approach holds value for further exploration, enabling organizations to better understand the impact of online crowds on their campaigns and make data-driven decisions to enhance their social media strategies. To facilitate this research, we make available a publicly accessible dataset containing our research findings, including the full dataset and code for the analysis: https://crowdimpact.github.io/. The dataset can also be accessed directly via GitHub at: https://github.com/crowdimpact/crowd-impact/tree/main/Charity_Crowds_Data_Package. This paper proposes a novel approach to sharing cyber threat intelligence by leveraging federated learning, an AI technique that enables collaborative model training among multiple entities without exchanging private data. Our framework facilitates decentralized training of a machine learning model to identify malicious network traffic, utilizing anonymized packet capture data from participating organizations. By extending the federated learning process to include cyber threat intelligence exchange, we can overcome limitations in current threat intelligence systems that suffer from data privacy and sovereignty issues. Our primary contributions are the development of a cyber threat intelligence exchange framework based on federated learning and the implementation of a PoC system to demonstrate its effectiveness in detecting network breaches from an anonymous traffic dataset. Furthermore, we investigate the privacy-performance tradeoff associated with different federated learning configurations. The proposed approach provides a promising solution for organizations to share cyber threat intelligence while maintaining data privacy and sovereignty, an area that needs to be addressed due to the growing significance of cyber security across organizations. In the future, we aim to expand the PoC model to include intrusion detection through the incorporation of anomaly and confusion techniques. Moreover, we intend to investigate the application of federated learning in generating adversarial examples for enhancing the robustness of network breach detection models. Lastly, we will evaluate the adoption of a decentralized cyber threat intelligence exchange framework based on federated learning across various industries, an area that we believe will become crucial due to the increasing prominence of cyber security among organizations. The proposed framework may also have potential applications in other fields beyond network breach detection, an area that we will explore in a subsequent study. The novel approach presented in this research can be applied to various domains beyond detection, demonstrating its potential to revolutionize the exchange of cyber threat intelligence. The development of a decentralized cyber threat intelligence exchange framework is pivotal in addressing the challenges associated with data sovereignty and privacy in the future of cyber security research. The exchange of cyber threat intelligence through a decentralized framework based on federated learning is a key area of study that we will continue to explore in a subsequent investigation. This study presents an efficient algorithm for sequencing tasks in multiple robotic systems. The method excels at processing a high volume of task data, outperforming existing solutions. A novel clustering approach is developed to minimize execution time, leveraging robots' mobility to perform tasks close to where materials are needed. We introduce the Avaricious Clustering Algorithm (ACA), which optimizes task ordering by reducing unnecessary movement of the manipulators. For validation, a simulation environment was set up using Unity, recreating a real-world scenario of a bin-picking task. ACA demonstrates better performance than existing solutions in terms of execution time and cluster efficiency, with significant improvements seen in specific scenarios. Detailed analysis of ACA is provided, along with proposed future research directions based on the observed results. 

Keywords: Multiple Robot Manipulation, Task Sequencing, Clustering Algorithm, Bin-Picking Task, Avaricious Algorithm, Clustering Efficiency, Simulation Testing.

A next-generation semiconductor technology based on Silicon-on-Insulator (SOI) is presented, featuring a 20nm gate layer. Unlike traditional MOSFETs, which employ a fixed gate placement, this novel structure allows for a gate-to-source/drain distance of less than 300nm, thereby enabling the integration of highly capable trigate designs at lower cost through a standard 300mm CMOS process. In comparison to traditional MOSFETs, the implemented devices demonstrate significantly reduced short-channel effects, along with increased current drive and higher robustness against short-channel ratios. Moreover, the unique design includes a distinctive characteristic in the drain current conduction, resulting in elevated mobility compared to conventional trigate MOSFETs, thereby potentially replacing existing MOSFETs while also facilitating the efficient design of more advanced logic circuits such as 5T and 6T logic, static RAM, and SONOS flash memory cells. Additionally, the study highlights the feasibility of a 3D stacked CMOS integrated circuit, promoting a more aggressive processor manufacturing technique, known as aggressive-slope (or agressive-velocity) or constant field (emulation of constant voltage) to reduce variability in the 3D-bonded packages. The research successfully produces functional devices with improved performance through a standard CMOS process followed by a simple etching process. Several innovative techniques were also employed to enhance the agility, including the incorporation of a thin gate material. The resulting agile SiMOFETs exhibit distinctive characteristics such as increased source/drain doping, reduced threshold voltage, increased oxide thickness under the gate, and decreased effective channel length, thereby enabling the performance required for the construction of efficient, high-output logical circuits. The unique properties of the agile SiMOFETs were studied and demonstrated across three different gate materials: the thin gate material, a thin metal gate layer, and a thick gate layer. A 20nm gate length was achieved with a 300nm gate-to-source/drain distance, thereby enabling the integration of highly capable trigate designs at lower cost through a standard 300mm CMOS process, along with improved robustness against short-channel effects, increased current drive, higher mobility due to a distinctive characteristic in the drain current conduction, and the potential to replace existing MOSFETs while also facilitating the efficient design of more advanced logic circuits such as 5T and 6T logic, static RAM, and SONOS flash memory cells. Our objective is to evaluate how search outcomes change when users access video search platforms through multiple devices or sources, such as mobile, tablet, and PC, which often yield inconsistent user experiences due to varying device capabilities. To achieve this, we created a virtual agent-based testing framework for video search, based on user testing methodologies such as think-aloud sessions, across seven source variations, covering popular mobile and PC devices, plus a unique source simulated to mimic a real-world scenario. Our results show that search outcomes exhibit significant source-dependent variability, exacerbated by additional factors like distinct search bar queries and uneven result loading behaviors. Further analysis reveals that PC devices generally perform best, followed by tablet sources, which often experience loading issues, mobile sources ranking third, and a distinct, yet inferior, performance from the unique source and a bot variant. Our study's findings indicate a need for video search platforms to ensure smooth access across diverse devices, which could be compromised by source-related discrepancies in user experience. To address this, we suggest several design and optimization guidelines for video search platforms to mitigate source variability bias and provide better access to relevant video content for users across different devices. Building upon previous research on monodromy preservation in supersymmetric field theories, we present a new finding. Specifically, we have successfully demonstrated that the Wess-Zumino model, when analyzed through a careful examination of its supersymmetric gauge theory within the context of three-dimensional AdS space, exhibits a non-zero "monodromy anomaly". This anomaly arises from the precise calculation of a topological crossing amplitude following a bootstrapping approach. Our research further reveals an intriguing relationship between this anomaly and a previously identified constant, known as the "monodromy invariant". Notably, this anomaly is found to be proportional to the product of these two quantities. It is hypothesized that this anomaly may serve as a essential building block towards understanding the preservation of monodromy under the three-dimensional reduction of four-dimensional supersymmetric gauge theories. Our research also suggests an important connection between the topological crossing amplitude and a previously unidentified component of the Wess-Zumino model's four-point correlation function, which we have successfully managed to reproduce through our analysis. This finding represents an important advancement in the ongoing research on bootstrapping four-dimensional superconformal field theories. Lastly, our research concludes by proposing an important comparison between our work on the topological crossing amplitude and an analogous quantity identified in the framework of the Wess-Zumino model, known as the "anomalous monodromy invariant". It is hypothesized that the latter may serve as a reliable signal for the presence of supersymmetry within a particular class of three-dimensional theories. These theories are characterized by their adherence to a specific type of supersymmetry known as $U(1)I$. These theories are significant as they may serve as a useful tool in the study of the four-dimensional Wess-Zumino model through the application of the "anomalous monodromy invariant". However, due to a significant computation required to calculate it, it remains to be further investigated in the future. Furthermore, our research concludes by highlighting an interesting relation between the Wess-Zumino model and a well-known three-dimensional theory known as the "maximally supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory". It is hypothesized that the latter may serve as a useful model for the study of the four-dimensional Wess-Zumino model through the reduction of a more complex four-dimensional gauge theory, in particular one with a high level of supersymmetry. These theories are significant as they may provide valuable insights into the behavior of the four-dimensional Wess-Zumino model

Uncoordinated deployments of wireless networks are prone to interference conflicts that worsen with increasing network size. To address these interference issues, we propose a novel stochastic medium access approach, utilizing an online learning algorithm that adjusts transmission rates based on instantaneous feedback and long-term average SINR estimates. This algorithm enables cells to determine an optimal transmission rate, minimizing packet delays while adhering to a bounded queue occupancy. Through analytical and simulation analyses, we demonstrate that the stochastic algorithm achieves lower packet delays and higher throughput compared to traditional coordination methods, while ensuring seamless network operation despite packet queuing during transition periods. Moreover, simulations reveal that the stochastic algorithm can surpass the performance of optimal co-channel coordination schemes in dense network scenarios. Key implementation benefits include simplified implementation and minimal dependency on network parameters, such as channel assignment and interference patterns. These attributes, coupled with the ability to effectively mitigate interference in uncoordinated networks, make the proposed stochastic medium access mechanism an attractive solution for ensuring smooth network operation. Furthermore, our work directly addresses the common challenge of interference in uncoordinated wireless networks, yielding insights that can be applied to other dense network scenarios. To validate our findings, we conducted thorough analytical and simulation studies that isolate the impact of interference, confirming our proposed solution's efficacy in a range of network scenarios. Specifically, we demonstrated that the proposed stochastic medium access mechanism can achieve performance comparable to optimal co-channel coordination schemes, thereby validating our design goal. Furthermore, our results showed that the online learning algorithm can effectively capture the statistical properties of instantaneously varying channel conditions, such as Rayleigh fading, using a limited set of training data. This capability, coupled with the ability to analyze the algorithm's performance using tools from online learning theory, yielded precise bounds on packet delay and throughput, thereby enhancing our understanding of the design and verifying the stability of the stochastic medium access mechanism. To further refine our design, we employed the Lagrange duality technique to analyze the complex optimization problem, thereby validating the viability of the proposed stochastic medium access mechanism as a solution. Additionally, our results showed that the stochastic medium access mechanism can be easily implemented using well-established QAM modulation and MIMO techniques, thereby alleviating concerns about practical implementation. Lastly, we conducted a detailed performance comparison between the proposed stochastic medium access mechanism and existing coordination schemes, revealing that our design outperforms these schemes by achieving lower packet delays and higher throughput in dense network scenarios. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) excel in semi-supervised node classification, but their effectiveness heavily relies on accurate graph pseudo-tagging, which can be both time-consuming and computationally expensive to optimize. To streamline this process, we propose a novel approach where precise pseudo-tags are derived from a limited number of labels through intelligent sampling of high-quality pseudo-tagged nodes, which in turn facilitate better model performance and faster training. This technique is particularly useful for large graphs, where transformation operations can be performed efficiently to generate a vast number of pseudo-tags with minimal human intervention. Moreover, our method offers enhanced model generalizability and a significant training-time efficiency of up to 12 times over conventional techniques. Furthermore, we have observed a notable 8.5% improvement in accuracy over baseline models, confirming the efficacy of our approach. The proposed method has been thoroughly evaluated on diverse graph datasets, showcasing its versatility and reliability. The source code for this research is publicly available at https://github.com/ShivamYSharma/GraphPseudoTagging. The dataset can be obtained from https://dtf.is.informatics.indiana.edu/Datasets.html and the TIP-NLP repository at https://github.com/ShivamYSharma/TIP-NLP. Additionally, the GNN model architecture can be accessed via the PyTorch implementation at https://github.com/ShivamYSharma/PyTorch_GNN.

In recent years, computer vision has experienced rapid advancement in creating artificial intelligence models to process video content, with a notable surge in the creation of video inversion and manipulation tools. These tools, although highly versatile, pose a significant challenge due to the large number of input frames, requiring advanced memory and processing capabilities. We present PatchNet, a novel model designed to tackle this challenge by breaking down video content into manageable patches and processing them individually, thus enabling efficient video handling on smaller devices and without requiring frame-wise processing. Unlike existing patch-based approaches, Patchnet incorporates a short-distance attention mechanism that enables seamless template correspondence establishment even at patch-level. It leverages a customized transformer backbone to consolidate patch-level inputs, effectively capturing long-range spatial and temporal structure in video content. Through an extensive suite of detailed experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of Patchnet in achieving patch-level video manipulation, outperforming existing inversion and manipulation techniques by a notable margin, especially on mobile devices. The source code of Patchnet is publicly available at https://github.com/VisCam/patchnet.

In a repulsive SU(N) Fermi mixture, we find that the point where two clouds of fermions attract each other the most is consistently solvable for any number of components N, and this phenomenon holds true even when these fermion clouds are extremely far apart. However, the majority of our research focuses on the 2-component and 3-component systems, as they are representative of the two most general scenarios. Our study reveals that in a 2-component system, the minimum of the potential energy occurs at a specific, consistent value for any degree of fermion cloud overlap, and this potential energy is directly proportional to the product of N and the squared value of the overlap. Conversely, in a 3-component system, the minimum of the potential energy not only depends on the degree of fermion cloud overlap but also depends on the value of N; this potential energy is comprised of terms that are proportional to the squared value of the degree of fermion cloud overlap and terms that are proportional to the degree of fermion cloud overlap raised to the power of three, and further scaled by the value of N. We demonstrate that these findings from a repulsive SU(N) Fermi mixture have notable analogies with the findings of a recent experiment involving fermions, where it was discovered that the minimum of the potential energy exhibited non-General properties. Our study provides a mathematical proof of these findings and extends them to be applicable to a wider range of situations. Our research also reveals that in a 3-component system, the minimum of the potential energy can exhibit negative values for certain negative values of loop degree, and this phenomenon has analogies with the findings of a category of mathematical equations known as negative risk models. We further show that these findings can also be extended to situations where the degree of fermion cloud overlap is quite high, and the results of these investigations exhibit close similarities with the results of a study on the properties of bosonic raspberry potential. Our research has the potential to be experimentally verified, and our study also exhibits close similarities with the findings of a study on the homogeneity region of a mixture of fermions. In this paper, we'll explore the concept of the AI Incident Repository in depth, defining its scope, benefits, and potential structure, as well as outlining a strategy for maintaining and utilizing the repository. Finally, we'll discuss potential hurdles and future areas of research related to the AI Incident Repository. By presenting this concept, we hope to inspire a community of researchers and practitioners to collaborate on establishing a comprehensive system for sharing and promoting best practices in AI, thereby making the field's contributions more responsible and beneficial in the long run.

Theoretical foundations for Quipner, the functional version of Quipper, were established in a previous paper, but a more practical, embedded variant, proto-quipper-m, was introduced without equivalent theoretical foundations. In this work, we provide a complete formalization of the machine semantics for proto-quipner-m by expanding upon the existing theoretical foundations of Quipner and developing a corresponding denotational semantics. Additionally, we demonstrate that the embedded quotient domain, used in the machine semantics for proto-quipner-m, behaves equivalently to the greatest fixed point domain established in our previous work, and establish that the machine and denotational semantics are equivalent by showing that the translation from machine to denotational semantics is a total equivalence relation. This achievement not only validates the design of proto-quipner-m against the existing Quipner design but also lays the groundwork for future research by demonstrating that the machine and denotational semantics provide equally strong means for specifying and reasoning about quantum circuits. Furthermore, we extend the equivalence between machine and denotational semantics to include the original proto-quipner-m with composite commands, and show that its evaluation is defined as either a total or partial function by applying a mathematical property called continuous monotonic convergence, which simplifies the proof of its soundness. In another contribution, we establish that the correspondence between the embedded quotient domain and greatest fixed point domain used in our proto-quipner-m design is universal and applicable to any other domain with the same structure, and that this design can be embedded into any such domain while maintaining equivalence; this design can also be embedded into itself while maintaining equivalence, and we demonstrate that these correspondence and embedding properties can be proven independently of the specific design of the domain, and thus these results provide a general design principle for the machine semantics of any other such domain. Finally, we apply these high-level theoretical results to establish a new proof of the equivalence between the machine and denotational semantics for Quipner, and provide a translation from proto-quipner-m to Quipner while maintaining equivalence between their machine and denotational semantics. One of the most efficient methods of ordering functional data is the statistical depth approach, yet a major limitation of most depth definitions and applications is the necessity for data to be within the interior of its domain. Several alternative depth definitions have been proposed for functional data, but those depths fail to meet the perfect order preservation property completely. This paper introduces a new functional depth definition that can effectively handle inaccessible regions of the domain and simultaneously satisfies the perfect order preservation property completely. Our method is grounded in the isometric log-chord (ILC) transformation, which makes the corresponding distance metric a special type of Fréchet mean on the functional plane, while the original distance metric used to order the data remains undefined for some points, particularly those with functional data missing or located on the boundary of the domain. This issue is resolved by applying the ILC transformation, which changes the point's location to the ILC hyperplane before calculating its distance from the mean. This approach yields a new depth definition called the ILC depth, which possesses key properties such as symmetry, monotonicity, and the ability to effectively handle points located on the boundary of the domain without distorting their original positions. A comprehensive set of simulation experiments and real-world data analyses are included to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed ILC depth definition. Its superiority is shown through comparisons with four other depth definitions, which reveal its ability to outperform them in both robustness and the ability to effectively handle points located on the boundary of the domain without distorting their original positions. A free R package named 'RFSILCD' has been developed to implement the proposed ILC depth definition and used to generate the results shown in the paper. This package can also be accessed via the following link: https://github.com/tjchien/RFSILCD. Please note that the R package 'RFSILCD' has been previously known as 'RFSID', but its name was changed recently to better reflect the method it implements, which is based on the ILC transformation.
