High-energy particle collisions involving protons and nuclei can create a vast number of hadronic particles.  Among these interactions, the presence of top quarks and their corresponding antiparticles is exceptionally rare because they require extremely energetic collisions to form.  In the past, detectors at high-energy particle accelerators have successfully detected top quark productions in proton-proton collisions but identifying them in proton-nucleus interactions is a more challenging task.  To achieve this goal, advanced analysis techniques must be developed to distinguish top quark productions from background noise.  Given that top quark productions in proton-nucleus interactions are expected to be significantly suppressed at very low energy levels below 100 GeV, the detection process primarily relies on low-energy collision events at the LHC.  In this analysis, we demonstrate a new method to identify top quark productions in proton-nucleus interactions at the LHC using low-energy collision data.  The proposed strategy involves selecting events that contain at least one jet with high transverse momentum and an oppositely moving b-quark particle, while also incorporating other analytical techniques to minimize background noise.  To evaluate the effectiveness of this approach, we utilized the SHARK and ATLAS simulations to create a realistic picture of top quark productions in proton-lead collisions at the LHC.  The results indicate that these simulations can significantly enhance the detection rate of top quark productions in proton-lead collisions, thus confirming the feasibility of this new detection method.  With a more advanced detection technique like this one, the top quark generation can be detected in proton-nucleus interactions at the LHC with high accuracy, opening up new research avenues in high-energy nuclear physics.  Additionally, this detection method could potentially be utilized in future electron-ion collider projects, where the detection of top quark generations in electron-ion collisions may become a significant area of research in high-energy nuclear physics.  The development of this new detection method could pave the way for pioneering research in high-energy nuclear physics in the future. Furthermore, this detection method may have broader applications in high-energy research, such as the study of quark-gluon plasma at extremely low energy levels and the investigation of high-energy nuclear physics in the partonic phase of very low energy collisions. Developing a text-to-sQL parser that's both accurate and comprehensive is an extremely challenging task, primarily due to the diverse patterns in human language. To overcome this hurdle, we propose a novel parsing framework, referred to as M$^2$Parser, which leverages an end-to-end text-to-SQL model to generate semantic trees. The core idea is to utilize the output of the text-to-SQL model as guidance to assemble meaningful sentences during parsing. To enhance the diversity of parsed sentences, we introduce a supplementary task called sentence augmentation. Furthermore, we define two comparison metrics, F1$_{len}$ and F1$_{mask}$, to evaluate sentence-level parsing performance. Experimental evaluations of M$^^$Parser on multiple datasets reveal its superiority over existing state-of-the-art parsing methods. The proposed framework also outperforms baseline models in terms of parsing accuracy and sentence augmentation performance. Importantly, the analytical results show that parsing accuracy and sentence augmentation performance are interdependent. To demonstrate the effectiveness of M$^$Parser in generating practical SQL queries, we report the top three parsed sentence candidates for a sample spurious text. The source code of M$^$Parser is available at https://github.com/Chen-123456/MParser.

We've investigated the stellar mass function and the complex process of biasing in the initial data release of the LOFAR Two-metre Sky Survey. To do this, we've relied on semi-empirical models of galaxy formation to understand how certain properties of galaxies relate to their stellar mass. By using these templates, we've estimated the average spectral energy distribution of galaxies at various stellar mass levels. Our findings reveal that lower-mass galaxies tend to have bluer spectra, while higher-mass galaxies have redder spectra. This pattern holds true across multiple wavebands. Initial data release observations cover 212 bright galaxies with known spectral energy distributions, allowing us to accurately model the stellar mass dependence for a narrow range at around 10^10 solar masses. However, creating a more comprehensive spectral energy distribution dataset at higher stellar masses for larger galaxy samples is crucial for validating our current models and better understand biased galaxy sampling, particularly in radio observations, at higher stellar masses. Moreover, we've found that the estimated spectral energy distribution bias remains consistent across multiple brightness limits but needs to be studied further in darker environments to make more precise bias predictions. Finally, we've developed a first-order model to explain how galaxy bias changes in response to stellar mass variations, mainly due to the inherent spectral energy distribution bias that affects light distribution in galaxies at different stellar masses. This novel model effectively models galaxy bias up to a stellar mass of around 10^10 solar masses with a low level of uncertainty but needs to be improved by incorporating more detailed galaxy physics at higher stellar masses. Further survey data will allow us to refine both the spectral energy distribution bias model and the galaxy bias model, which will help to interpret future survey data accurately and make more informed observational design choices. Moreover, our approach, incorporating semi-empirical galaxy spectrum models and radio biasing based on stellar mass, can potentially be applied to other large-scale biased galaxy sampling surveys with multi-wavelength data, such as the Square Kilometre Array Galaxy Evolution Pilot. Finally, our work highlights the significance of radio data in interpreting galaxy bias, particularly at higher stellar masses, and the potential of the upcoming SKA to advance our understanding of galaxy bias through radio observations. Moreover, our study demonstrates the usefulness of combining optical and radio data to study the galaxy spectral energy distribution bias and galaxy bias, highlighting the tremendous scientific potential of joint optical-radio datasets from future surveys like SKA. Moreover, our work reveals the considerable value of utilizing semi-empirical galaxy spectrum models that incorporate radio data to interpret large-scale biased galaxy sampling

Utilizing a microscopic model based on single particle dynamics, we investigate how individual particles respond to external stimuli in both weak and strong scenarios. These stimuli cause rapid, microsecond fluctuations in the particles' positions. One characteristic of this response is the particle's velocity profile over time, which varies significantly depending on whether the external stimulus is constant or changes over time. When the stimulus is constant, the entropy produced per particle follows a linear trend, represented by a fluctuation-driven convolution of the velocity distribution and the rate of entropy production. This convolution introduces an inherent time-averaging effect, effectively making the contribution of higher velocity moments negligible. As a result, the entropy production becomes a convex, experimentally verifiable function of the average velocity of the particles. Furthermore, this convex dependence can be further optimized, resulting in a function that has a larger slope and exhibits larger deviations from equilibrium conditions over a broader range of velocities. Additionally, we explore the implications of our findings on second-order transport coefficients associated with nonlinear driving forces. These insights into the mechanism of entropy production also shed light on the fundamental, thermodynamic characteristics of individual particles based on their behavioral responses to external stimuli. When the stimulus varies over time, we found that the entropy production takes on a more complex, nonlinear form and is characterized by a characteristic time scale associated with the rate at which the stimulus changes. Our research also demonstrates that the convolution integral is replaced by a simpler, local relationship between the velocity and entropy production, thereby eliminating the effective time-averaging effect typically associated with entropy production. Based on these findings, we further analyzed the mechanism of entropy production and revealed additional features of the particle's dynamic behavior, thereby providing a deeper understanding of the thermodynamic properties of individual particles. These insights also underscore the significance of considering the external stimulus's temporal variation to extract meaningful thermodynamic information from experimental data. Our analysis further reveals the flexibility of single-particle dynamics in exhibiting either super- or sub-Darwinian behavior, depending on the stimulus's characteristics, thereby expanding our understanding of the thermodynamic properties of individual particles. Lastly, we investigated the mechanism of entropy production during rapid driving and revealed key features of the particle's dynamic behavior, including a relationship between velocity and entropy production that is characterized by a large slope and exhibits large deviations from equilibrium conditions over a broad range of velocities. Additionally, we analyzed the nonlinearity of transport coefficients associated with second-order driving forces and predicted a future research trajectory, thereby providing a theoretical basis for the experimental verification of entropy production's convex dependence on average velocity. The rising prevalence of artificial intelligence poses questions about its impact on the natural world. Ecological modeling, a field that investigates the interconnections between species and their environment, can provide valuable insights into the long-term consequences of integrating artificial intelligence systems. By analyzing AI systems through an ecological lens, we uncover previously overlooked effects of these systems, revealing them to be akin to invasive species that alter their surroundings. To address these concerns, we examine various ecological modeling methods that can serve as tools for assessing AI systems' impact on the environment, including mass-action models, differential equations, machine learning, and probabilistic simulations. Further exploration into the distinct benefits of these approaches could lead to the development of a framework for accurately predicting the ecological effects of AI systems, ultimately informing decision-making processes and guiding the design of AI systems with the capacity to positively influence their surroundings. Unlike existing AI assessment metrics that focus on computational efficiency and data management, our proposed tool can evaluate AI systems based on their long-term ecological impact, thus providing a broader evaluation spectrum. Ultimately, we aim to facilitate a comprehensive understanding of the ecological implications of AI, thereby enabling these systems to achieve their full potential of benefiting both the technology and ecological ecosystems. To assess the effectiveness of control policies in process engineering, authors often employ procedural monitoring, analyzing the impact of interventions on system behavior through the lens of nonlinear control theory. In this context, our work focuses on prescriptive procedural monitoring, where the monitored process is influenced by an external agent following a predetermined protocol. We establish a general framework for prescriptive monitoring, based on optimal control, and then consider two specific scenarios, analyzing the monitored process evolution under a leading agent's direction, and developing a new approach for identifying the underlying control policy when the monitored process behaves predictably. Ultimately, our method is applied to a STEPS model, demonstrating its utility in inferring the action of an unseen controller and assessing the validity of assumed control policies. The novel algorithms introduced in our study enable the computation of an alignment metric between predicted and actual process trajectories, providing valuable insights into the efficacy of applied control policies in analyzing procedural data. Additionally, our method contributes to the development of more accurate disease progression models by identifying the optimal intervention policy, and thus the most suitable trial arms in clinical settings, when only a limited number of treatment options are available. The presented methods are further validated through numerical simulations, analyzing the impact of variations in trial durations and disease model parameters on predicted treatment timelines. Our work introduces a versatile concept - prescriptive procedural monitoring, potentially applicable to a broad range of processes, such as disease intervention and cyber-physical systems, beyond traditional process engineering contexts. The proposed algorithms are implemented as open-source software, available at https://github.com/AE-KIS/PPM. The stepps_prm tool is specifically designed for analyzing STEPS model applications, while the built-in python package, ppm, can be utilized for applying the introduced methods to any other prescriptive procedural monitoring scenario. Furthermore, a corresponding ipython notebook is provided, demonstrating the step-by-step application of our approach to a STEPS model, and is available at https://nbviewer.ipython.org/12345678. Furthermore, we demonstrate the adaptability of our method by integrating an additional goal focused on heat transfer. Our technique remains versatile and can be applied with different goal functions, as illustrated through our numerical results. In this research, we explore if kernelization can be achieved for a specific category of problems by limiting the size of input strings, and we're looking at'stacking' problems, a type of combinatorial optimization issues, for a special case. Our findings reveal that these types of problems can be solved efficiently with a fixed-parameter tractable algorithm and can also be reduced to a more manageable size, allowing for a simpler, solution-based dimension-reducing technique. Furthermore, our study indicates that kernelization is feasible even in the presence of approximate solutions for these types of problems, thus contributing to a deeper understanding of the complexity of these problems. These results emerge from our examination of a broader theoretical model, the'stacking context', which encompasses 'tagged' combinatorial optimization problems and reveals a useful framework for this particular type of problems. In contrast, our study also shows that certain problems involving constraints cannot be reduced to a simpler form, even with approximate solutions, which provides further insight into their complexity. Ultimately, our research provides valuable insights into the complexity of optimization problems with specific parameters. These insights could be useful in designing more efficient algorithms for these types of problems. In certain situations, individuals hold differing opinions on how relationships between key entities interconnect. A new model, called the Linked Dynamics of Structural Equilibrium and Views, creates a unified framework that can handle both assurance and forward-looking analysis within this context of multiple perspectives. When there is a single dominant view, the model simplifies to mirror the classic assurance paradigm. However, when there are multiple views, each with its own probability of occurrence, the model yields a unique solution for each possible scenario, which can then be examined for potential instabilities and optimal policy applications. Through this expansion, the model can now account for a wider array of life insurance purchase motivations, encompassing not only a single, dominant view but also a spectrum of possible scenarios as well. As a result, the most pressing policy concerns surrounding limited assurance and forward-looking analysis are addressed in a comprehensive manner. Furthermore, a critical examination reveals that, in certain instances, policy action may actually drive individuals further away from a stable equilibrium. A thorough exploration of a particular in-action scenario, coupled with numerical examples and a graphical visualization, demonstrates how differing views can either reduce or increase the price of limited-term insurance, thereby highlighting the complexities of structural analysis and the need for precise model representations. Finally, a discussion on the challenges and controversies surrounding the reliance on structural models in practice is presented. These observations stem from an examination of a scenario in which a single individual holds two distinct views of the world, resulting in two distinct equilibrium outcomes with varying insurance prices, thereby illustrating the inherent ambiguity of a structural model prediction and the inherent uncertainty of a researcher's assessment. Additionally, the resulting solutions rely heavily on the researcher's subjective interpretation, thereby raising concerns about objectivity and the inherent limitations of a structural model in capturing unknown aspects of an individual's behavior, as evident in the case of a college-educated individual seeking assurance, where a more comprehensive understanding of the situation is required to make a precise prediction. Finally, a crucial recognition is made that a structural model may never fully capture all aspects of an individual's behavior, as exemplified by a situation where a frequent traveler seeks assurance, thereby underscoring the necessity of non-structural methods that can effectively incorporate individual specifics into a more comprehensive analysis. As a result, the utility of a structural model is significantly constrained, and a more flexible approach that combines both structural and non-structural elements is necessary to yield a reliable and accurate understanding of limited assurance and forward-looking insurance analysis. Several possible avenues for achieving this are presented.

Using advanced high-throughput technologies, scientists now measure the levels of messenger RNA directly within cells. This information has significant implications, as it enables the comparison of gene activity with its corresponding DNA. These new tools have motivated researchers to re-examine the relationship between a gene's DNA and its messenger RNA by simulating transcription on a massive scale. This large-scale simulation allowed scientists to accurately model RNA synthesis in human cells, revealing a surprising pattern - a significant delay between creating RNA and translating it into protein. This pattern held true across cells that were growing normally as well as those under stress. Further analysis of these simulations uncovered additional insights, including the prevalence of active gene regions within the human genome and changes in RNA production rates in response to external stressors. These results validate existing observations about the human genome's functional nature and provide new insights into gene regulation. This work has the potential to improve the interpretation of RNA-seq data, a widely used technique for measuring messenger RNA levels, and enhances the BIO tools suite with new capabilities. This suite is an online platform that enables researchers to model biological systems on a large scale. It has various tools that enable the simulation of transcription, translation, and other cellular processes, ultimately predicting the levels of proteins in a cell. These predictions can be compared to real protein data to validate models and explain observed trends. This is particularly useful, as a protein's function can be understood much better than a gene's, allowing scientists to link a dormant gene to a protein with known function and understand its purpose. These predictions have shown a surprising accuracy of 90%, higher than earlier expectations. This work has the potential to improve the accuracy of predicting protein function based on gene data and provides a new framework for combining different models and data sources. It also demonstrates how large-scale simulations can validate experimental data and reveals a comprehensive picture of a cell's functioning components. This knowledge can be used to inform models of rare human diseases and how they are inherited. This is made possible through the use of vario, a tool that enables researchers to simulate how mutations in a person's genetic DNA affect their health. This is a difficult task, as there is limited information available about the effects of mutations. However, by combining these simulations with real DNA data from families affected by a rare disease, scientists can propose new hypotheses about the underlying causes of a disorder and how it is passed down through generations. These predictions have shown a surprising accuracy of 90%, demonstrating a comprehensive understanding of a cell's functioning components and the potential to improve the interpretation of RNA-seq

Our research extends this concept to a larger framework, allowing for the distribution of group codes into multiple codes with interconnected overlaps. We introduce a new graphical model representation, 'brief function depiction',
which redefines the exact maximum probability expectation framework through
variable factorization. This novel approach leads to a quicker exact MPE algorithm
and facilitates a more efficient search for optimized solutions in the sum-product framework.
Our experiments demonstrate that brief function depictions can lead to a substantial
reduction in computational time and a marked decrease in memory usage for complex models. 
This new representation also offers a clearer and more compact model representation, 
especially when there are unobserved variables involved. 
We provide a geometric interpretation of the state space organization to explain its benefits. 
Additionally, we present an optimized implementation of the MPE algorithm and propose a 
further refinement to speed up computations, along with an efficient method for optimizing
parameters through a localized search strategy. 
These innovations enable a significant improvement in performance, 
particularly when dealing with large-scale or highly complex models. 
We support our claims with extensive empirical evidence and
illustrate the efficacy of our approach through a thorough evaluation of its
effectiveness, simplicity, scalability, modularity, reliability, and user-friendliness. 
Finally, we showcase the versatility of our technique by applying it to a range of
applications, including computer vision and the analysis of biological sequences. 
Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/parralx/bfd_mpe. 
This contribution is under consideration for an CC BY ND 4.0 license. 
It introduces three novel concepts: 
i) the brief function depiction as a compact model representation for exact MPE, 
ii) the factorization of the state space, and 
iii) the optimization of solutions. 
It presents empirical evidence of its effectiveness and showcases its applications.

In this study, we develop a location estimation system for objects positioned on the ground in front of a visual camera. Asynchronous audio and visual data are used to determine the object's location. Our method employs deep learning to process AV signals, allowing for the precise location of objects within a specific area. To enhance accuracy in challenging conditions, the proposed system integrates information from both modalities. For example, the audio signal can provide the distance of an object from the camera's axis, while the visual channel can pinpoint the object's location horizontally and verify the initial distance estimation. Leveraging the asynchronous fusion of the two signals, the object's 2D location can be accurately calculated, and its prone orientation also determined. Our novel approach enables location estimation with minimal overhead, as visual and audio data are regularly collected by smart devices. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed system achieves high accuracy in locating objects, specifically a precision of 0.83 meters when the axis distance is known and 1.04 meters otherwise, using widely available benchmarks. The integration of audio and visual cues significantly improves precision by a margin of 0.21 meters. The code for this research is publicly available at https://github.com/yhj3300/AxialLocation. Our work contributes to the development of location estimation systems that can function optimally in AV settings. Additionally, the method's design and testing on publicly accessible datasets using standard experimental protocols facilitate replication of the findings. Our research bridges the gap between small and large scales, offering a framework for widespread application that can be computationally simplified with the inclusion of a single non-Newtonian parameter, thereby facilitating global stability and control over shear thickening phenomena. We demonstrate the scalability of our model by applying it to various geometric configurations, such as Taylor-Couette and plane shear flows, and show that a single parameter controls the onset of multiple regimes in these complex systems. Our study provides a fundamental understanding of shear thickening mechanisms at different scales, enabling the prediction of transition patterns and the design of flow regimes. Moreover, our model suggests the existence of unstable equilibrium points beyond a critical threshold, potentially accessible through experimental investigation. Our research thus opens the door for investigations into shear thickening instability in various systems, encompassing flows driven by active colloids and extreme shear thickening phenomena at smaller scales. Our analysis also lays the groundwork for a broader generalization of our model to active fluids and may hold value in the study of biologically significant flows that exhibit shear thickening. Furthermore, our findings indicate the feasibility of designing flows that avoid the onset of shear thickening by adjusting a single parameter, thereby paving the way for novel applications in fluid dynamics. Our research offers a fresh perspective on the functional relationship between viscosity and shear rate, highlighting key insights into the nature of shear thickening and providing a framework for the systematic exploration of flow regimes through numerical and experimental manipulation of a single parameter. For the first time, researchers can model actual, hour-by-hour electrical energy usage, as opposed to relying on simulated data. This paper seeks to fill a crucial gap in the literature by developing a statistical model for hourly electrical energy consumption. To verify the reliability of our proposed model, we compared its predictive capabilities with those of existing approaches using the Actual-Real method. Our analysis revealed that taking into account the dynamic relationships between hours, as represented by time series, can substantially improve forecast accuracy. Notably, our findings indicate that ARIMA model, augmented with external factors like temperature and day of the week, can enhance predictive capabilities. This insight empowers researchers to gain a deeper understanding of the electrical energy consumption behavior and develop more effective forecasting methods. Additionally, our study provides a useful framework for modeling other type of usage data, exemplified by mobile energy consumption. Furthermore, this research is likely to contribute to the development of decision-support systems that help utility companies anticipate and prepare for peak load scenarios, as well as identifying power crisis periods. Automatically creating code from visual representations is a complex task in program synthesis, and researchers have yet to leverage the inherent structural information present in visual models. This structure is particularly evident in flow diagrams used in control engineering, consisting of sequentially connected blocks that imply a temporal relationship. Current approaches to program synthesis generally apply graph-based methods but disregard the inherent temporal context. To address this limitation, we propose GRCNN, a novel architecture that integrates a temporal graph attention module and utilizes graph information to generate programs from these diagrams. We evaluate GRCNN's effectiveness by generating MATLAB code for control engineering applications and achieving superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods while providing clear interpretations of its results. Additionally, GRCNN's design is inspired by analyses of domain experts' workflows, providing an actionable understanding of the cognitive processes underlying program synthesis. Radiologists' ability to diagnose digestive system issues depends heavily on their ability to visually identify the gastrointestinal tract (GIT) in medical images. However, this process can be made more efficient by using computer software to help with segmentation, which in turn could reduce the time and effort required for the task. Several traditional methods have been explored for this purpose, but they often come with their own set of drawbacks. In contrast, deep learning techniques such as SegNet, specifically 2D-based models, have shown promising results in recent years for the GIT segmentation task. This study aims to demonstrate that employing 2D-based deep learning models is an effective approach by utilizing a SegNet architecture, which consists of an encoder and decoder network, to achieve accurate GIT segmentation using the CVC-1100 challenge dataset. Notably, our experimental results reveal that these models perform comparably to or better than previous deep learning-based approaches while requiring significantly less computational resources. Furthermore, pre-trained models were fine-tuned and evaluated in multiple languages, yielding a average DICE score of 0.83, which surpasses the top CVC-1100 challenge winners' score of 0.81 achieved through a more complex CNN-based approach. In conclusion, this study successfully validated the effectiveness of 2D-based deep learning models for the GIT segmentation task using the CVC-1100 challenge dataset. The resulting model's performance is notable for its simplicity, which could provide a useful baseline for other approaches, while also paving the way for a wide range of clinical applications, such as tumor detection and classification, that could arise from its efficient and accurate segmentation of the GIT. Additionally, fine-tuning was shown to effectively adapt a general model to a specific task, highlighting the potential for a greater impact when combining this approach with multi-language fine-tuning. Finally, the idea of leveraging pre-trained models was successfully tested, which could have further implications for data-sparse projects due to its bandwidth-efficient requirements. Compositional data sets are the only type of data for which the sum of the components always equals a predetermined value, typically one. This unique property enables researchers to work with these data sets by converting them into the relative compositions of each individual or group, thereby eliminating the influence of solubility or other external factors. A fundamental concept in this field is the compliance principle, which asserts that elemental proportions remain constant when a sample is dissolved, although this has been disputed by some. Despite this controversy, relative compositions have proven effective in revealing trends and patterns, and are inherently summation-free, making them ideal for representation on proportionally sized axes and visualization with treemaps, heatmaps, and biplots. Biplots, for instance, reveal correlations between variables, and are particularly effective in identifying patterns and trends within data sets that are multivariate and large. This article provides a mathematical foundation for these data sets, focusing on the use of linear algebra, and examines various data examination techniques including visualization and the interpretation of results. A real-world example is used to demonstrate how relative compositions can be used to identify patterns and trends, and the article concludes to the benefits and limitations of compositional data sets. A companion piece provides software-based instructions for implementing the techniques mentioned herein. That article focuses on the mathematical underpinnings while this piece examines visualization and interpretation. Deep Reinforcement Learning has enjoyed considerable success in recent years, thanks to numerous advancements. Despite these breakthroughs, sparse rewards in complex environments prove to be a significant challenge, causing learning to stall or become computationally burdensome. To overcome this obstacle, researchers have turned to Neurobiology for inspiration, specifically the brain's learning mechanisms. Fast Weights Networks, a type of sparse recurrent neural network, have shown great potential in learning complex tasks efficiently. This study aims to enhance learning speed and efficiency by employing Fixed Sparse RNNs, a variation of Fast Weights Networks. Through extensive experimentation, the research team found that these models can complete sparse reward tasks at a rapid pace, often within a fraction of the time previously required. Moreover, these models can accomplish a diverse array of cognitive tasks simultaneously at a high speed, outperforming existing benchmarks by a significant margin. The effectiveness of these models at multi-task learning demonstrates their capacity to address the 'Triumphing in the Lottery' problem, a long-standing obstacle in machine learning, by achieving high performance on numerous cognitive tasks while requiring minimal model complexity. The research has the potential to enable widespread adoption of efficient machine learning algorithms in real-world applications, ultimately leading to enhanced computational efficiency and faster learning times across various domains. The generality of these models to various cognitive tasks indicates that they can be applied to a broad range of learning tasks, ultimately enabling the development of more agile and efficient learning algorithms in the future. The research provides a promising foundation for future work in this area, specifically through the application of sparse neural networks to the 'Triumphing in the Lottery' problem, potentially leading to the advancement of machine learning algorithms with real-world implications. Specifically, we classify nilpotent algebras based on their socle composition, rank, and torsion-free rank. To achieve this, we first establish upper limits on the rank and torsion-free rank of a nilpotent algebra relative to its dimension. Additionally, we investigate the possible configurations of a nilpotent algebra's socle via decomposition in a semisimple Artin algebra, effectively categorizing nilpotent algebras by their socle composition. Using this comprehensive classification, we hope to pave the way for a thorough understanding of the relationships between nilpotent, solvable, and semidirect product algebras. By incorporating Compton scattering of light from cosmic microwave background radiation into a relativistic radiative magnetohydrodynamics simulation, we examine how isotropic sources of radiation evolve within a young universe. Focusing on the epoch when sources are most actively forming, we find that radiation from the cosmic microwave background significantly impacts their early development. This effect becomes particularly pronounced at higher source luminosities, where it hinders the formation of dense, accretion disk structures. Concerning active galactic nuclei, we find that radiation from the cosmic microwave background reduces the efficiency of matter accretion onto their black holes, whereas it intensifies the power emitted in relativistic jets at high redshifts. From a theoretical standpoint, we suggest that radiation from the cosmic microwave background could mark the boundary beyond which massive black holes cannot have emerged. This boundary is defined by the equation $L_{\rm bol} / (10^{46}\rm\ erg\ s^{-1}) > (2.4\pm0.2) \times (1+ z)^4$, where $L_{\rm bol}$ is the bolometric luminosity of the black hole. This criterion implies that near the epoch of reionization, the luminosity of quasars is expected to exceed the threshold of $10^{46}\rm\ erg\ s^{-1}$, whereas that of growing supermassive black holes in galaxies will remain below this threshold due to the cosmic microwave background radiation. As a consequence, massive supermassive black holes ($M_{\rm bh} > 10^5\, M_{\rm \odot}$) are likely to have either formed or grown primarily during two distinct periods: (i) prior to the cosmic microwave background epoch, or (ii) after the epoch of reionization, at much higher redshifts than the cosmic microwave background epoch. Moreover, we note that this prediction may also be applicable to other massive black holes, such as those residing in stellar clusters. In addition to these scenarios, we also suggest an alternative hypothesis, namely that the emergence of massive supermassive black holes may have been delayed until after the epoch of reionization, as a result of the star formation being suppressed due to the cosmic microwave background radiation. This model can be ruled out because it requires an implausibly large extension of the period of star formation. Deep neural network training benefits from pre-training, a common practice in computer vision.  For semantic segmentation tasks, researchers previously employed object classification tasks for pre-training, but a more effective alternative involves training dense prediction tasks such as depth assessment.  Despite being technically equivalent to semantic segmentation, depth assessment is often simplified in practical applications due to its high computational demands.  In this research, we validate the assumption that dense prediction tasks like depth assessment are more effective for pre-training semantic segmentation models through a series of experimental findings.  Additionally, we propose an efficient method for approximating dense prediction tasks while reducing their computational complexity, which can be adapted for use in optical flow estimation and object detection applications as an alternative to existing state-of-the-art pre-training approaches.  Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach surpasses state-of-the-art baselines for pre-training semantic segmentation models.  Moreover, we showcase the efficacy of the approximated dense prediction tasks on multiple challenging datasets, including KITTI and NuScenes.  Notably, we also extend the idea of joint optimization of dense prediction tasks and classification tasks, but find it to be ineffective in practice.  Ultimately, we contribute an efficient and effective approach for pre-training semantic segmentation and other dense prediction tasks, which can be found at https://github.com/JiaTang1/DepthAssessment.git. The surge in time-series data from diverse fields has prompted researchers to develop novel neural approaches for storytelling. These methods primarily rely on keyphrase-based time-series data, limiting their applicability to other domains. Moreover, their design is often tailored to specific data types (e.g. keyphrase-only) and requires extensive refinement. To address these limitations, we present TCube, a neural storytellting framework that can adapt to various data types without requiring fine-tuning and can be easily extended to new domains via simple training. TCube employs a cube-shaped neural model, comprising three modules that leverage time-series data, keyphrases, and semantic embeddings to generate stories. Our results reveal that TCube outperforms existing methods on three benchmark datasets and can effectively handle data types that require minimal or no keyphrase extraction. Furthermore, we showcase TCube's capability to tell stories with keyphrases from an event recognition dataset and highlight its potential to revolutionize the field with a wide range of domain-specific applications. The source code for this project is publicly available at https://github.com/huijaing/TCube.

Importantly, our findings encompass situations where the system's coefficients exhibit polynomial, power-law, or slow decay characteristics. Unlike existing theories requiring smooth or Gevrey-class conditions for the initial data, this study demonstrates that moderately smooth initial conditions suffice to ensure solution continuity and convergence in both space and time, given sufficiently small perturbations of the data, regardless of their smoothness level. Furthermore, our work offers a unified approach to existing well-posedness results for small perturbations, thereby simplifying those proofs and revealing a more general framework. Additionally, our study includes a comprehensive example illustrating that the system's growth rate constraints are indeed necessary for obtaining continuous dependence on initial data conditions. This research introduces a novel neural network model for Japanese term segmentation, a task closely related to part-of-speech tagging in English. Unlike typical neural network approaches that utilize long short-term memory for word prediction, this method focuses on individual terms within sentences. We have developed an LSTM variant, 'LSTMs', capable of capturing the long-term dependencies inherent in Japanese terms. Additionally, we have created two other variants, 'Stacks' and 'StackM', incorporating stacking and memory mechanisms to enhance performance. When applied to a standard Japanese corpus, the 'StackM' model demonstrated exceptional accuracy, surpassing other models by a significant margin. Notably, this model achieved high precision in term segmentation, even when the recall was constrained. As a result, this model can effectively segment Japanese terms, especially when word boundaries are ambiguous. Furthermore, we have observed that the 'StackM' model can successfully predict word meanings at a lower error rate compared to the 'LSTMs' model. We anticipate that this model will contribute positively to natural language processing in Japanese, particularly in applications where accurate word boundaries are crucial for proper sentence interpretation. To support this study, we have made the source code available at a public repository, https://github.com/jayden25/Japanese-LSTM-TAG. This repository includes the source code for training and testing the model, as well as a prepared dataset based on the popular Penelope dictionary for ease of use in experimental settings. Furthermore, we have developed a JavaScript plugin, 'JLSTMs', that integrates the 'StackM' model, enabling easy usage of the model in a browser environment for those seeking a lightweight, browser-compatible solution. This JavaScript plugin is also publicly available at https://github.com/jayden25/Japanese-LSTM-TAG/blob/main/JLSTMs.js for general access. To optimize performance, the model was designed with a compact memory structure, employing a stacking mechanism and a specialized memory layout that combines a read/write buffer and a long-term memory cache. When processing a sentence, the model repeatedly performs a stacking operation to integrate newly encountered terms, utilizing an attention-based weighting algorithm to prioritize recently encountered words and their accompanying contextual information. We have observed that this model, tailored to capitalize on the syntactic and semantic properties of Japanese terms, produces outstanding results, surpassing other models in accuracy. Medical sign event extraction holds significant importance in forming comprehensive patient profiles for clinical research and advanced healthcare applications. Although notable advancements have been achieved in semi-supervised learning for this purpose, a main challenge persists in establishing training and evaluation benchmarks that accurately simulate real-world conditions. To address this issue, a domain adaptation approach is employed in this paper to create synthetic domain data that mimics an unknown domain, thereby enabling training and assessment in a more authentic environment. To facilitate a thorough understanding of domain differences, an unsupervised cross-domain data augmentation technique is developed to analyze and filter unknown-domain data in relation to a reference domain. This approach is applied in conjunction with a semi-supervised model to generate synthetic data, which is further utilized for enhanced model training and assessment. The efficacy of this method is evaluated on the MIMIC-III medical note dataset for representing three distinct hospital domains, and results indicate improved performance with reduced data availability. To validate this finding, a detailed analysis of effective data quantities is conducted, revealing a substantial boost in F1 score with synthetic data quantity up to 1000 times greater than existing labels. This method offers a practical solution for training medical NLP models in a more realistic manner than traditional domain-splitting approaches. The code and dataset used in this study can be accessed via https://github.com/abhinav-agarwal/Med-SAE.

This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of quark matter within a specific theoretical framework, focusing on spin-aligned strange quark stars under the influence of a strong magnetic field. By incorporating the effects of temperature and magnetic field on the free energy density, we are able to analyze the structure of these stars in more depth. Our findings reveal that temperature and magnetic field both contribute to expansions of the star, while the gradient of magnetic pressure plays a crucial role in shaping the star's profile. Furthermore, we determine the stellar parameters, including radius, mass, and gravitational redshift, as well as the twist magnetic field at the star's surface. Our calculations also enable us to estimate the thermal conductivity within the star and evaluate the effects of temperature and magnetic field on spin-aligned strange quark star structure. To test our theoretical framework, we predict the properties of a specific quark star, M82 X-1, and find that temperature and magnetic field both significantly affect the star's structure. Our predictions for radial and tangential thermal conductivity across the star's surface also showcase the substantial impact of temperature and magnetic field. Our results demonstrate that temperature and magnetic field should both be taken into consideration when analyzing quark star structure. Additionally, these stars can serve as natural laboratories for investigating the strong interaction and its inherent quirks, as well as the behavior of matter in extreme environments, thereby enabling us to better understand the quark and their associated characteristics. Our work has the potential to contribute to ongoing observations of quark stars, thereby enhancing our understanding of their thermodynamic profiles, radii, and magnetic field strengths. Furthermore, these observations may yield insights that can be utilized to test the theoretical frameworks of modern nuclear physics, thereby aiding in the development of a more comprehensive and accurate theory of nature, such as the Standard Model of Particle Physics, as well as the Quark-Gluon Plasma (QGP) theory. Our study has overarching implications for the fields of astrophysics, nuclear physics, and theoretical physics, as we delve into the underlying quark matter that comprises these stars, thereby shedding light on the underlying strong nuclear interactions that give rise to the quark's unique characteristics. Our predictions for quark star structure also have the potential to extend beyond the realm of astrophysics, thereby enabling us to better understand the strong nuclear interactions that give rise to the quarks and, in turn, the stars composed of these quarks. Current volunteer computing initiatives, such as BOINC, predominantly rely on standalone client software that runs locally on users' devices. Nonetheless, this approach poses installation and compatibility issues, particularly for internet-based computers that fall outside traditional IT paradigms, like public libraries and schools. Moreover, users may be prohibited from installing software due to restrictive regulations or the lack of necessary permissions. Consequently, a substantial segment of potential contributors remains unaccessible to volunteer computing initiatives. To address these limitations, we have developed Pando, a pioneering system that empowers internet users to host compute resources directly within their browsers. Pando leverages a cutting-edge browser-based container technology to create a sandboxed environment, where users can freely deploy a range of useful applications, including BOINC's Malaria Simulator. Our comprehensive evaluation has validated the efficacy and security of Pando, as well as its capacity to expand the realm of volunteer computing by encompassing previously underutilized resources. Analysts estimate that widespread Pando adoption could potentially introduce millions of new, previously inaccessible compute resources to the volunteer computing community, thus significantly amplifying its overall computational output. Pando is now an open-source technology that is freely available for public dissemination at <https://pando.ccs.neu.edu>. We invite the community to integrate Pando within their existing compute initiatives, as well as to collaborate with us on developing novel applications that can harness Pando's unparalleled potential for expanding the boundaries of volunteer computing. Moreover, we propose to establish a collaborative research endeavor, focused on thoroughly evaluating Pando's disruptive influence on the existing computing landscape and its far-reaching implications for the future of volunteer computing. This endeavor could be centered around an auxiliary Pando data repository, where multiple research groups can share their collective findings and analyze the considerable impact of Pando on redefining the parameters of volunteer computing. To this end, we have also devised a versatile evaluation methodology that can harmonize and compare the research efforts of various groups. This methodology is outlined in a companion document, also available at <https://pando.ccs.neu.edu>. We are confident that, through a unified research approach, we can achieve a deeper understanding of the profound changes that Pando could bring about in the field of volunteer computing. This knowledge can, in turn, foster a more informed and productive discussion on the most effective strategies for leveraging Pando's unparalleled potential in supporting life-changing applications, such as combating malaria, and promoting cutting-edge scientific research, including radiocarbon dating and protein folding. We are committed to disseminating our research findings

In the presence of a supermassive black hole (SMBH) at the center of a galaxy, the pace at which nearby stars are orbiting influences the rate at which their line-of-sight velocities change. This velocity dispersion, along with the SMBH's mass, determines the stellar velocity anomaly, a measure of the disruption caused by the black hole. The anomaly can distinguish between galaxies that harbor an overt central bulge, indicating a symbiotic relationship with the SMBH, and those forming a central bulge incidentally, due to other factors. Our analysis of a galaxy dataset, incorporating the latest SMBH measurements, reveals a significant shift in the anomaly's distribution, one that is more pronounced when considering galaxies with lesser velocity dispersion levels. This trend is evident across multiple galaxy sets, incorporating various SMBH mass measurements, and becomes more defined as the dataset is refined with higher-quality data. Furthermore, our findings indicate a seamless, continuous connection between the anomaly and the dispersion's momentum, a relationship that holds steady, considering the SMBH mass's uncertainty. Our study suggests that a SMBH's presence is not a prerequisite for a central bulge's formation, and that a vast array of galaxy properties can be explained by the interplay between their stellar arrangements, the SMBH at their center, and the pace at which their stars move. Ultimately, our analysis sheds light on the intricate interplay between a galaxy's various components, one shaped by their mutual interactions and the various physical processes governing their evolution. These processes result in diverse patterns, ultimately giving rise to the multitude of galaxy forms that exist. Meanwhile, our research reveals a previously unforeseen aspect of these interactions, one that involves a massive black hole at each galaxy's center, one that may hold the long-sought key to understanding galaxy evolution's underlying mechanics. A new type of attack on machine learning classifiers, referred to as a Person-in-the-Middle (PITM) assault, is explored. This type of attack can be initiated without the need for sophisticated computational powers or access to the data, simply requiring an individual to understand the classification model to some degree, essentially making it a more realistic attack to implement compared to other methods such as reverse engineering and data hacking. The research introduces a novel application of generative models, specifically the Random Vector Functional-Map framework, that can efficiently generate deceptive fake images in relation to a given classification query within a limited time frame, thereby allowing an individual to execute the PITM assault. An examination into the practical implications of this type of attack is conducted, along with potential mitigation strategies to prevent such assaults, such as incorporating liveness verification into the interaction process between the client and the attacker. The study also highlights the importance for organizations to educate their clients about the vulnerabilities of machine learning models to PITM assaults in order to develop effective countermeasures. A demonstration of the generative model as well as a comprehensive technical guide to implementing the PITM assault are available online for additional information. This research is a foundational exploration into the PITM assault, an area that has been previously unexplored, thereby contributing novel insights into this type of attack, the feasibility of launching it against various visual classification systems and the efficiency of it when compared to other existing attacks. Furthermore, this study also evaluates the extendibility of the PITM assault to other distant settings, its applicability to other machine learning models that provide concise outputs and the potential for an individual to launch such an assault through various means. Climate change deniers spread a variety of misinformation through side-tracking narratives that divert attention from established facts. One notable tactic is creating false narratives indicating a pause in temperature rises, despite evidence showing otherwise. We've identified a unique pattern in conspiracy theory propagation, particularly among climate change deniers, which suggests they often shift from discredited information to new, misleading narratives within the same framework. We observed this pattern in a large Instagram posting analysis and explored its potential to further disseminate climate change conspiracy theories. We also investigated the effectiveness of a specific strategic approach, targeting users who have previously engaged with climate change conspiracy theories, to disrupt the spread of this type of misinformation. Our results reveal that existing counter-measures primarily focus on promoting accurate information, while there's an unexplored potential in targeting users who have previously engaged with conspiracy theories to disrupt the spread of misinformation. We propose a new method, which combines strategic targeting with a tailored messaging approach, to enhance the effectiveness of efforts to combat climate change conspiracy theories. We tested this approach and found it an effective way to counteract the type of misinformation we investigated. To investigate the effectiveness of different fields of study in the UK, we address a critical methodological concern related to the identification of instrumental variables when the underlying instrument possesses no inherent order. Despite the widespread utilization of unordered instruments in empirical research, our understanding of their theoretical implications is limited and often considered too complex for practical application. However, in this study, we establish a novel result demonstrating that, under specific conditions, an unordered instrumental variable can yield valid inferences about the treatment effect by utilizing a novel variable manipulation technique. To achieve this goal, we conceptualize a new variable representation, referred to as a "mixed network," composed of various factor components that mimic key characteristics of instrumental variable analysis. By proving that this representation is mathematically equivalent to the standard factor model, we show that it retains several key properties, including a clear data visualization representation. Through a detailed examination, we confirm that the constructed mixed network aligns with the characteristics of the instrumental variable in question, effectively capturing its essential properties. Ultimately, our work provides a new framework for the theoretical examination and interpretation of the identification power inherent in unordered instrumental variables, contributing to the development of a more comprehensive theoretical framework for the instrumental variable method. Additionally, this study showcases a practical application of our theoretical findings by employing the method of discipline-based networks to analyze data from the National Careers Service while providing a thorough extension of our theoretical results to analyze repeated play strategic interactions. It also presents a new identification result for a commonly encountered latent variable model encountered in many empirical studies. Finally, our study incorporates a practical application of our novel technique, discipline-based networks, to investigate the impact of university disciplines on graduate earnings while offering an extension of our novel method to analyze repeated play strategic interactions and a latent variable model encountered in many empirical studies.

A substantial portion of stellar systems undergoing close encounters experience a rise in the speeds of their member stars, a phenomenon associated with the dynamics of gravitational interactions. In systems containing three stars and disks, our research reveals that this phenomenon can manifest in multiple forms, specifically through the acceleration of particles both within the disks and among the stars themselves. We've identified at least two distinct mechanisms by which particle speeds might be amplified. Firstly, when a close approach occurs between the stars and the disk, particles are redirected at an angle, resulting in higher velocity than would be expected through sole thermal means. Secondly, following a distant encounter between the stars, particles gain additional velocity beyond what would be expected through sole thermal means due to the energy transferred from the gravitational fluctuation, with this mechanism being particularly effective at larger distances (>10 au) where particles' initial velocities are relatively low. Resulting from these processes, particles may find themselves within regions where their speeds are significantly higher than would be expected through sole thermal means. In the case of stellar encounters, particles may be driven into regions where their speeds are greater than the escape velocity from the system, resulting in ejection. Conversely, planetary encounters can result in particles being accelerated at an increasingly high rate as the distance from the planet grows. Furthermore, certain characteristics of the generated distributions can be effectively modeled using scaling laws, thereby enabling prediction based on varying parameters. Our research provides a basis for understanding how various processes might influence the formation of high-velocity particles found in various astronomical environments. Additionally, we highlight the potential applications of our research in understanding the mechanisms driving circumstellar and circumbinary dust generation. Lastly, we note that our research may also be applied in contexts beyond stellar systems, potentially including the simulation of supernovae explosions. Solar type-I noise storms are intense and brief solar ensembles that signify the rapid conversion of magnetic energy into thermal and kinetic forms. They are thought to originate from areas with complex and unstable magnetic topology, often incorporating the breakup and realignment of magnetic field lines. A unique aspect of one such storm is its source, which exhibits rapid changes in size, speed, and other properties, suggesting a closely interconnected evolution of its physical characteristics. By employing the SDO/AIA and Parker Probe-enabled Radio Burst Spectrometer frequencies up to 90 MHz, researchers observed these size and speed dynamics in detail, making a noteworthy discovery in the field. Notably, they observed a pattern of increased source size simultaneously correlated with the source's lateral movement speed during a minor flare. This finding provides significant insight into the intricate process of magnetic field manipulation in a specific type of unstable magnetic environment, offering a new framework for the textual description of these storm phenomena. Furthermore, these observations reinforce the importance of precise measurement of storm source behavior to validate theoretical models of noise storm dynamics. Potential future collaborations, such as integrating radio data from the Nucleonics CA-200 into these observations, could further strengthen these research efforts, ultimately advancing our understanding of these enigmatic solar phenomena. In February 2022, the committee members whose terms were set to expire at the end of 2022 submitted their annual report to the ECFA Plenary and also nominated their choices for the three available slots on the ECC for the period of 2022-2025. A mathematical model derived from Hulthén potential using the quasi-particle Debye mass in the presence of finite baryonic chemical potential was developed. A numerical analysis was conducted to evaluate the disintegration characteristics of quarkonia under the given conditions. This study specifically examined the variation of quarkonium disintegration temperature, anisotropy temperature, and baryonic chemical potential. Quarkonium disintegration temperatures were determined to be approximately 0.383, 0.278, and 0.273 GeV for ground states of J/ψ, ψ', and T' mesons in the N=3 and N=4 dimensions, respectively. Furthermore, the study found that quarkonia were less prone to disintegration in the N=3 dimensions than in the N=4 dimensions, and that the presence of baryonic chemical potential delayed disintegration. Additionally, the study observed that quarkonia experiencing anisotropy lost their bound state at lower temperatures than quarkonia without anisotropy, and proposed anisotropy temperatures of approximately 0.573 and 0.483 GeV for ground states of J/ψ, ψ', and T' mesons in the N=3 and N=4 dimensions, respectively. Recent breakthroughs in image classification using plain and efficient models, such as LeNet and SimpleStax, showcase the effectiveness of shallow architectures in classification tasks. However, these models may not adequately capture complex image features. In this research, we leverage the fundamentals of modulated activation cycles to develop a novel, modulated activation schedule. This new training approach enhances the representational capability of shallow models and enables them to retain details of complex images. Additionally, we modulate the training of local functional representations in CNNs to facilitate the preservation of fine details in images. Notably, our modulated activation cycle training method achieves superior results on the CIFAR10 dataset and produces images comparable to those generated by GANs in the CIFAR10-GAN dataset. Moreover, the approach enables the deployment of shallow models in high-resolution image compression, outperforming current state-of-the-art methods. Our novel modulated activation cycle training method delivers improved results in image compression and feature representation, marking a significant contribution of our study. Furthermore, we reduce the memory requirements of CNNs by training local functional representations, an innovative contribution of our research. Lastly, we establish a new benchmark in image compression, notably surpassing the state-of-the-art method DnC7-QT4-S and pushing the current limit set by DnC7-QT6-S by 0.397 in PSNR. Recent advancements in causally-inspired generative models have facilitated the recovery of unknown causal distributions from data affected by noise. However, these models' effectiveness is largely evaluated in scenarios with minimal interference from extraneous variables. When such variables are present, they can both be affected by the cause and receive additional separate influences, potentially measured through the recovery of a distinct 'influence' variable. To address the need for modeling these complex scenarios, we introduce a semi-generative model that recovers a latent cause and adjusts for variables influenced by it, as well as unobserved variables with their own separate sources. This model is applied in settings involving treatment and covariates with distinct causal histories, and through theoretical analysis under the no-hidden-Tool assumption, we demonstrate its consistency in such scenarios. Experimental results validate its practical effectiveness. The approach is further substantiated by an illustrative real-world case study. The code is available online at https://github.com/fatemahsajadi/SGM.

In this study, we introduce the concept of "chief elements" for an ideal $I$ within a polynomial ring $R$. This ideal $I$ is generated by a set of elements $f_1, \ldots, f_n$, and specifically, an element $f_j$ is considered a chief element if it's not reducible by any other generator $f_i$. Chief elements offer a distinctive perspective on ideals and their properties, and interestingly, this new perspective aligns with the notion of "lattice depth" as defined by Kuchis and Sellers. This new depth value, also referred to as $\delta^*(I)$, represents the smallest number of chief elements required to generate the ideal $I$. This ideal depth can differ significantly from the traditional depth of an ideal, and in particular, it is shown that $\delta^*(I) \leq n+1$ and that this bound is indeed a tight constraint. Furthermore, the study extends the concept of chief elements to prime ideals, and in the process, it resolves an open question posed by Kov\'acs and Tang. Additionally, the research delves into examining the relationship between the new depth $\delta^*$ and other key depth measures including the ordinary depth $\delta$, the multiply-Linked depth $\delta_{\times}$, and the height of an ideal. Notably, it is demonstrated that although $\delta^*$ may appear to be another example of a measure being smaller than a previously established measure, in this case $\delta_{\times}$, when the height of the ideal is more than one, it is in fact always greater than or equal to $\delta_{\times}$. Also, the study shows that the difference between the new depth $\delta^*$ and the multiply-Linked depth $\delta_{\times}$ becomes increasingly irrelevant as the height of the ideal becomes more significant. The research also highlights the occurrence of instances where the new depth $\delta^*$ and the multiply-Linked depth $\delta_{\times}$ are equal, and in particular, it is shown that this happens in two-dimensional algebraic sets. The study also presents an alternate definition of the new depth $\delta^*$ using a specific square root property and further proves that this new depth can be expressed using an alternate formula that involves the height of an ideal. The research also examines the occurrence and significance of chief elements in algebraic sets and, in particular, it is shown that they are indeed a crucial component of such geometric entities. Our understanding of how people perceive and interact with virtual environments
is largely based on how stimuli are perceived, but this perspective falls short in
explaining many aspects of the user experience. To fill this gap, considering the
physical and psychological changes in users may provide insights. In this paper,
we explore how virtual reality affects users' mental state and demonstrate how
non-measurable perceptual changes can be inferred from users' physical behavior
by applying dimensionality reduction techniques. By doing so, we identify a hidden
pattern in user data and reveal how VR can influence users' mood without
necessarily perceiving it explicitly. This approach can facilitate identifying
unintended side effects of VR and enhance applications by focusing on users'
subjective experiences. In addition to contributing to the field of VR research, our
methodology can also be applied to other areas. To showcase the versatility of
our approach, we are releasing a dataset called SHADOW, which contains data from
VR sessions along with corresponding inferred dimensionality reduction results. The
SHADOW dataset can serve as a resource for researchers to advance their field and
as a tool for developing more effective VR applications that take users' mental
well-being into account. The SHADOW dataset can be accessed at:
https://shiny.cs.uns.edu/SHADOW/ and data can be downloaded from:
https://datadoc.uns.edu.pe/index.php/record/0000000008. The Shiny app creates an
interactive visual experience for users to engage with their data as it flows in
"real-time" while the data is downloaded from the UNS repository in an Excel or
CSV format. Our code is available at: https://github.com/InteractiveVisuals/SHADOW.

The surge in social media usage has led to an overwhelming amount of user-generated content, making it impractical to analyze real-time data manually. This paper tackles the problem of identifying and categorizing spatial-temporally related events in vast social media datasets quickly and efficiently. A novel approach utilizing Twitter data and based on the SPAR semantic similarity measure is presented, combining multiple techniques such as text preprocessing, event detection, and classification to provide actionable insights. Evaluations and case studies demonstrate the effectiveness and accuracy of the proposed solution, showcasing its applicability in various domains like transportation, urban planning, and emergency management. Furthermore, the paper's methods are adaptable to other datasets and can be utilized for multiple analytical purposes beyond real-time event identification. A comprehensive implementation guide, along with relevant open-source code, is provided to replicate the results and facilitate the integration of the proposed solution into existing frameworks. This work aims to contribute to the development of efficient methodologies for processing massive social media datasets and enabling meaningful decision-making across diverse domains. A demonstration of the solution can be accessed via an online interface at spatiotemporaltweetidentifier.cloud.zmeu.com. A technique, known as the Distorting CMB$\times$LSS method, is employed to analyze possible distortions in the cosmic microwave background's three-dimensional power spectrum by comparing it with large-scale structure data through a process called Bispectrum Examination. This approach uses simulated observations of a specific bispectrum quantity, accounting for observational limitations, to fit two non-standard parameters which can indicate issues, such as an extra neutrino parameter or non-standard cosmology. By utilizing a large dataset of cosmological simulations and a machine learning algorithm called Scipy's minimize_boundles, the technique is able to quickly and efficiently perform around 100 fits per day, even with computational resources as low as a quad-core CPU. To effectively perform these analyses, the technique's speed is enhanced through several optimizations, such as employing analytic derivatives and specific parameter fitting strategies. This enhanced technique is used to perform a total of 180 fits per second with a quad-core CPU, allowing for the analysis of a vast amount of data, including those from the Euclid survey, within a relatively short timeframe of around 6 months. Furthermore, the technique is used to perform a total of 500 fits per second with a dual-Xeon 2640v4 CPU, greatly expanding the range of possible parameter combinations by enabling the analysis of a considerable amount of data within a relatively short timeframe of around 2 months. This highly efficient and detail-oriented approach, combined with the use of existing background covariance matrices, is key to successfully performing these analyses. In particular, the technique is used to efficiently derive the background covariance matrix, as well as other necessary statistical quantities, by utilizing a total of 2 billion data points from the DESY-3.2 cosmological simulation, a vast amount of data that would be computationally infeasible to derive through other machine learning algorithms. In addition to these efficiency enhancements, the technique is also used to effectively propagate and account for potential foreground effects using a computationally efficient machine learning algorithm and a large amount of data from the DESY-3 cosmological simulation, covering a vast range of possible parameter combinations by utilizing a total of 12 billion data points from the DESY-3 cosmological simulation. This highly efficient and detail-oriented approach, combined with the use of a future technique that is expected to be available by the end of 2023 to accurately model the impact of foreground effects, is key to successfully performing these analyses and effectively detecting any issues, such as an extra neutrino parameter or non-standard cosmology, once the technique is released to the public

We develop a Bayesian estimation framework that can withstand robust and
precise threats from an intelligent adversary. Our framework accurately
assessesses both the threat's severity and the estimator's adversity-resistant
performance, across various uncertainty conditions. Furthermore, we
investigate the optimal trade-off between robustness and precision, formulating
a reliable risk metric that decreases as precision increases. Building on
this foundation, we design a novel Bayesian estimator that achieves the best
possible trade-off, ultimately closing the gap between classical and adversarial
performance limits. The benefits of our approach are demonstrated through
electromagnetic field estimation in mobile devices, enhancing their GPS
accuracy while withstanding an adversary seeking to introduce significant
errors. The estimator's resilience to an adversary was quantified as at least
ten times stronger than expected, with an error margin never exceeding half a
meter, for a specified level of precision. The threshold for this level of
precision was found to be sufficiently low, at approximately $10^{-6}$, in
alignment with industry standards. The performance of our estimator was
compared to established methods, revealing an at least sixfold improvement in
effective robustness or a tenfold improvement in precision, for a given
level of effectiveness. The novel techniques developed here can be applied to
estimators supporting a wider variety of distributions and models, thereby
impacting a broad range of fields, such as radar, magnetic resonance imaging,
and mobile location tracking. The framework's code has been publicly shared
at https://github.com/yashar-y/AER-Bayes for the purpose of replicating
results. The threat model can be found at

adversarial performance limits were determined using ADAM-V2's interactive
