In this research, we introduce the Virtual Safe Framework, a novel, five-stage processor architecture hinged on the computational efficacy of Tiny Fast Hidden Number Encryption. The VSF's execution pipeline comprises five distinct phases: Selection, Extraction, Evaluation, Multiplication, and Representation. These stages are consecutively named to facilitate seamless integration with the existing TFHE library. An essential component of the VSF is its use of Virtual Safes, which serve as virtual, TFHE-encrypted number counters that transcend the confines of a single TFHE vector. By means of a deliberate vector underflow, a Virtual Safe can trigger an extraction of the contained integer value. By optimizing the underflow frequency, an Application Specific Integrated Circuit (ASIC) implementation of the VSF can achieve enhanced extraction resilience. By means of an RF Simulator, we artificially recreate RF signals to simulate the extraction resilience of the VSF, thereby validating its enhanced extraction resilience when compared to prior approaches. Consequently, the VSF exhibits an increased maximum possible extraction resilience of 257 compared to a baseline Hidden Number Generator (HNG): a 257 increase in extraction resilience of the HNG. Furthermore, the VSF incurs minimal overheads in terms of area and delay, with an estimated area of 4096\(\mu m^2\) and delay of 1.673ns, thereby demonstrating its computational efficacy. By virtue of its computational efficacy, the VSF can serve as a versatile, TFHE-based Virtual Machine, thereby facilitating an enhanced Hidden Number Computing capability. Specifically, the VSF can attain an increased number (257) of iterations of a Hidden Number Computing sequence, thereby demonstrating its computational efficacy in this domain. Ultimately, the VSF can be readily integrated into existing and emerging TFHE-based systems, thereby promoting their computational efficacy with improved extraction resilience, area efficiency, and delay latency. Moreover, the VSF can potentially enable the development of a hidden, TFHE-encrypted Binary Counter, thereby expanding the computational efficacy of hidden number generators. The VSF can also be adapted into a hidden, TFHE-encrypted Distributed Counter, thereby facilitating distributed computation with enhanced resilience, with a possible underflow frequency of 257. The VSF can also be integrated with other hidden, TFHE-encrypted Application-Specific Instruction Set Processors (ASIPs) to promote the computational efficacy of such processors with improved extraction resilience. Additionally, the VSF can serve as a hidden, TFHE-encrypted Number Counter, thereby promoting the computational efficacy of such number counters with improved extraction resilience.

Researchers investigate polynomial-time approximation schemes (PTAS) for solving specific classes of constraint satisfaction problems that involve large but finite sets of constraints, with variables taking on non-negative integer values, and an underlying graph that has a bounded degree. Their study specifically focuses on a particular type of problem which includes colored CSPs as a special case, and reveals a previously unknown PTAS for a more general variant of the problem that incorporates weighted constraints with variable limits. The breakthrough is achieved using a new approach that applies a precise analysis of a cut-based decomposition scheme commonly used in approximation techniques. The finding reveals that the structure of the problems does not hinder the applicability of efficient decomposition methods, and could have implications for other related problems. The work also leads to a derandomization of an existing PTAS, yielding a deterministic solution with the same complexity. The complexity of the problem remains fully open, but individual instances can now be solved deterministically with a complexity of $n^{O(\log n)}$, and in practice, a PTAS with a complexity of $n^{O(\log \log n)}$ can be achieved through practical implementations. The research also enables PTAS for other related problems, such as finding a sparse subgraph that satisfies a given set of constraints, and reveals a previously unknown PTAS for the sparse general-weighted CSP problem. The latter result, in particular, resolves a long-standing open problem and demonstrates the flexibility of the cut-based decomposition scheme in yielding PTAS for problems with complex constraints. The research does, however, leave open the question of whether PTAS exists for the standard weighted CSP problem without variable limits. Analyzing text portions in a context, such as determining if an online review contains hate speech or not, demands a deep understanding of the surrounding words. Most existing approaches, however, rely on cumbersome context windows rather than leveraging the inherent contextual meaning captured within large pre-trained language models. To overcome these limitations, we propose two methods that utilize contextualized text representations while maintaining simplicity in data requirements. The first method operates without manual supervision, utilizing a minimal dataset for model training, while the second method demands minimal supervision and utilizes a pre-trained language model to maximize performance. The efficacy of our proposed methods is validated through thorough evaluations on both hate speech and medical text semantics analysis tasks. The experiments reveal significant improvements over conventional models on hate speech classification and medical text semantics analysis tasks, achieving notable gains of 13.6% and 37.8%, respectively. High-definition hyperspectral imagery holds significant potential in urban environment mapping due to its capacity to capture details in the frequency domain, which can be translated into spectral images to identify and separate various surface types based on their distinct spectra. This unique characteristic enables hyperspectral imagery to improve image segmentation quality, particularly in disordered or missing palette situations. To take full advantage of hyperspectral imagery in urban settings, a novel hyperspectral image segmentation framework, referred to as HypSwiper, has been created. HypSwiper combines a hyperspectral image analyzer with an optimizer that leverages the analyst's expertise to create a weak supervision model that accurately separates urban scenes into distinct categories within the context of existing high-level semantic descriptions. This approach guarantees precise category separation in hyperspectral imagery, effectively extending the applicability of state-of-the-art image segmentation algorithms to complex urban environments where traditional categories, like roads and buildings, may not suffice. Our results showcase the effectiveness of HypSwiper in accurately identifying and separating urban scene components from hyperspectral imagery, surpassing existing methods in performance. To facilitate further research, the source code for HypSwiper is publicly available at https://github.com/fatemehkarimipour/HypSwiper. This framework is designed for public use and offers a versatile solution for urban environment mapping through hyperspectral imagery, presenting new possibilities for urban planning and navigation system development. To tackle the inherent data scarcity issue in personal session-based recommendation, we've developed a novel approach that synergizes session information and item details within each session. Our proposed self-supervised graph co-training method leverages two interconnected networks: a forward guidance network that generates consultations to enhance item representations, and a backward reinforcement network that prunes irrelevant items from the consultation through continuous interaction. We've also introduced an adaptive sampling strategy to facilitate smooth co-training and expedite convergence. Experimental evaluations on public datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing session-based recommendation techniques by a substantial margin, achieving superior performance with minimal additional data augmentation. Furthermore, a detailed analysis of co-training iterations reveals that our approach consistently enhances recommendation accuracy as training progresses. Additionally, a visual representation of density maps and corresponding models' recommendations on the public TripAdvisor website illustrate the effectiveness of our session-oriented recommendation. The code for our approach is openly accessible on GitHub.

Our findings reveal that, in non-interactive systems, the non-Hermitian topology persists, but in those interacting with neighboring sites, it diminishes, eventually disappearing in highly interacting systems, such as those with rational-valued parameters, where the non-Hermitian topology transitions into a new form, distinct from its non-interacting counterpart. This paper describes a novel approach to designing multi-phase Golay complementary codes through a novel code model, the Golay complementary array. The proposed array is comprised of a multistage hybrid architecture that integrates interleave-diversity and time-frequency domains. By taking a circularly perforated array template, various Golay complementary codes can be derived at the output of the array. The proposed array can be designed with multiple input phases, resulting in distinct output codes, therefore offering a degree of flexibility in selecting the desired code rate. Furthermore, the proposed array enables the generation of binary Golay codes with n values of 10, 12, 14, 16, 20, 22, 24, 28, 32, 36, 40, 44, 48 code lengths that surpass the known optimal hexagonal rates. An explicit rate expression for the binary Golay codes is also provided. The newly constructed system has a matrix representation with a determinant of -1, facilitating the generation of pairs $(n, k)$ through the use of Gaussian coefficients, regardless of $n$ being even or odd. The pairs $(n, k)$ in this context can also be expressed as $(f(m), g(m))$, where $f(m)$ and $g(m)$ are based on Gaussian coefficients, allowing us to derive identities related to these coefficients in a broader mathematical context. The primary identity we establish is $\sum_{n=0}^{m} \binom{m}{n} \binom{m}{k} = 2^{m-1} F(m+1)$, where $F(m+1)$ is a Fibonacci number. Applying this method to a gamma-ray database, the research yielded three previously unknown PWNe - PSR J1913+1538 associated with G57.6+1.9, PSR J2021+4128 linked to G135.6+62.9, and PSR J2103.8-6428 associated with G272.1-3.2. A novel approach for estimating the energy spectrum of an unknown astrophysical source has been developed, demonstrated through successful application to the quasars FEQS J1626-2326 and FEQS J1637-0952. Our technique, which is based on machine learning, reconstructs the energy spectrum of an astrophysical source from observed spectra by minimizing the difference between observed fluxes and those calculated from the model spectrum. By leveraging a large dataset of simulated spectra, our algorithm can effectively distinguish between varying energy spectra, even when faced with limited observational data. Notably, our technique can accurately determine the power law index of an astrophysical spectrum even at a low photon flux of $10^{-15}$ erg s$^{-1}$ cm$^{-2}$ in the energy range of 1-300 keV. Furthermore, our approach remains unbiased and resilient to incomplete coverage of simulated spectra. A larger dataset of observed quasar spectra, along with a broader range of energy coverage from future telescopes like the XARM, will significantly enhance the precision of our technique and expand its applicability to a wider range of astrophysical sources. This new method can effectively determine the energy spectra of diverse astrophysical sources, including those associated with active supermassive black holes. A comprehensive evaluation of our approach's performance with a larger dataset of observed quasar spectra is presented. Additionally, our technique is capable of accurately determining the energy spectra of various quasars, confirming that the typical spectrum consists of two components - a soft power-law and a comptonized continuum. A detailed analysis of our findings reveals that the soft power-law component of 14 FeLoQs quasars can be described by a spectral index of $n_{\mathrm{s}}=1.34 \pm 0.14$. A full description of our approach, along with the associated code, can be accessed at https://github.com/FRGQuasarsReconstructionEnergy Spectrum/tree/main/description. A detailed report outlining our methodology and results can also be obtained via arXiv: arXiv:220.02.09. The reconstructed energy spectra of the 20 quasars from the FeLoQs sample, as well as their corresponding best-fitting spectral indices, can be found at https://github.com/FRGQuasarsReconstructionEnergy Spectrum/tree/ main/energy_spectra. A summary of our findings is also available at https://frgquasars.infn.it/ReconstructionEnergy Spectrum/index.html.

In the context of large and complex networks, uncovering the underlying causal relationships between individual components is a task that has garnered significant interest across various disciplines. Numerous methods have been proposed to infer causality from non-interacting systems, but these approaches fail to account for the emergence of causal interactions within integrated systems. To address this limitation, we present a novel framework called the Signaling Game, an interactive system consisting of two neuro-symbolic agents tasked with a common goal. Through a two-stage process, the Signalling Game facilitates the discovery of causal exchanges between agent signals, which are represented as symbolic variables. Moreover, we find that the strategy profiles of this game, known as Nash Equilibria, provide a reliable representation of the system's emergent causality. To verify the efficacy of our approach, we apply it to real-world data from brain regions and a synthetic network of genetic interactions. The results reveal promising outcomes, with the Signalling Game yielding accurate causal models and enabling the prediction of target outcomes. The implementation details, including source code and data, are made available on GitHub. With its capacity for large-scale integration, the Signalling Game offers a powerful tool for modelling complex systems, making it an invaluable asset for scientists and engineers working on extensive projects. Furthermore, the distributed nature of the Signalling Game enables it to be an ideal candidate for applications requiring real-time causal inference, such as biomedical interventions and autonomous vehicles. To broaden its applicability, we explore the application of the Signalling Game to biomedical case studies, including a scenario involving seizure-related brain changes. With its potential for system-wide deployments, the Signalling Game presents a groundbreaking approach to causal inference, with a particular advantage lying in its ability to capture the dynamic nature of causal interactions. To showcase its efficacy in real-world settings, we provide a detailed analysis of a Signalling Game application to brain regions connected through emergent causal exchanges. Furthermore, the Signalling Game's capability for large-scale integration by means of Nash Equilibria provides a reliable solution to target outcome prediction in modern therapeutic approaches. To illustrate this, we apply the Signalling Game to a network of interconnected brain regions, with a particular focus on areas involved in seizure-related brain changes. A comprehensive source code is available on GitHub for replicating the results presented in this study. Additionally, the research findings are further discussed in an open contribution to the neuroinformatics community, with connections to the iCME logo representing the integration of causal models in biomedical research. This project presents a hybrid approach to term forecasting in online publishing, combining the strengths of two techniques: naive Bayes and latent topic modeling. A novel forecasting framework is developed, incorporating the predictions of two distinct models to yield better outcomes. To accelerate computation, a strategy involving the simplification of naive Bayes is explored, particularly by assuming mutual exclusivity among dominant topics. Experiments were conducted using a dataset of 3,000 terms from actual publishing content, demonstrating that the hybrid method excels over a standalone naive Bayes model due in part to reduced error rates and enhanced diversity of outcomes. Furthermore, the hybrid method exhibits a faster processing speed for term forecasting, making it more suitable for online publishing applications. Notably, the hybrid method achieves an average error rate of 12.4% less than naive Bayes, while also reducing processing time by a factor of 10 compared to the more complex Bayesian topic model. Notably, the enhanced processing speed allows the hybrid method to reach a processing speed of 280 terms per second, surpassing the performance of the simpler latent topic model by 30%. Moreover, the hybrid method demonstrates a processing speed that is 101 times faster than the more complex hierarchical naive Bayes model. In summary, the proposed hybrid approach merges the predictive capabilities of two distinct models, yielding a more compact and efficient solution that surpasses the performance of its individual predecessors in term forecasting. The Seidel matrix is an important tool used to analyze graph properties, particularly in understanding graph symmetry and alternate generalizations of the Ramanujan conjecture. However, the range of the Seidel matrix is limited to a specific set of numbers greater than one, except in certain exceptional cases. For a specific type of graph, the characteristic polynomials of the Seidel matrix have a maximum range of $\zeta_5$ or $\zeta_7$, where the $\zeta_n$ denotes the Riemann zeta function. Additionally, we investigate the Seidel matrix spectrum and establish bounds on its non-zero eigenvalues, similar to those of the Laplacian matrix. By combining these eigenvalue bounds with the range constraints, we prove that certain inequality inequalities do not apply to sequence graphs, thereby solving a previously unsolved problem. To confirm our results, we developed a computer program that generates sequence graphs and tests their inequality compliance. Our study demonstrates that, unlike many other graph theories, the sequence graph theory is inherently incomparable to the established Laplacian matrix theory. Furthermore, we explored an alternative matrix, known as the middle laplacian matrix, that correlates with the Seidel matrix and sequence graphs, and can be used to analyze their properties, particularly the range and spectrum. Our research has resolved several unresolved issues and provided key insights into the middle laplacian matrix, thereby paving the way for further research. A detailed step-by-step proof is provided in the appendix. Our findings also highlight the significance of combining diverse mathematical tools, such as the Seidel matrix, analytic number theory, and matrix perturbation theory, to analyze graph properties, thereby fostering cross-pollination between graph theory and other established mathematical fields. Moreover, our study demonstrates the practical applications of graph theory, such as solving unsolved problems and expanding theoretical frameworks, and highlights the importance of using computer programs to validate theoretical findings, as well as the limitless creative possibilities they offer. Our research also raises several intriguing questions and speculation, and encourages fellow mathematicians to build upon our findings, particularly by investigating whether our results can be extended to other graph theories, such as circulant and pseudo-circulant matrices. Furthermore, we conjecture that sequence graphs can be generalized to higher dimensions, and that the correlation between the Seidel matrix and its inverse will provide a breakthrough in the study of positive semidefinite matrices, particularly the long-unresolved Ramanujan conjecture. Finally, our research has crucial implications for real-world applications, such as cryptography and coding theory

Extensive simulations are conducted to generate over 100 billion bits, which reveal that vehicle relays offer approximately 30% better performance than V2I, and create a network pattern characterized by the matróska effect. Relaying from infrastructure and other vehicles on the same frequency yield similar outcomes, but using roadside units as relays on a separate frequency provide significantly better performance. This research provides crucial insights for designers and engineers, which can be used to develop efficient systems and implementations. It is found that positioning an RSU in the middle of a road or at an intersection enhances the system by as much as 210%, which underscores the importance of road layout and deployment strategy for optimal performance. This paper introduces a novel metric, diversity ratio, which explains the system's performance and shows that an additional frequency used by an RSU can improve the system by as much as 210%, which may be seen as a variety of perspectives for a better outcome. Ultimately, this paper suggests that a hybrid approach with an RSU on the main frequency and another on a frequency divide could provide the best performance, which is supported by the data. The extensive information housed in Wikipedia's databases is dependable due to its community-driven approach, which effectively filters out malicious edits from registered users. However, unregistered users can still cause harm through edits, despite Wikipedia's reliability. Previous research focused on detecting unregistered users' malicious edits using natural language patterns, while this research builds upon that by investigating relationships between editing activities and content quality. Editors who regularly make low-quality edits develop patterns characterized by infrequent contributions, related changes, and persistent material deletion. Infrequent contributors are more likely to engage in low-quality editing, which is further indicated by words related to confusion, chaos, and misinformation in their content. By combining these factors, Wikipedia articles can be automatically labeled as low-quality without considering the identity of the editors involved. This process can serve as a starting point for an automated system to detect and potentially rectify low-quality content across the platform. Moreover, our underlying model enables the detection of Infrequent Contribution Patterns (ICPs) through machine learning or deep learning techniques, which can be applied to fields beyond Wikipedia that rely on volunteered content, including online forums and media files. Our approach demonstrates a high level of accuracy in identifying low-quality content, with scores of 0.9336 for macro-averaged precision, 0.9347 for macro-averaged recall, and 0.913 for micro-averaged F1-score. Our proposal is comprised of a theoretical framework, a tagger model, and an experimental analysis, which together provide a comprehensive understanding of the interplay between editing activities and content quality. Furthermore, our findings are substantiated through a robust set of qualitative results, which highlight the distinct patterns of editors making low-quality edits, as well as the properties of high-quality content. Finally, our study identifies areas for future research, specifically the potential misuse of our proposed theory for harassment, as well as the necessity of developing automated tools that can aid editors in enhancing content quality. In practical scenarios with limited knowledge of the underlying system, decision-based reinforcement learning algorithms can provide valuable guidance. This paper explores a novel approach where an external knowledge source, unaffected by the target system's specifics, supplies decision-making information. Through repeated interactions with a black-box environment, the learned policy adapts and refines itself, utilizing the transferred knowledge more effectively over time. Two frameworks - Black-Box Policy Search and Black-Box Optimization - are examined in detail, with empirical analysis conducted using both simple and complex environments. The results demonstrate that the proposed strategy can achieve notable performance improvements, specifically in finding more optimal solutions in challenging environments. Given its reliance on minimal environmental assumptions, this approach could potentially bridge the gap between theoretical and practical stochastic optimization challenges. The code used in this study has been publicly shared for ease of replication. Additionally, the developed framework shows promise in real-world applications, such as its initial application in personalizing the interaction of a robotic agent with its internal decision-making module. This personalized integration is anticipated to enhance interactions between various system components and potentially lead to further generalizations. The associated project can be found on GitHub at: https://github.com/cwenger/decision-based-rs. The knowledge transfer framework, specifically the dbbk module, can also be accessed through the following link: https://github.com/cwenger/decision-based-rs/blob/main/decision_based_black_box_framework.py. A video showcasing the results can be found at: https://youtu.be/3U6R6D9heHk. A geometric representation of geometric T-duality on a twisted torus is developed,  applying the concept of locally free sheaf geometric T-duality to twisted torus fibrations.  The  result is demonstrated by constructing a geometric T-duality transformation for sheaf gerbes over a twisted torus.  The associated class in the Brauer group of the twisted torus is shown to be invariant under geometric T-duality.  This sheaf gerbe geometric T-duality is applied to a specific example involving a holomorphic volume form on a twisted torus.  The class of the associated sheaf gerbe is computed and found to be non-zero,  and its Brauer class is invariant under geometric T-duality.  This provides a novel application of sheaf gerbe geometric T-duality to the study of holomorphic volume forms on twisted tori.  A related question concerning the closure of the image of the map from the first cohomology group of the twisted torus to its Brauer group is also addressed.  It is shown that the map is monomorphic when the twisted torus has a trivial ramification,  and that this result is optimal.  Additional properties of the Brauer class of a sheaf gerbe over a twisted torus are also investigated.  It is shown that the Brauer class is trivial whenever the twisted torus has a ramification degree that is a fifth power,  and that this result is also optimal.  The topological T-duality of a twisted torus is recalled and compared to the sheaf gerbe geometric T-duality.  It is demonstrated that the Brauer class of a sheaf gerbe over a twisted torus is invariant under topological T-duality.  A specific example of a sheaf gerbe geometric T-duality on a twisted torus is computed,  and is found to be consistent with the topological T-duality of the twisted torus.  A general method for computing the Brauer class of a sheaf gerbe over a twisted torus is developed.  It is shown that the map from the first cohomology group of the twisted torus to its Brauer group is an isomorphism when the twisted torus has a ramification degree of three or five.  A related class in the cohomology group of the twisted torus is defined and found to be a multiple of the Brauer class when the twisted torus has a ramification degree of three or five. The emergence of the Co-Observation Learning (CoOL) paradigm addresses the limitation of traditional specialist reinforcement learning, which necessitates extensive expert input and thus hinders practical application. CoOL learns from observations shared among agents without expert supervision, facilitating self-discovery through exploration. Our research aims to validate the feasibility of CoOL in real-world scenarios, specifically in the context of vehicle following, an inherently cooperative setting that necessitates rapid learning for safe navigation. We integrate the CoOL paradigm into a Proximal Policy Optimization (Proximal) framework, experimenting with four observation-sharing methods: individual, pairwise, group, and global sharing. Our findings reveal that the pairwise and global sharing approaches outperform the individual sharing method by promoting more efficient learning, while also demonstrating comparable results to a control group using specialist demonstrations without sharing. These results confirm the viability of the CoOL paradigm for real-world cooperative scenarios. The source code for this project is publicly available at https://github.com/tjdcstudent/Cool-vehicle-following.

This paper tackles the efficient decoding of ACCL codes, which are a type of PAC code. Specifically, we examined linear ACCL codes of size n, consisting of m nonzero vectors in a subspace of dimension m, and an active set of size k, where l elements of the set are chosen from the topl largest coordinates of the vectors. Our study focuses on two decoding problems: one where the active set is already known, and another where it needs to be determined as part of the decoding process. Notably, we identified that both problems can be framed as a form of maximum independent set (MIS) problem in a graph, whose construction we described as an edge-colored multigraph. By analyzing the decoding of linear ACCL codes, we observed that certain code properties hold. Furthermore, we analyzed a proposed algorithm for computing the active set during decoding, providing it along with some theoretical validation of its performance. Our work also covered the measurement of ACCL codes, and we established a connection between their ACCL and code rate. Additionally, we investigated the influence of top-l coordinates on the accuracy of measuring the active set size in an ACCL code. Our findings are supported by numerical results. Lastly, we explored computational experiments to compare the performance of ACCL codes of various types, including bipolar, binary, and multivariate. Our research was facilitated through a recently developed software tool for computing ACCL codes, ACCL Compute, which we described and used to conduct the experiments. The study concludes by specifying future research directions prompted by our observations. These directions pertain to enhancing ACCL code property validation, accelerating the decoding of ACCL codes with unknown active sets, and further developing the ACCL Compute tool to include additional features. Our work is publicly accessible through a corresponding arXiv document. Additionally, the ACCL Compute tool used in our research is freely available at https://cimm.columbia.edu/accIcompute under the terms of the GNU General Public License, version 3.0. Reconstructing and tracking hand-object interactions within unstructured real-world environments poses a difficult problem in computer vision.  To approach this challenge, we developed a novel, engaging hand-and-object reconstruction pipeline, which can be applied directly to in-depth depth sensor data.  To enhance accuracy in unpredictable settings, we presented a multi-frame reconstruction repair strategy, which utilizes data-from-data tracking information to fix potential reconstruction errors.  Experimental results on a real-world, unedited dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in comparing various engagement states and accurately tracking reconstructions over time.  To facilitate replication, we released both our reconstruction pipeline and the entire unedited dataset publicly.  These reconstructed pointcloud series can be accessed through our website under the name CP3D-Engagements.  We found that our method surpasses every alternative approach in accuracy, with particularly notable improvements in tracking and reconstruction repair.  Notably, we found our reconstruction repair strategy alone boosts accuracy by at least 10% in monitoring and reconstructing hand-object interactions within unstructured real-world settings.  To evaluate the feasibility of our approach in practical applications, we also carried out a user study, in which participants participated in grasping tasks while wearing a specific type of hand-tracking technology.  We analyzed the resulting data to confirm our hypothesis that by rebuilding hand-object engagements in every frame, we can enhance precision in various engagement monitoring tasks.  These findings contribute to the field by supplying previously unquantified evidence for the benefit of engaging hand-and-object reconstructions in unedited real-world settings.  Additionally, we discovered that current state-of-the-art hand-tracking technology experiences occasional failures, which we found can be partly attributed to the straightforward nature of the used baseline grasping motion.  These outcomes present potential avenues for enhancement in tracking accuracy by incorporating additional robustness, particularly in detecting various hand-and-object interaction types.  To facilitate replication, we released the code for our reconstruction pipeline through our website, where users can also access the engaged reconstructions, referred to as CP3D-Engagements.  We anticipate these pointcloud series to become a valuable resource for various computer vision tasks involving hand-and-object interactions, as they supply highly accurate, unedited depth sensor data spanning a range of engaging poses and rigorous testing to ensure reconstruction accuracy across every frame. We establish a noncrystallographic type of collection, referred to as a tail-triangle C-collection, in a 4x4 grid. Two distinct forms of this collection are presented, both of which possess an interleaving number of 2. Moreover, we establish a crystallographic type of subset, referred to as a triangle collection, in a 4x4 grid, for which the interleaving number is 1. Additionally, we introduce an efficient algorithm to generate all triangle collections in a 3x3 grid. Furthermore, this research extends existing findings on hexagonal honeycombs by revealing a 2-interleaving number for a specific class of these collections, encompassing both regular hexagonal honeycombs and a previously discovered spiral honeycomb. Existing proofs of 1-interleaving numbers for regular hexagonal honeycombs can also be applied by utilizing a transformation to 30-120-150 triangle honeycombs. Lastly, this research provides a comprehensive listing of all C-collections in a 3x3 grid, along with their associated interleaving numbers. These findings also hold significance beyond the realm of honeycombs, as they possess broader applications. The concepts and techniques utilized in this research also have potential applications in other areas of mathematics, such as tilings and mesh theory. Additionally, the results of this research may be useful in solving open problems related to tilings and mesh theory, such as the generalization of triangle collections to n-dimensional tilings and the application of mesh homotopy to the solution of the strong tilting conjecture. The findings of this research also offer potential avenues for resolving other open problems in honeycombs and tilings, such as generalizing the spiral honeycomb to higher dimensions and finding a proof for the weak tilting conjecture. A novel learning-based approach is proposed to determine the optimal position and orientation of a robot's end-effector in unmarked environments. By combining images from a depth camera and kinematic data from the robot, an unsupervised method estimates the location of the end-effector using a conditional normalization technique. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach can accurately calculate the end-effector's location across various configurations without requiring any pre-defined parameters or training. Moreover, analysis of depth images enables efficient calculation of the end-effector's pose, making this method suitable for applications requiring high precision and real-time calculations. A numerical evaluation of the technique's accuracy is also presented. Crucially, both the depth camera and robot kinematics serve as the foundation for this approach, ensuring its reliability and simplicity in practical applications. An example use case is provided to illustrate the method's capabilities in adjusting the robot's configuration and local coordinate system for optimal task performance. This technique has potential applications in a wide range of tasks, such as adjusting the robot's field of view, ensuring a safe working distance, and optimizing task efficiency. A video showcasing the robot's interactive capabilities in a dynamic environment is available online at: https://youtu.be/S6u4POB8yeU. To effectively implement a treatment, it is essential to comprehend how various individuals interact with each other. One widely adopted framework for achieving this is the k-nearest neighbors (KNN) interference model, which enables the identification of treatment disruption - a situation where a patient's response to treatment is negatively impacted by another patient receiving the same treatment. Previous studies have established conditions under controlled laboratory conditions that yield precise mathematical formulations for identifying treatment disruption in both the static and dynamic KNN models. Notably, these conditions become complex to meet when data is drawn from a non-unique probability distribution known as the mixed Bernoulli-Gaussian distribution. Our primary objective is to create a condition under which the treatment disruption in the KNN model can be accurately identified when data is drawn from a more general probability distribution than previously considered. Our approach involves a novel hybrid of two distinct data sets - one generated from the mixed Bernoulli-Gaussian distribution and another generated independently - to create a data set that adheres to a unique probability distribution, thereby allowing us to formulate a condition under which the treatment disruption in the KNN model can be accurately identified. Our technique addresses a critical challenge in the field of treatment disruption by providing a precise mathematical formulation for its identification in the KNN model even when data is drawn from a complex probability distribution, thereby enhancing the understanding of treatment disruption in big data applications. Our approach is further validated through simulations conducted on real-world and simulated data sets, which demonstrate its efficacy in identifying treatment disruption in various scenarios. Calculations of neutrino emissions from Dark Matter annihilations within Neutron Stars are crucial for ongoing and future observations. This work refines those estimates by incorporating previously unconsidered processes involving Dark Matter interactions with nuclear matter via a pseudoscalar mediator. We examine how neutrino emissions are impacted by this mechanism and adapt our results to apply to both Dark Matter composite models and cases involving multiple Dark Matter components. We demonstrate that the improved neutrino emissions could have a significant effect on the cooling of Neutron Stars, potentially affecting their observable radius or heat emission. The modified neutrino emissions may also affect the detection of signals from Supernovae, specifically in the Pulsar Wind Nebula of the famous SN 1054, the Vela Pulsar, and others. Furthermore, the modified neutrino emissions could have a significant effect on the detection of signals from Hickson 62, the densest galaxy system and a potential source of DM signals, as well as from the nearby Rho Oph cloud complex. We conclude by noting that our refined estimates of neutrino emissions from DM annihilations may lead to reduced expectations for DM-related signals from Neutron Stars in the near future. Insufficient accurate galaxy shape measurements have long impeded cosmological studies that utilize weak lensing, a technique that's increasingly important for researching dark matter and the expansion of the universe. To address this limitation, we've developed ShapePipe, a precise and efficient pipeline for assessing galaxy shape measurements that's adaptable to various data sets. We employed ShapePipe on a vast dataset combining the UNIONS project and CFIS data, yielding over 300,000 distant galaxy clusters that serve as effective lenses. Our analysis exploited half a billion galaxies, covering a wide range of redshifts, to generate accurate weak lensing signals that we leveraged to study the distribution of cosmological matter clustering as a function of redshift and scale. However, we noticed that our investigation was constrained more by our data's noise level than by the precision of our galaxy shape measurements, highlighting the need for further research. We've publicly released ShapePipe and encourage its application to other data sets, thereby enriching the range of applications for this versatile pipeline. We've also contributed to the field by providing detailed documentation and guidance on utilizing ShapePipe. To facilitate the exchange of spin information in quantum computers, it's crucial to understand how nearby spins interact. This is particularly essential in planar Heisenberg magnets which exhibit Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless behavior characterized by long-range correlation and unconventional melting points. The magnetic properties of these systems can be manipulated through the application of a magnetic field. This research investigates the impact of a controlled magnetic field on the spin correlations in a square-lattice Heisenberg model with neighboring spins interacting. We find that the field can adjust the spin correlation to conform with either 2D or 3D systems, thereby altering the melting behavior and scaling exponents of the system. This control over exchange interactions could enable the development of a new class of quantum gates based on Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless physics. Moreover, this research provides a crucial link between two-dimensional systems that exhibit BKT physics and those that are three-dimensionally bound. The final results were obtained via simulations using Monte Carlo method. The field-adjustable magnetic behavior may exist in other systems that exhibit the same type of spin interactions and we believe that this phenomenon is not unique to the specific system that we studied. Therefore, it is possible that quantum computers using similar systems could be vulnerable to errors due to their connection to the BKT phase. However, this could also provide a potential strategy for implementing a type of quantum gate known as a $\pi$ gate. Hardware-generated truly random numbers are highly valued in scientific and cryptographic applications for their unpredictability.
A widely used method for obtaining such numbers involves exploiting SRAM array voltage fluctuations during fabrication.
Although this approach seems efficient at first, it's hampered by several drawbacks: the costly and time-consuming process of bringing these arrays into true random states, the vast number of SRAM bits required to generate a single binary number, and the challenge of extracting a single high-quality random bit from a SRAM array.
Our proposed system, TuRaN, tackles these issues by utilizing a novel approach to extracting multiple random bits from a small SRAM at once.
To achieve this, TuRaN integrates a full binary counter that identifies and discards undescaled SRAM bit patterns, providing a fixed latency period and high-quality random outputs regardless of the SRAM size.
Additionally, TuRaN features a customizable architecture that allows the user to choose between two low-energy operating modes in underscaled SRAMs.
Our performance evaluation indicates that TuRaN generates the highest number of random bits per SRAM bit, and its fully-automated random number extraction eliminates the need for frequent SRAM reinitialization, making it an ideal solution for the task at hand.

During the training process of a neural network, its architecture undergoes significant changes, leading to the reduction of its capacity to process complex inputs. This phenomenon is closely linked to the prevalence of simpler representations within the parameter space of neural networks, as evidenced by various experiments conducted in the field. In this study, we initially demonstrate that certain common architectures of neural networks, such as those employing ReLU or max-pooling, incorporate features which effectively limit the complexity of the inputs they process, resulting in the reduction of intricate geometric patterns within those inputs. By examining the effect of global features including the architecture of layers, the dimensions of inputs, and the positions of neurons, we show that these features act as effective simplifiers of geometric patterns within the parameter space of neural networks. Subsequently, we design a modular circuit based on the Allen-Cahn type that is capable of detecting patterns at scales ranging from a few to hundreds of pixels, thereby extending the scope of pattern detection to larger scales. Notably, our findings are corroborated by both the examination of regularizers derived from dynamical systems and the analysis of neural networks trained using the gradient descent algorithm. The latter reveals that the preference for simpler geometric patterns can be attributed to the prevalence of smaller-scale features within the data, as demonstrated through the analysis of representations at distinct scales within the parameter space of neural networks. Ultimately, our work highlights the influence of geometric complexity as a regulating factor in neural network training, thereby laying the groundwork for the exploration of topological complexity as a further regulating factor in neural networks. Additionally, our research enables the design of low-level circuits capable of detecting patterns at a wide range of scales, thereby surpassing the current capabilities of circuit designers. The proposed circuits can be extended to applications in biology and medicine, where patterns at various scales often emerge, such as those observed in microcosms and normal human cells. Furthermore, our research may be extended to the detection of macroscopic patterns in the world around us. The key concepts of our research are illustrated through applications in geology and meteorology. This approach relies on four $q^2$ dependence-based ratios of hadronic matrix elements, which are accessible with $e^+e^-$ collider data. As an immediate benefit, this technique enables Wilson coefficient extraction without standard model precision assumptions regarding these matrix elements. Additionally, ratios of hadronic matrix elements are directly extracted, and given current uncertainties, their values are centered on 1. This approach is versatile and can be applied to various decay processes such as $B^0\to K^{*0}X$. Furthermore, with anticipated $e^+e^-$ data from BESIII, a notable reduction to zero can be observed in certain ratios, providing crucial new information that will significantly enhance the accuracy of standard model Wilson coefficient determinations. Music composition automation poses a complex problem, due to its intricate nature.
Composing music involves multiple aspects like melody, harmony, and rhythm,
which must be specifed correctly to produce coherent output.
Different composition systems face unique challenges in addressing these
aspects, highlighting the problem's complexity.
This complication also hinders the development of a universal evaluation
metric for composition systems, making it a third major issue.
To tackle these challenges, our approach involves leveraging pre-trained
Transformer-based models, combining them with data augmentation techniques
to expand the versatility of composition systems and improve their overall
performance.
By applying magnetic augmentation to a melodic dataset, we observe a
substantial improvement in evaluation scores for the melodic component of
the MuseGAN system, ranging from a moderate 5% boost in LSML scores on
the Minimusic dataset to a notable 26.52% improvement in MuseScore scores
on the Compproxy dataset.
Furthermore, we discover that applying magnetic augmentation to a harmonic
dataset HarMoNet, enhances the harmonic quality of the generated music,
as measured by the Compproxy metric, with an average increase of 13.81%.
These findings support the use of magnetic augmentation for music
composition, indicating its potential to benefit other composition systems
as well, thus expanding the repertoire of available data augmentation
techniques for automated music composition. 
We make our code available for replication of results at https://github.com/jbousquet6/Magnetic-Music.

The marginal dependence framework is a widely-used approach for analyzing
contingency tables, offering a simple and intuitive way to model complex
dependencies between variables while allowing for efficient maximum
likelihood estimation. This chapter summarizes research in developing various
marginal dependence frameworks, highlighting their key benefits and
considerations. Different types of models within this framework are explored,
along with discussions on their respective advantages and the way they
comparatively fit real data. Additionally, the chapter examines the
flexibilities offered by the marginal dependence framework in terms of its
potential applications to handle big data and its versatility in analyzing
multi-response data. Furthermore, potential future areas of research within
this framework are identified and possible directions are proposed. Lastly,
the chapter concludes by reiterating the significance of considering models
within the marginal dependence framework, particularly in practical
applications, and the need for future studies on this topic. In various computer science fields, solving structured linear equations is a crucial task. It plays a key role in multiple areas, such as solving polynomial equations or matrix nearness problems. While it has been proven possible to solve unstructured linear equations in space that is proportional to their size, the same question for structured equations remains unresolved. In this research, we provide an affirmative answer, showing that solving structured linear equations can be done in space that is proportional to the size of the input for equations with a specific pattern. Specifically, we can handle monic equations with Pascal and matrix-powers of 2 patterns in logarithmic space, and matrix-powers of 2 patterns in poly-logarithmic space, respectively. Our approach also offers a direct transformation for converting algorithms that use poly-logarithmic amounts of memory into ones that use logarithmic space, thereby addressing an previously unanswered question. Additionally, we extend the boundary of solving near-pivotless linear equations, reducing the space requirement for this task to log(n) bits, an improvement over the previous space complexity of n*log(n) bits. This research further enables solving linear equations with a space requirement of log(n) bits when accompanied by a constant-size near-pivotless pivot-finding component, answering an affirmative question in the process. Finally, we expand the boundary of solving linear equations with poly-logarithmic space complexity by incorporating additional patterns, specifically clonable and product of term (POT) patterns. Our innovative direct transformation technique, developed in this research, is the first to establish a connection between algorithmic techniques that use poly-logarithmic memory and those that use logarithmic space, thereby offering significant insights into the underlying problem. Recent breakthroughs in AI have led to a surge in accurate digital replicas of complex systems, but their widespread adoption is hindered by a catch-22: models require substantial, rarely available data, and generous computational resources to predict uncertain future events. This circular dependency renders many systems inaccessible to modeling. We propose a novel approach, Collaborative Data-informed Modeling (CDM), an online AI-facilitated collaboration model that addresses this data scarcity by creating multiple smaller models among various entities, each refining its results with feedback from others and adjusting its predictions based on the others' distributions of possible outcomes. This CDM surpasses traditional modeling methods by demonstrating superior performance, higher data efficiency, and greater scalability, while effectively managing computational resources. Additionally, our model promotes transparency and explainability through human interpretation of each contributor's results and fosters trust through the integration of multiple perspectives. We showcase CDM's efficacy by creating a 1,500-member collective that successfully maps the dynamics of a highly non-linear, hidden system with only 12 initial data points and limited environmental context, outperforming individual modeling efforts and highlighting CDM's potential to bridge the gap between individual intelligence and collective intelligence. CDM can empower various fields to navigate complex, data-scarce environments by providing a collective, collaborative understanding of the world. The code for this research is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/donk-art/cdm and on GitHub.io at https://donk-art.github.io/cdm. Related data can be found at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/19s6T1G1k1C7__R3x. Please visit our website at https://donk-art.github.io/cdm for a detailed demonstration of CDM's capabilities. The researchers welcome feedback, questions, and collaborations, and encourage other researchers to test the model and join the collective. They have established a dedicated Slack channel for the collective (https://slack.com/invite-code), and can be reached via email at contact-donk@art.com for further information. We have developed a tutorial (https://docs-donk.github.io/learning-cdm), and a set of frequently asked questions (https://faq-donk.github.io/cdm), as well as a public GitHub issue for general inquiries (https://issues-donk.github.io/cdm). Please don't hesitate to reach out; we are excited to collaborate!

This paper presents a novel coding strategy that incorporates degree-degree connections in low-density parity-check (LDPC) code construction. By doing so, it surpasses traditional LDPC code performance, achieving higher error-resistance capabilities on binary erasure channels. To explain this enhancement, this study develops a degree-degree linking model and proves it through analysis. Computational experiments confirm that the proposed degree-degree linked LDPC codes yield superior performance compared to conventional LDPC codes of similar density and sparsity. In particular, these codes display improved error-resistance capabilities, particularly in scenarios involving erasure patterns that mirror the LDPC code parity-check matrix structure. As such, they are an ideal choice for applications requiring robustness against such pattern-specific errors. Furthermore, these degree-degree linked LDPC codes have been found to be highly suitable for binary erasure channels with unknown noise patterns. Our findings indicate that degree-degree linked LDPC codes can provide superior decoding performance relative to conventional LDPC codes when the channel noise pattern is unknown. This research contributes to the ongoing effort to develop LDPC codes capable of overcoming pattern-specific errors, highlighting novel degree-degree linked structures as an advantageous design choice. Ultimately, these degree-degree linked LDPC codes are shown to be an effective tool for addressing the remaining gap in LDPC code performance, specifically for binary erasure channels characterized by unknown noise patterns. As such, they hold significant potential for LDPC code application in various challenging channel scenarios. To validate these findings, this study presents and analyzes degree-degree linked LDPC code examples across various code sizes and densities. Specifically, it examines density and sparsity characteristics, error-resistance capabilities against channel noise, and the degree-degree linked LDPC code performance in scenarios involving both known and unknown channel noise patterns. Moreover, this study evaluates and compares LDPC code designs that incorporate degree-degree links and examines how these designs interact with channel-specific noise patterns. It is found that degree-degree linked LDPC codes yield superior performance in both deterministic and probabilistic decoding contexts. Nevertheless, our research reveals a new type of attack that exploits a flaw in the proposed system, where partially randomised states can be distinguished without limitation. Recent research has identified a phenomenon called 'in-context learning,' where a vast language model can generate outputs in context, without requiring task-specific fine-tuning.  In-context learning typically leverages data from a large, self-supervised pretraining dataset, and selecting an appropriate dataset can lead to improved performance.  Past studies have shown that using tailored pretraining datasets can enhance in-context learning, but a more extensive analysis of the influence of diverse datasets is needed.  In this research,, we examine the in-context learning capabilities of a state-of-the-art language model when prompted with eight different datasets, including datasets for zero-shot sentiment analysis, natural language inference, and data-to-text.  Our investigation reveals that using an appropriately aligned pretraining dataset significantly enhances in-context learning performance, and under optimal conditions, can achieve comparable performance to that achieved through task-specific fine-tuning.  Conversely, utilizing a misaligned pretraining dataset significantly decreases in-context learning performance, highlighting the challenges and limitations of this approach.  Additionally, our research provides insights into the specific elements of in-context learning data that can affect performance, and suggests various potential applications of vast language models for tasks that were previously thought to require more specialized resources. This study employs smoothed particle hydrodynamics simulations to delve into the historical impact of cooling on gas within these groups, focusing on how magnetic fields and thermal conduction affect the process. We discovered that in systems lacking strong magnetic fields, high levels of cooling occur as gas collapses onto the center, but this leads to over a decade's worth of excessive cooling. When magnetic fields are present, they prevent excessive cooling due to a low beta factor, yet slow down the cooling process overall. Thermal conduction has a minimal effect, primarily inhibiting cooling in the presence of magnetic fields. This leads to an reduced mass loss through thermal conduction and a reduced thermal pressure in the halo. A reduced thermal pressure in the halo prevents hot gas from reaching its equilibrium state, resulting in a lower excess cooling compared to systems with strong magnetic fields. However, magnetic fields are ultimately ineffective in preventing reduced cooling in the long term. Ultimately, a lower mass of gas remaining in the group and high rates of star formation both contribute to decreased levels of excessive cooling. A critical challenge in voice synthesis without annotation involves deriving essential phonetic information directly from acoustic data. To overcome this, a method is developed that converts wideband speech into acoustic primitives, which are then used to extract essential phonetic information. This information is subsequently represented in a space that aligns with the underlying linguistic structure, where it is learned in an unsupervised manner. Furthermore, a technique is created to align these acoustic units with the underlying linguistic structure in a way that mimics linguistic patterns. To validate the effectiveness of this approach, voice synthesis experiments without annotation are conducted, demonstrating that voices synthesized based on this method outperform others in terms of overall similarity. Additionally, when annotation is available, it is shown that this approach leads to voice synthesis metrics comparable to those of state-of-the-art models. Importantly, this method enables voice synthesis without requiring transcription, but when annotation is available, it is shown that this approach leads to improved results when combined with annotation. To further enhance the synthesis quality when annotation is available, a neural audio unit synthesis model is developed, which utilizes these transcriptions as input to produce high-quality audio units. To train this model, a novel, efficient method is developed that converts wideband speech into audio units, which are then used to derive the necessary phonetic information. Experiments show that this model leads to a significant improvement in synthesis quality when annotation is available. Notably, this approach and another method that also converts wideband speech into audio units were previously known to be effective, but it is shown that this model leads to a more precise alignment of acoustic units with the underlying linguistic structure, which in turn leads to improved synthesis quality. To further investigate the efficacy of this model, additional metrics are created to gauge its performance from a linguistic perspective, which show that this model leads to voice synthesis metrics closer to those of human speech. Decentralized learning techniques are increasingly popular due to their ability to process large datasets and withstand failures. Despite their effectiveness, decentralized learning algorithms may be susceptible to distributional shifts in data, which can impair their performance. In response to this challenge, we develop a distributionally robust decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent method, allowing multiple clients to collaboratively learn a robust model in the face of changing data distributions. By integrating bilinear modification with a standard decentralized learning algorithm, we prove that our method achieves a robust convergence rate comparable to the best-known results in standard decentralized learning scenarios. Furthermore, we tested our method in a communication-efficient decentralized setting and found it to be more resilient to data distribution changes than the current state-of-the-art decentralized learning methods. Additionally, we provided empirical evidence demonstrating the efficacy of our method in a communication-efficient distributed training scenario involving Google Colab machines with different hardware capabilities. The source code for our method is available at https://github.com/learn2connect/DR-DSGD.

Through frequency-domain analysis, the amplitude and phase responses of an object's acceleration transients can be understood. A new statistical approach is proposed for determining the required sample size in basket trials by incorporating learning between subgroups within a single trial. This involves using Bayesian methods to calculate the necessary recruitment for each patient type based on available data. Two scenarios are considered: one where treatment effects between subgroups can be similar, and another with differing treatment effects where subgroup comparisons are compared to a control group. By employing Bayesian posterier prediction, this approach valves the average outcomes of unknown patient types, and estimates the required sample sizes for uninvestigated types based on historical data and ongoing trial findings. The proposed method is assessed through simulations, and further illustrated with a real-world example from an acute myeloid leukemia study. Simulation results indicate that this approach is reliable, precise in sizing trials for new patient types, and adapts effectively to varying numbers of subgroups, degrees of freedom, and types of outcomes. The case study demonstrates the eligibility of this approach for use in trials involving continuous data and illustrates its application in determining the required recruitment for a new subpopulation. Simulation data also reveals the influence of non-informative priors on sample size estimates and suggests that the lower bound of the predicted range provides a more conservative estimate. Furthermore, this approach is found to be more efficient in sizing trials for new patient types compared to frequentist methods. The latter's performance, however, improves when subgroup effects are similar. The proposed method enhances the flexibility and efficiency of basket trials by allowing for simultaneous investigation of multiple patient subgroups and improved recruitment accuracy for uninvestigated types. By leveraging information between subgroups within a single trial, this approach optimizes statistical power and efficiency in basket trials. The approach offers a versatile solution that can be applied to various clinical trials involving continuous data and is compatible with different Bayesian priors, including the use of frequentist priors for maximum conservatism. The latter's upper bound provides a conservative estimate in the case of priors with varying levels of belief. The influence of non-informative priors on sample size estimates and the effect of prior choices on the predicted range are areas that require further investigation in the future. The novel approach offers a pioneering solution for incorporating interim data in basket trials, and its extension to account for covariates in the Bayesian posterior predictor has also been explored. The possibility of incorporating covariates in the approach may offer additional advantages and enhancements to the method in future research. Additionally, we provide an overview of the previously documented results for the generalized solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups, as well as establish new findings, including some previously unverified conclusions. A highly efficient method for analyzing time-resolved data is developed, allowing it to be processed either as response surfaces or in high-dimensional trajectories. By treating an experiment's results as noisy observations, an optimized path is sought that aligns with those observations. Initially, the simplest form of this path, a low-dimensional representation, is determined through conventional least-squares optimization. However, we demonstrate that introducing a constraint on observation count leads to a robust, low-dimensional path that is resistant to outliers and can effectively handle the limitations of quantum dynamics simulations. Furthermore, its application is not confined to least-squares optimization; any quantum forward model can be utilized to calculate a sturdy trajectory compatible with a variety of quantum simulation results. The development of this sturdy trajectory approach, termed 'Sturdy Trajectory Extraction Algorithm', yields a range of benefits, including enhanced stability of analytical results and a decrease in spurious results associated with noisy data. The algorithm comprises two distinct versions - STEA-SLS and STEA-LB - which cater to least-squares and Laplace-based data analysis respectively, while a general form of the algorithm, STES, can accommodate any quantum forward model to compute a sturdy trajectory even in the presence of data gaps. The stability of results can be visually estimated through the 'Sturdy Score', a metric that represents the reliability of a trajectory. The approach is detailed through applications to three datasets, namely those related to the multi-state photoinduced dynamics in cobalt-phthalocyanine, the photodynamics of the charge-separated state of a model trimer, and the photoinjection of phthalocyanine, showcasing its robustness and efficiency in analyzing dynamic quantum phenomena. The STES algorithm is devised such that its components can be scaled up to analyze data from quantum simulations involving vast numbers of steps, thereby making it a valuable tool for analyzing the outcome of high-throughput quantum simulations. The stable trajectories it generates can also be used as a starting point for theoretical studies of the underlying dynamical quantum phenomena over extended time periods. The novel approach to time-resolved data analysis presented here is expected to contribute to the analysis of the dynamic quantum phenomena resulting from the interaction of light with various materials. It is furthermore an integral component of a forthcoming high-throughput analysis tool, PHANTOM, that generates sturdy trajectories from simulation data sets to facilitate the analysis of their contents. A novel approach called Cycle Division GAN is proposed to split data into distinct groups based on their characteristics, without requiring pre-defined labels, by using an unsupervised divide-and-conquer strategy that combines cycle-loss and divisional operation. 

We apply the Cycle Division GAN to separate images captured from multiple modalities, such as RGB and depth, or RGB and semantic segmentation, by using transformation-encoding GANs to transform samples into a reference group's domain. 

Experimental results show that the Cycle Division GAN effectively splits data into two parts and accurately transforms samples across domains, while also demonstrating its ability to achieve consistent results multiple times due to its deterministic nature. 

Comparison experiments reveal that the Cycle Division GAN outperforms existing methods in splitting RGB and depth images, and also produces lower reconstruction errors for RGB images transformed from depth and vice versa. 

Furthermore, the Cycle Division GAN is capable of splitting RGB and semantic segmentation images into three parts, a task that earlier methods were unable to accomplish. 
Such a capability makes the Cycle Division GAN a versatile tool for a range of applications, including data utilization, processing, and synthesis. 
As such, the Cycle Division GAN presents a useful unsupervised approach to instance partitioning.

Predicting actions in advance allows healthcare and security systems to identify potential issues at an early stage, enabling more effective prevention and mitigation of harmful events. This paper outlines an innovative method for forecasting future actions, incorporating a radial basis function (RBF) kernelized feature mapping mechanism within a long short-term memory (LSTM) network. By transforming the LSTM output from a density distribution into a discrete action, our approach enhances the precision and efficiency of prediction. Furthermore, we introduce an adaptive Gaussian kernel size that optimizes performance in various scenarios. Experimental evaluations confirm that our model surpasses competing alternatives in a real-world hospital dataset. Additionally, we conduct thorough analyses to assess performance under different data availability conditions. Source code for this project has been publicly released at https://github.com/NicoScheller/RBF-Kernel-LSMT.

This leads to a relationship between nearly parallel forms and the curvature of the canonical connection. Additionally, our findings extend the concepts of and relations between G2-instantons, deformations of G2-instantons, and zero instantons to the broader context of nearly G2 structures, and can also be applied to the specific case of G2-manifolds. ambiguous and semi-implicit time relationships. To address these issues, we

of a time-independent score function, employing time-noise augmented samples for training.

datasets, while the integrated time embeddings also facilitate the comprehension
of implicit temporal relationships. To address the issue of ground noise in audio synthesis, we investigate its impact on speech enhancement models. Ground noise is persistent background noise characteristic to robocalls, making audio synthesis relevant. We analyze the effect of ground noise on speech enhancement models by comparing their performance on clean and noisy speech. Our research shows that ground noise is difficult for models to filter out, as it significantly lowers their quality even after enhancement. This is evident from speech translation metrics like WER and WERM. To mitigate this issue, we try various filtering methods, including magnitude spectrum filtering, but find that ground noise remains difficult to eliminate. Consequently, we propose a strategy involving signal approximation after filtering out noise above a threshold. We also explore the use of early termination in neural taintment models to minimize the impact of ground noise. Our experiments suggest that early termination can improve speech quality, as measured by WERM, at the cost of greater resource usage, indicating a tradeoff between quality and efficiency. Code for our work is available at https://github.com/RockyAndersen/efficient_speech_synthesis_with_ground_noise_rejection.

A new compound called hydrogen boride (H3+2B) exhibits high chemical potential and high electron correlation, which are reminiscent of hydrogen compounds that show superconductivity under high pressure. Therefore, it has been suggested that it could also exhibit superconductivity. We used ab-initio calculations to investigate its possibility. However, our study revealed that the superconducting property of H3+2B is unlikely because it tends to undergo a chemical reaction with its own components under high pressure, forming boron and hydrogen gases. Furthermore, created mock superconducting compounds (HxBx+1 with x = 2, 3) exhibit inferior electrical properties compared to H3+2B and do not satisfy standard superconducting criteria. Our investigation shows that high-pressure stability is a vital prerequisite for a hydrogen compound to exhibit superconductivity. We expect our findings to contribute to the further exploration of superconducting hydrogen compounds at high pressures.

This study develops a comprehensive analysis of Leibnizian calculus within three modern mathematical systems: real analysis, non-standard analysis, and smooth infinitesimals. Real analysis is examined through the lens of a detailed historical reconstruction of Leibniz's thought, while non-standard analysis and smooth infinitesimals serve as alternative approaches to understanding Leibnizian concepts. The author draws upon Leibniz's writings, particularly a letter to Clarke, to frame a precise mathematical representation of Leibnizian calculus within real analysis. A thorough comparison of this construction with non-standard analysis and smooth infinitesimals reveals a striking similarity between the latter two approaches. Furthermore, the study introduces a new framework for smooth infinitesimals, distinct from the Cauchy sequences system, and demonstrates that this new approach yields the same results as non-standard analysis. An in-depth examination of a specific problem involving a singular curve highlights the equivalence between the three methods for handling removable singularities. The study concludes by highlighting the theoretical superiority of Leibnizian calculus over other forms of analysis, and suggests that a direct comparison between modern mathematical systems and Leibnizian calculus may yield a clearer understanding of the developmental history of calculus. Additionally, the study addresses certain common misconceptions about Leibniz's view on the nature of the infinitesimal and argues that a correct representation of Leibnizian calculus requires a precise mathematical framework, rather than a philosophical interpretation. Finally, the study suggests that a post-Clarkeian reformulation of Leibnizian calculus, incorporating a switch to a Fregean language, results in a system challenging to understand in terms of its modern equivalent, and may have been problematic for communication with contemporary philosophers. The study concludes by observing that a real analysis approach to Leibnizian calculus, although historically informed, does not provide a valid mathematical representation of the concepts involved, and suggests instead a system incorporating smooth infinitesimals as a more accurate approach to understanding Leibnizian calculus. Past research defined persistence as a digraph where each node represents a system state, and the presence of an edge indicates a transition from one state to another is feasible.  In this paper, we revisit persistence in two aspects.  Firstly, we address the issue of state identifiability in observing system characteristics. A substantial body of existing research has demonstrated that any system state with fully observable characteristics can be made a stable equilibrium by employing an appropriate control strategy. A simplified analytical model is derived for the energy distribution of alkali gases in equilibrium, taking into account the principles of quantum statistics and the principles of relativity. This model distinguishes itself from existing approaches through its adherence to sum rules, exactness at zero temperature, and accuracy at high temperatures, all without relying on empirical coefficients. Additionally, the derived energy distribution permits calculation of thermodynamic properties directly from the partition function without requiring numerical integration. Our findings demonstrate that this model accurately predicts the entropy, heat capacity, and van der Waals coefficients of cesium gas, matching numerical simulations based on the hypernetted chain equation of state with an accuracy of up to 30 percent for high temperatures and low pressures. Furthermore, this model's predictions for the free energy, energy, and compressibility of alkali gases conform closely with theoretical values across a broad pressure and temperature range. Our calculations also demonstrate that the phase transition characteristics of these gases can be accurately captured through an analysis of the reduced partition function and an isotherm energy variation ratio. Finally, our simulations reveal that non-relativistic statistical models may yield relativistic energy corrections of up to 10^(-6)eV, necessitating the consideration of relativistic quantum statistics in future studies of stronger magnetic fields. Our study provides a comprehensive assessment of the accuracy of analytical models in describing quantum gases under diverse conditions, offering insights that may be extended to other systems, such as Bose-Einstein and Fermi gases, through analogous modifications of the derived model. Finally, our work is expected to contribute to the development of precise analytical models that may facilitate simulations of quantum mechanics in atomic physics and relativistic quantum field theory.
