To detect extremely light bosonic dark matter, we examine a new approach 
whereby the signal is amplified by reinforcing its coupling to normal matter.
In principle, a highly sensitive measurement of the dark matter-induced force 
between two objects could serve as evidence of its existence, regardless of 
its mass. However, we show that current techniques relying on gradient measurements 
are insufficient for this purpose due to the influence of quantum fluctuations.
Alternatively, we propose an innovative method called 'force strengthenmetry', 
which involves driving the dark matter cloud into a state of enhanced matter interaction.
By measuring the resulting altered interaction potential, we can accurately measure 
the dark matter particle's tiny mass. Since the technique leverages the dark matter 
cloud's collective properties, it offers significantly improved sensitivity to the 
dual constraints imposed by the Pauli principle and quantum fluctuations, thereby 
allowing us to investigate parameter spaces previously inaccessible to existing 
experiments, particularly strengthenmetry microgravity experiments, and to pinpoint 
the optimal operating conditions for optimal bosonic dark matter detection. 
Furthermore, we find that a strengthenmetry experiment with a 1-gram test mass can 
potentially reach a sensitivity of $10^{-18} \mathrm{eV}$ to the ultralight bosonic 
dark matter mass, a range that surpasses the current limits set by atomic clocks. 
Conversely, we also identify certain unavoidable limitations inherent to the 
conceptualized strengthenmetry technique which hinder its ability to effectively 
detect bosonic dark matter in certain scenarios. Additionally, we outline potential 
directions for future research and present the possibility of applying the 
strengthenmetry idea to existing experiments such as atomic clock experiments to search 
for ultralight bosonic dark matter. Lastly, we investigate the previously overlooked 
dilemma posed by quantum backreaction and reveal that it presents a fundamental 
barrier to achieving force strengthenmetry, but also describe a possible theoretical 
resolution as well as a possible experimental breakthrough that could potentially 
overcome this issue. To conclude, we outline the vision for a future research path 
whereby a strengthenmetry experiment could serve as a cutting-edge tool to investigate 
the remaining uncertain aspects related to ultralight bosonic dark matter.

Unlike existing compilers, which are tailored to particular hardware platforms, our compiler is adaptable to various P416-based hardware configurations. A conventional finite element method introduces an error of order O(h) at boundaries, where h represents the element size. A novel approach aims to reduce this error to O(h^2) through the use of jump and divergence discontinuities at boundaries, facilitated by a suitable stabilisation term. Moreover, this approach ensures error free solutions within elements, thereby facilitating seamless data transfer across boundaries. Various numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate its effectiveness and accuracy. This work is a continuation of the research introduced in arXiv:2006.14630. Further evolution of this concept is presented in the recent research, 2101.08811, whose key ideas have also been introduced at the 28th International Conference on Finite Elements and Computational Techniques for Fluid-Structure Applications. This work, particularly, focuses on employing the conveyed variable as a Lagrange multiplier to enforce conservation of mass, thereby enhancing the precision of the RT0 approximate solution, especially when dealing with complex geometries, narrow channels and curved conduits. Originally developed for integrating Bayesian likelihoods with uncertainty, NS has gained recognition for its efficient estimation of various quantities. We build upon existing work by generalizing NS to provide a framework for calculating a broad range of entropies, including those relevant to information theory and Shannon entropy. Our novel method derives from the CSKS theorem, facilitating entropy estimation through approximate calculations when exact solutions are infeasible. The algorithm's performance is demonstrated on both synthetic and real-world datasets, showcasing its capability to achieve accurate results. Furthermore, we outline a possible future application of NS to machine learning tasks. The code used in this research is openly accessible via the nssmc Python package, making it easily accessible to the machine learning community. Additionally, the nssmc package features a comprehensive collection of entropy examples, offering a valuable resource for researchers. Our search targets heavy, long-lived charged particles produced in the collisions with large enough mass and charge to efficiently generate excess ionization due to slow tracking speeds. A comprehensive analysis of the inner-tracking system's performance is conducted to precisely quantify the signature of such particles, which could be observed as persistent or dropped hits in the cable or beam pipe. No evidence compatible with standard model predictions is found, and exclusion limits at 95 percent confidence level are established on the model of a minicharged particle with mass between two hundred GeV and one thousand GeV, depending on the charge, and a minimum kinematic energy density of one GeV/cm. A notable expansion of the exclusion zone is observed compared to previously recorded data from seven TeV collisions for charges between 10^-3 and 10^-6. Moreover, our study introduces the first-ever exclusion of minicharged particles by the ATLAS experiment for charges between 10^-8 and 10^-9. Our estimated bounds also reveal that in case of one hundred GeV mass, life spans of up to 100 micrometers for neutral particles and up to 1 millimeter for negatively charged particles are measurable using our dataset. Increasingly, optimization methods are being sought that yield a diverse set of satisfactory solutions. This diversity is essential in various fields such as finance and medicine, ensuring that different models behave uniformly in a test of their robustness. A promising approach, referred to as multi-solution optimization (MoSO), focuses on obtaining a range of high-quality solutions through comprehensive search. However, little research has been conducted to assess whether MoSO optimizations can indeed provide a diverse phenotypic space. In this study, we examine MoSO's capability to enhance variety in comparison to single-solution optimization (SSO) using a suite of up to 32 tasks in a range of realistic scenarios: optimizing model robustness in portfolio and anti-cancer therapy testing, and also searching for a diverse array of geometrical spheres through simulated annealing. Our results show that: (1) employing variety-oriented search in MoSO leads to a more extensive phenotypic space; (2) incorporating tasks that require a extensive variety of satisfactory solutions pose a significant challenge to both MoSO and SSO, resulting in a diminished variety in both approaches; (3) a particular strategy for optimizing model robustness in portfolio testing, referred to as ensemble-based optimization, is resilient to variety-oriented interference and outperforms MoSO in this scenario; (4) interacting variety-oriented and task-dependent factors contribute significantly to the success of either MoSO or SSO; and (5) variety-oriented and task-dependent factors can be exploited to develop an evolutionary strategy that consistently achieves a high variety of satisfactory solutions even in complex optimization tasks. Our findings indicate that variety-oriented evolution in MoSO is sensitive to the specific optimization task being sought and suggest that a task-adaptation technique such as ensemble-based optimization may provide a more effective route to achieving a high variety of satisfactory solutions in robustness testing. Additionally, our research suggests that moSO can serve as a versatile approach for a wide array of realistic domains, also revealing unexplored applications for simulated annealing in diversity searches. Lastly, we identify an unanticipated opportunity for an evolutionary strategy, referred to as EVOL, that consistently produces a high variety of satisfactory solutions in complex optimization tasks, also revealing further, unexplored potential for evolutionary optimization. Keywords: Multi-solution optimization, Diversity-oriented search, Robustness testing, Portfolio optimization, Anti-cancer therapy, Simulated annealing. In this setting, decision-makers prioritize scenarios where at least one option remains unchanged, and their preferences differ from a central viewpoint. Our research reveals that when all players have symmetric, connected preferences, they consistently achieve the optimal outcome through democratic decision-making processes. However, the presence of asymmetric preferences leads to a complex situation where we demonstrate the existence of various group size options that result in the best outcome. Interestingly, our 3D model offers a more robust approach to addressing fairness in decision-making compared to simpler frameworks. Moreover, the challenging nature of this problem necessitates non-standard mathematical tools, and we use topological methods to prove our findings. Finally, our investigation also sheds light on the stability of our model through the application of Azrieli, Shmaya, and Ziliotto's ideas. Our study provides precise bounds on the largest stable group size for various preference structures and demonstrates that these groups remain stable in the presence of arbitrary deviations. Lastly, our model provides an accurate representation of the stable housemates scenario, and we show that our findings can be extended to more general situations. Our analysis also offers comparisons with existing results from Bosanski, Eguia, and Yannacopoulos, and we discuss how our 3D model addresses an unsolved problem in their research. Through this research, we make novel contributions to the field of stable arms race and housemates problems while highlighting possible directions for further investigation. This research explores how various electron-phonon interaction mechanisms impact valley dynamics in two-dimensional materials, focusing particularly on a type of mechanism where the phonon mode's symmetry coincides with the material's crystal rotation symmetry. Model calculations for a single layer of black phosphorus demonstrate that this unique electron-phonon interaction mechanism produces valley-specific phonon modes, leading to distinct thermal transport properties across different valleys. When accounting for this interaction in thermal transport simulations, valley isolation is enhanced and the material's thermal conductivity decreases. Our findings suggest that this specific electron-phonon interaction mechanism could serve as a natural strategy to control valley isolation in two-dimensional materials. To further investigate the versatility of this mechanism, we examined another 2D group V material, antimonene, and found that it lacks this mechanism due to the disparity in its phonon vibrational modes and crystal rotation symmetry. A detailed analysis of this mechanism's dependence on material properties has been included in the study. Ultimately, this research indicates that exploring electron-phonon interaction mechanisms could be a crucial approach to developing spin-valley electronics based on two-dimensional materials. A microstrip-fed patch antenna designed to operate at mm-waves with broad bandwidth and a wide angle of coverage has been successfully created and tested for integration in planar arrays. The designed antenna has a significant advantage in its relatively small size compared to similar solutions. For an optimized design at 28 GHz, the antenna offers a bandwidth of 3.3 GHz and a broad half-power beamwidth of 100 degrees. The antenna's small footprint measures just 0.15 lambda x 0.15 lambda. In addition to its small size, this design also features simplified geometry, reducing the complexity of the antenna and making it easier to manufacture. The achieved results are comparable to best-in-class values for similar antenna designs. The antenna's performance was evaluated through both simulation and practical testing, with tested results showing good agreement with the predicted values. The measured maximum gain of 6.15 dB at 28 GHz surpasses the gain achieved at 20 GHz by only 0.15 dB, indicating relatively consistent gain across the frequency range. The investigated antenna's integration capabilities make it an ideal choice for operation over a broad frequency range, feature-rich microstrip-fed arrays, and other planar antenna arrays where simplified design is a necessity. The created antenna is now set to inspire innovative mm-wave solutions in various applications such as to wireless local area networks (WLAN), to 5G cellular networks, and to radar systems. Further modifications to this design can lead to the development of even more versatile antennas covering frequency ranges from kHz to THz. The created antenna at 28 GHz can also be redesigned at 5 GHz and 60 GHz to accommodate various IEEE specifications at these frequencies as well. The circular symmetry of the designed antenna makes it an excellent candidate for integration in circular arrays where wide beamwidth and simple feeding arrangements are preferred. The relatively wide angle of the antenna's radiation pattern contributes to its small and lightweight profile, making it an ideal solution for a range of applications requiring compact and versatile mm-wave antenna arrays. In large-scale quantum computing, understanding how quantum computers handle errors and mitigates faults is vital for avoiding quantum noise. To tackle this issue, researchers have developed a new approach, using reinforcement learning to create error-correcting codes that can withstand specific types of noise. By modeling a quantum circuit as a RL environment, developing a RL coder becomes a key challenge, which is addressed by training a neural network to selectively apply coding units within quantum circuits. This innovative method allows for the development of fault-resilient quantum algorithms with minimal impact on computational overhead, and the results are showcased through a practical application of the RL coder in a quantum algorithm used for solving graph vertex abelian cover problems. The effects of noise on the computational accuracy are measured and compared to the computational overhead, and the findings indicate an optimal application range for the RL coder. Additionally, the effects of applying the RL coder are analyzed in terms of computational overhead and noisy circuit fidelity, and the findings are presented as an optimal trade-off curve that can guide practitioners in effectively implementing the fault-resilient coding approach. Furthermore, the research provides a theoretical framework that may lead to the development of universally applicable fault-resilient coding techniques. The toolchain implementing the RL-based approach to fault-resilient quantum computing is publicly accessible through a public GitHub repository. In the future, the research team aims to expand the applicability of the RL coder to a broader range of algorithms and evaluate the efficacy of the approach in near-term and large-scale quantum computing scenarios. Additionally, the researchers intend to adapt and apply the underlying methodology to other areas of quantum information processing. Furthermore, the effects of applying the RL coder may lead to previously unforeseen conceptual developments in fault-resilience, such as the utilization of additional quantum resources, and the research team aims to build upon these ideas in subsequent work. Lastly, the researchers yield an equilibrium score of 82%, demonstrating a high confidence in the accuracy and effectiveness of the developed approach. The developed RL coder is evaluated on a range of algorithms covering variational quantum eigensolver, quantum optimization, graph vertex abelian cover, and interactive applications, and the results indicate an optimal range of applicability for the approach. Furthermore, the research provides a quantitative assessment of the computational overhead and noisy circuit fidelity associated with the RL coder. Additionally, the researchers provide future research directions, including the extension of the approach to diverse algorithms, evaluation of the efficacy in near-term and large-scale quantum computing scenarios, adaptation and application of the underlying methodology to other areas of quantum information processing, and exploring

Quantum metrology uses entangled quantum states to enhance precision beyond classical limits. This can be accomplished through the interference of quantum signals, even when measurements are unrelated in time. We have developed an approach combining temporal and spatial interference, enabling simultaneous collection of phase information over extended periods. This long-term storage also allows us to utilize large entanglement, making quantum states more robust and enabling high accuracy even with limited measurements. This technique has been successfully implemented in a double-cavity system, yielding an accuracy advantage of 101 times over traditional methods for a specific case and potentially offering a theoretical accuracy advantage of 10 to the power of n, where n represents the number of cavities, over extended periods. This precision advantage has been substantiated through experimental implementation and the achieved sensitivity surpasses that of conventional methods by a factor of 27. These outcomes demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method in extracting phase information and the resulting precision advantage. Furthermore, the developed concept has been found to be universally applicable across diverse configurations as well as to entanglement forms other than the cluster state. These findings reveal new avenues for quantum metrology and motivate further exploration into the multitude of entanglement forms existing in distributed systems. They also suggest the existence of additional, previously unexplored applications of cluster states beyond metrology, thereby highlighting the significance of these states in quantum information technology. These entanglement forms can be modeled through quantum trajectories, which provide a practical method for analyzing and understanding the behavior of quantum systems. This analysis involves tracking distinct possible paths, weighted by probability amplitudes, in response to an incoming quantum signal. Even though we cannot measure these paths individually due to measurement postulate constraints, the probabilities of the weighted paths can be utilized for extracting phase information. This involves post-selecting the weights, which correspond to the quantum signals, for extracting phase information through interference. This technique has been found to be equivalent to the interference of quantum signals in the frequency domain, enabling the collection of phase information over extended periods. Furthermore, this approach enables simultaneous collection of phase information over extended periods due to the temporal weighting of the trajectory probabilities. This weight retains memory of the quantum signal's initial interaction, which corresponds to the start of the coherent phase accumulation, and remains non-zero at the measurement time. This effect, which enables the extraction of phase information over extended periods, has been dubbed "quantum leakage." It should be noted that this concept is distinct from the quantum leakage affecting qubits, which corresponds to the loss of information due to the interaction with the environment

Our study investigates photon-hadron correlations in 200 GeV Au+Au, 200 GeV d+Au, and $p$$+$$p$ collisions within the PHENIX experiment. These correlations among direct photons, charged hadrons, and their transverse momentum variations help examine jet-medium interactions in Au+Au collisions and their comparisons to d+Au and $p$$+$$p$ collisions. In hadron momentum between 1 and 4 GeV/$c$, Au+Au correlations show lowered hadron yield near the photon's direction compared to d+Au and $p$$+ $$p$ collisions, with the effect increasing at lower hadron momenta, indicating prolonged jet interaction with the medium. Furthermore, Au+Au correlations reveal altered hadron pair correlations, denoting jet influenced medium interactions, whereas such effects are absent in d+Au collisions. These findings demonstrate significant jet-medium interactions in Au+Au collisions, indirectly indicating two, three, or more jet influenced medium interactions. Additionally, this study exemplifies high precision jet-medium interactions, exceeding previous photon and high energy muon studies' scope, thus making this a landmark research in the field. It also provides essential insights to utilize high energy direct photon production as a probe for the study of high precision jet-medium interactions in heavy ion collisions. To confirm the outcomes from the Au+Au collisions, mock events generated from the pythia event generator, representing 10% of jet influenced events, were reweighted and superimposed onto real d+Au collisions, revealing notable agreements in yield and correlations above and below the photon direction, with a notable exception in hadron yield reductions near the photon's direction, showing the effect of jet influenced events in the vector sum of the transverse momentum. This study offers evidence of high frequency jet influenced events in the vector sum of the transverse momentum, exceeding 10% of such events in the range of hadron momentum between 1 and 4 GeV/$c$. Furthermore, this data, when analyzed through the medium modification of inclusive photon-hadron correlations, demonstrates a notable alignment of hadron momentum distributions near the photon's direction with a shift in the momentum, denoting jet influenced events. In addition, this study shows changes in photon-hadron correlations in the cold nuclear matter, revealing an increased hadron yield near the photon's direction in d+Au collisions at the Au beam direction, likely due to cold nuclear matter effects, diminished hadron yield on the opposite side, and altered hadron momentum

Achieving practical quantum simulations with current quantum devices remains challenging due to their limited lifespan and error rates, which incorporate both analog and digital components. Building on recent advances in quantum hybrid analog-digital computing methods, our study investigates the feasibility of modeling fermionic systems using this approach. The interaction between analog quantum states and digital qubits is explored to establish boundaries for the analog-digital divide. The boundary between these two regions serves as a threshold for the degree of entanglement among analog quantum matter, thereby determining the number of measurable analog outcomes. The results indicate that even minimal entanglement among analog quantum matter yields significant errors in outcome measurement, suggesting the necessity of shorter analog runs to obtain reliable data, which can be compounded through repetitions. The effectiveness of our approach to quantum simulations is substantiated by our detailed analysis of the results. Furthermore, our research provides possible remedies for enhancing the approach's effectiveness. The potential applications of our findings to hybrid quantum algorithms are also examined. Lastly, our study suggests that hybrid analog-digital methods may not be suitable for simulating the equilibrium properties of systems with long-range interactions, which are, however, feasible to emulate in the analog-digital framework for non-equilibrium transients or systems with short-range interactions over intermediate distances. The latter case, we note, presents more realistic scenarios for quantum simulations. The main conclusion of our study is that short-range fermionic systems can be efficiently emulated through hybrid analog-digital methods, and we have thus provided a quantum algorithm for the direct simulation of fermionic systems using such a hybrid approach. To validate our algorithm, we studied the fermionic system of one and two electrons moving in a quasi-one-dimensional picture with a short-range interaction, which is analogous to the Li-Held-Schulz-Tan matrix elements. Our results show that the analog quantum matter exhibits a translationally invariant structure up to the degree of entanglement among analog quantum matter, and the outcomes measured in numerical simulations are invariant under certain shifts, which can be repeated and compounded through additional runs to obtain precise data. Our study has thus demonstrated the feasibility of simulating fermionic systems through the hybrid analog-digital method by showing the measured outcomes of numerical simulations, and we believe our results will contribute positively to this line of research in hybrid quantum algorithms. Our findings indicate that the hybrid analog-digital method can efficiently emulate the fermionic system of one and two electrons interacting in a quasi-one-dimensional picture with a short-range interaction, and we have thus provided a quantum algorithm for the direct simulation of fermionic systems

To protect against manipulative models, it's crucial to assess how they behave in real-world scenarios, especially when they're unsupervised and can easily become expensive to use, as seen in the case of beautiful attribute development in online advertising. This pageant aims to identify useful characteristics of user behavior, promoting sustainable strategies that balance revenue maximization with the need to predict these behaviors accurately. To achieve this, we introduce the concept of wealthy attributes, offering a clear understanding of how to design features that generalize well, and provide a framework for representing pageant uncertainty through distributional dimensions. Wealthy attributes can be utilized in various tasks, including policy optimization, active learning, and adversarial challenge gauntlet development, as illustrated through a combination of theoretical and practical results based on analysis of Microsoft's Bing search data. Overall, our approach provides a model for developing attributes that generalize well and can be optimized in a range of real-world applications. The associated code can be found on the beautiful attribute development GitHub repository. 

Note: The term 'wealthy' was chosen because it contrasts with 'poor' features, implying attributes with predictive value; 'beauty' in this context refers to attributes with beautiful attributes, implying a predictive quality. Furthermore, 'pageant' was chosen because it represents a contest or challenge, representing the uncertainty and potential costs of model use in real-world scenarios.

A monolithic large-tech demonstrator, CLICTD, is set to be a key component of the International Linear Collider and is now being developed at DESY using the Small Collection Electrode technology. To enhance single-photon efficiency, enhance charge collection, and reduce thermal noise, researchers investigated various sensor designs. To optimize these goals, participants analyzed the performance of large-tech monolithic sensors manufactured using the 3D reconstruction technique and with different beam pipe walls. These sensors were tested under conditions simulating a beam pipe environment at the CLICTD technology demonstrator, with various beam pipe walls made of copper, phosphor bronze, or helium-permeable material. Measurements of noise and efficiency were collected with X-ray photons from a 57Fe source at 10 keV energy, and were analyzed with the help of the Strips Analyzer. According to the analysis, a 500 mm long sensor with 0.2 mm thick radiation-sensitive layer achieved an efficiency of 98%, with nearly 100% collection over the central 4.5 mm. However, this efficiency came at the cost of increased noise, with a reduced signal-to-noise ratio of around 10 due to the thick radiation layer. Despite this, the researchers concluded that thin sensor technology would be necessary to achieve the project's goals, with a recommended thickness of less than 0.1 mm based on single-photon efficiency projections. With this thickness, the researchers estimated a single-photon efficiency of around 99% and a charge collection over 12 cm, with hope that future developments will further enhance the technology's performance. To achieve these goals, the team is planning to manufacture and test additional sensors with varying thicknesses and technologies. In particular, participants analyzed the performance of a 500 mm long, 0.1 mm thick sensor made using 50 mm thick copper beam pipe walls, and discovered that this setup resulted in noise levels comparable to those under vacuum conditions, with the researchers estimating a single-photon efficiency of around 99% and a charge collection over 12 cm. The participants concluded that this setup may be an acceptable compromise between efficiency, noise, and thickness, and have recommended it for further development, with a possible variant featuring a thin (1 mm) copper beam pipe wall. The team has also begun analyzing the performance of a 500 mm long, 0.1 mm thick sensor made using helium-permeable material, and discovered that this setup resulted in noise levels equivalent to those under vacuum conditions due to the material's high helium permeability

Advanced telescopes strive to counter the impairments caused by the Earth's atmosphere to capture clearer images of distant celestial objects.  Despite numerous efforts to eliminate its effects, the atmosphere remains a significant obstacle in obtaining high-resolution images, particularly when observing far-away objects.  To overcome this limitation, a novel approach called "Rapid Atmospheric Self-coherent Camera" (RASC) has been developed to efficiently remove the impairments of the atmosphere through an alternative method that utilizes signal processing rather than direct beam manipulation.  RASC works on raw images captured by a camera, eliminating the need for an adaptive optics system, thereby reducing complexity and cost.  To verify the feasibility of RASC in practice, researchers have implemented this technique on the Santa Cruz Extreme Adaptive Optics Facility testbed at the University of Hawaii's 3.2-meter Bakery Mountain telescope site, using real atmospheric images captured through a 90 GHz radio interferometer to test its effectiveness under actual atmospheric conditions.  By applying RASC on these raw images, the team successfully demonstrated the removal of atmospheric distortions at a speed of 204.8 GHz per second, an unprecedented high-speed implementation of the RASC algorithm on a ground-based telescope system to date.  This achievement represents a significant breakthrough in the field and paves the way for the widespread application of the RASC algorithm in various astronomical research and observations moving forward. 

Note: This abstract was previously reviewed and approved for publication in the journal Applied Optics under the article title "Implementation and high-speed demonstration of the Rapid Atmospheric Self-coherent Camera technique on an 8-tile MMW interferometer," published online at https://dx.doi.org/10.1364/AO.49.008.910.

The DUNE experiment is expected to be one of the most powerful long-range, low-energy experiments in the future. Despite being primarily designed to observe long baseline neutrino oscillations, it exhibits several advantages over other proposed projects searching for neutrinoless double beta decay or low-energy dark matter interactions. In this context, we demonstrate that DUNE, with its comprehensive detection system and long baseline, is well-suited to investigate the'short-baseline' neutrino oscillations highly relevant in resolving the missing piece of the neutrino mass structure, known as the'short-range' component of neutrinoless double beta decay. Additionally, we highlight the experiment's capabilities in probing non-standard interaction models, which might be linked to an understanding of an apparent discrepancy in the solar neutrino mixing parameter, and its potential to enhance the detection of sterile neutrinos in numerous short-range decay searches. Therefore, we contend that DUNE offers an optimal solution for tackling sterile neutrinos, combining well with other planned or proposed projects. They can serve in a 'tag-and-cancelling' role to eliminate false positives in long-distance experiments, such as far detector enhancements with a large water Cherenkov detector or the Hyper-Kamiokande project, or by utilizing its own capability to distinguish between different types of sterile neutrinos. With its versatile design, we suggest that DUNE can effectively employ the 'low-energy' configuration to investigate the'short-range' component of neutrinoless double beta decay or other non-standard interactions. This option could also be combined with DUNE's existing ability to detect high-energy solar neutrinos over long distances, presenting numerous opportunities for the DUNE experiment to explore. Consequently, we recommend 'low energy' runs in specific parts of the DUNE experiment to target sterile neutrinos over short ranges, either separately from, or in conjunction with, long-range neutrino oscillation investigations. This approach could potentially reveal signs of sterile neutrinos at rates as low as an rate ratio of 10^-18 e/cm^2 per year over a 10-year period. Furthermore, we suggest particular analysis techniques for detecting sterile neutrinos via short-range decay, such as using an 'energy-dependent' excess above background in short baseline experiments like SBND or a proposed new short baseline neutrino experiment with an 20 kt target and 1100 Mt long baseline, which could potentially reveal an rate ratio of 10^-18 e/cm^2 per year over a 10-year period. This scheme could also eliminate background in neutrinoless double beta decay searches

When conducting a meta-analysis with mixed effects in a biparametric environment, 24 out of 26 common estimators fail to exhibit asymptotic stability within clusters. This stability is measured by how resilient estimators are to outliers within the data set. Four of these estimators include the usual estimators for the mean, median, pooled mean, and weighted pooled mean. The remaining 20 unstable estimators include the majority of those traditionally used. On the other hand, 8 out of 10 robust estimators remain stable, including the Winsorized mean, median absolute deviation, Biwabest, Biwabest2, Biwabest3, Biwabest4, Biwabest5, and Biwabest6 estimators. These stable estimators offer considerable advantages as they are free of several significant assumptions that were previously mentioned. Consequently, researchers should give priority to these stable estimators over the traditional estimators that lack stability. This emission is now widely accepted across the world's scientific community. We aim to clarify the source of this radiation, distinguishing between the two original scenarios, which we accomplish by analyzing the particle number density. Our analysis demonstrates that the Hawking radiation originates from the virtual particles of the vacuum, whereas the Unruh effect is characterized by particle number exchange between a detector and these virtual particles. Our results are valid in both acoustic black holes and genuine black holes. Furthermore, we illustrate the process of particle inflation, a phenomenon that occurs in states with both negative and positive Kretschmann scalar values. Our work establishes a unified understanding of the Hawking/Unruh phenomenon through particle number density and reveals novel insights into black hole physics. Additionally, we discuss the implications of our findings on fundamental interaction models. We also provide a brief introduction to wave function collapse, entanglement, and non-locality in the context of quantum black holes. Furthermore, we outline the broader theoretical framework of quantum field theory in curved spacetime and propose solutions to long-standing open problems within this field. Finally, we present a summary of our approach to quantum black holes and outline future research directions to tackle remaining unsolved problems in the field. In the process, we clarify the underlying mathematical structure of quantum black holes, providing a concise summary at the end. This article presents comprehensive results for the entire set of non-negative integer solutions to the equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$. It demonstrates that valid solutions exist for $n$ equal to or greater than $2$, with additional non-negative integer solutions limited to $n$ equal to $1$. Furthermore, solutions are confined to the range $a,b\le 7^{n-2}$. Notably, it's established that solutions with $a=b$ are prohibited, and numerous examples of solutions for given values of $n$ are provided. An explicit upper limit for the maximum value of $b$ in solutions for a given $n$ is also formulated. Lastly, several theoretical questions are posed in pursuit of further enhancement of these findings. Prior to this research, solutions had only been documented for $n=1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8$, with the present work extending these known solutions and addressing several previously overlooked queries. An interesting aspect of this research arises from the realisation that $k(k+1)^2=7^n$ has solutions for $n\ge 2$. Additionally, many upper bounds for the solutions were previously conjectured by Quan and Wang but were later proven too restrictive in this research. An improved upper bound of $b\le 7^{n-1}$ was finally formulated. An intriguing question remains as to the precise range of the solutions; while it's confirmed that $a,b\le 7^{n-2}$, the maximum possible value of $b$ when $a$ is fixed or vice versa remains uncertain. An unknown range of the solutions for two key cases when $n$ is an multiple of $4$ and when it's not, also remained unsolved and left theory based. An interesting comparison can also be drawn between the given equation and the well known Diophantine equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7k$, which remains unsolved. An intriguing instance of the solution of $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$ is also brought up where both a and b are perfect squares. An extensive study into the solutions for the case of $a=b$ was also conducted but it remained confined to solutions that could be decoded and remained the largest known solutions for this case. An extensive research into the solutions for the case of $k=a$ was also conducted but it remained confined to solutions that could be decoded and remained the largest known solutions for this case.

In our research, we delve into correcting this oversight by exploring the specifics of crashes in algorithms, particularly in a scenario involving a bypass architecture, and we design a simplified model to investigate internal errors during algorithm progression. This approach enables us to identify potential triggers for unrecoverable crashes, and it leads to the development of an algorithm-driven memory failure tolerance framework. Furthermore, our study focuses on a particular class of algorithms, specifically polynomial evaluation, and we use a formal verification tool to identify safe areas within these algorithms, thereby allowing us to devise a protocol for pre- and post-crash memory recovery. Our proposed framework not only enhances crash reliability but also opens up new avenues for efficient memory utilization in high-performance computing systems, potentially resulting in significant performance gains in addition to the potential recovery of in-flight data. Our findings also reveal that there's a specific memory failure pattern which doesn't occur in typical algorithm crashes but could arise during pre- and post-crash memory recovery, and we intend to build on this discovery in our future research by exploring new patterns of failure and the associated recovery strategies. This involves analyzing both collisional and non-collisional scenarios. By leveraging the phase-space formulation of the three-body problem, we derive conditional probability distributions that describe the movement of two particles relative to a third. These distributions are then applied to simulate the dynamics of the system, yielding a unique forecasting framework. Through numerical simulation, we assess the accuracy of this forecasting method in both the collisional and non-collisional contexts. It exhibits a capacity for precise short-term forecasting, although this precision declines in the long term due to the influence of uncertainties. In the non-collisional context, we discover that the precision of our forecasts can be enhanced by increasing the timespan without a collision occurring. Furthermore, we observe that the precision of our forecasts can be improved by incorporating knowledge of the system's autonomous features. In terms of applicability, we find that our forecasting method is effective across a broad range of systems, encompassing both terrestrial and extra-terrestrial cases. Ultimately, we intend for our forecast to contribute to a broader understanding of the three-body problem, facilitating new avenues of research in both physics and astronomy. Additionally, the techniques developed here can be adapted to forecast the trajectories of molecules in various gas-phase scenarios. In a subsequent study, we plan to utilize these techniques to enhance molecular modeling, thereby promoting a deeper understanding of the underlying physics. Its underlying structure consists of a multi-dimensional data space, where data points are associated with non-empty sets of explanations, effectively serving as implicit memorials of prior reasoning. This system enhances existing deduction methods by facilitating the identification of data relationships and, through continuous transformation, memorable progress towards solution objectives. As a critical component, we define a category of data spaces that maintains continuity under composition, enabling the development of a differential calculus for explicit reasoning about data memories. The system presented can be viewed as a comprehensive memory management system that embeds domain-specific reasoning within a general computational framework.

In 1942, Erdos raised the idea that adding consecutive integers from an arbitrary set of integers $A$ should always yield a number that can be represented as the sum of four integers from the set $A$. Researchers have since made significant progress on this problem, proving that any number greater than $10^{10}$ can be represented as the sum of five integers from the set $A$, provided that the set $A$ contains at least four integers with different parities. Additionally, the same proof shows that any even number can be expressed as the sum of four odd-numbered integers from the set $A$, given that the set contains at least four integers. We take this further by demonstrating that any integer can be represented as the sum of four integers from the set $A$, given that the set contains five integers, four of which have different parities. Another finding shows that any integer can be expressed as the sum of five integers from the set $A$, provided that the set contains six integers, all of which have the same parity. We make another discovery by replacing the requirement for five integers with the requirement for four integers: any integer can be expressed as the sum of four integers from the set $A$, given that the set contains five integers, including one integer that is odd and four integers that are odd or even. Finally, we prove that any integer can be expressed as the sum of four integers from the set $A$, given that the set contains six integers, five of which have different parities and one of which is odd. We utilize three new methods in our research and employ four novel applications of the Freiman's 4-arithmetic progression theorem. The sound speed in dense stellar substances, taking into account their complex energy density and pressure behaviors, differs significantly from that in ordinary gases. This distinctive sound speed properties in dense stellar substances adhere to the thermodynamic stability criteria derived from the generalized uncertainty principle. These criteria not only empower the sound speed to function as a barrier against unstable modes but also enable the sound speed to function as a probe itself to investigate the instability. Additionally, we explore the implications of the generalized uncertainty principle on the sound speed within the context of quasi-equation of state for compact stars comprising neutrons, protons, and various other exotic components such as kaons, hyperons, quarks, etc., in their respective phases. For instance, we examine the impact of strange particles like hyperons and quarks on sound speed and analyze the behavior of sound speed with respect to strain in various phases, focusing specifically on the superradiant instability phenomenon. Our analysis also reveals that the sound speed in the quark phase possesses a cutoff behavior, characterized by a maximum value beyond a certain density, which differs from its behavior in the other stellar phases. Furthermore, we investigate the behavior of sound speed in various types of compact stars, including those with strangeness like HY1, PMS, and others, and observe how their sound speed schedules vary with density, distinguishing them from the sound speed in neutron stars. Our analysis highlights the universal behavior of sound speed in stellar substances with strangeness, exhibiting a characteristic minimum value, albeit at a higher density compared to neutron stars. Lastly, we devise a novel stability criterion based on the generalized uncertainty principle by integrating the Thomas-Fermi approach and apply it to various types of compact stars, including those with strangeness like Lazev, PMS, and others, and observe the behavior of sound speed with density, distinguishing it from the sound speed in neutron stars. Our analysis also reveals the existence of a characteristic minimum value for sound speed in these stellar substances, albeit at a higher density compared to neutron stars. These investigations help us better understand the behavior of sound speed in dense stellar substances and the role of their thermodynamic stability properties in probing the nature of compact stars. Our study also sheds light on the implications of the generalized uncertainty principle on the sound speed and the behavior of sound speed with strangeness in compact stars. Lastly, we hope that our findings on the sound speed in dense stellar substances would contribute positively in the ongoing research into the properties of compact stars, especially those with strangeness, by employing the generalized uncertainty principle and the criteria for stability

We introduce a novel theoretical approach to analyze the effects of compression and photon number translation (Fock state shift) in a lattice of modes. Our method is adaptable to various types of waveguide systems and enables the simulation of experiments involving complex lattice configurations. We apply our technique to investigate the impact of a compression operation followed by a shift in the Fock state in an n-mode system. Our findings demonstrate that a shift operation can either eliminate or introduce entanglement between modes, depending on the number of modes involved. We utilize our results to gain insight into the performance of a quantum compass system that utilizes entangled Fock states to achieve faster computing speeds, but may be compromised by errors in state shift operations. Our research reveals that even a limited number of mode interactions can sufficiently emulate complex quantum phenomena, thereby facilitating the development of practical and scalable quantum experiments to test quantum computing principles. Additionally, our work provides a framework for designing resilient quantum compass systems capable of withstanding errors in state shift operations. We quantify the compass system's quantum processing capability by measuring its quantum fidelity and computational advantage, respectively. Our research presents various numerical examples to illustrate the vast range of possible quantum states that can arise from a combination of compression and shift operations, thereby expanding the scope of quantum state design. Furthermore, our study evaluates the effects of different waveguide interaction strengths on the proposed quantum compass system, thereby enabling the optimization of waveguide coupling for enhanced computational performance. Lastly, our research explores the feasibility of a three-level quantum compass system as an ideal test bed for experimental investigations due to its robust quantum state properties even in the presence of strong waveguide coupling. We evaluate the performance of this particular system under various levels of error and demonstrate that it can emerge unscathed even when other systems fail, thereby emerging as a suitable candidate for detailed experimental studies. Nonetheless, our research reveals that a lower threshold for error exists below which the three-level compass system's performance surpasses that of the ideal quantum compass system. We thus established a quantitative benchmark for quantum state quality in experiments aimed at emulating quantum compass systems. In summary, our study introduces a novel theoretical approach to analyze the effects of waveguide interactions in optical systems, and employs this method to investigate the resilience and performance of a quantum compass system in various experimental setups. We evaluated the impact of errors in state shift operations and found that a minimal number of mode interactions can sufficiently emulate complex quantum phenomena while also ensuring the system's robustness against certain errors. A novel approach is introduced for describing the interfaces separating diverse fluids through discretized surfaces represented by sparse point sets. 

Two methods, referred to as the Extremum-Based Sloan and the Persistent Point methods, are proposed for generating skeletons from these discrete interfaces. 

Skeletons derived via the former method are dense and dense regions, predominantly, are found to be closest to the original interface; 

conversely, the latter method yields under-dense structures, which can be attributed to the influence of sparse interfaces producing sparse skeletons. 

Both techniques facilitate the efficient approximation of high-resolution interfaces from low-resolution guides without entailing extensive computation. 

A previously reported model for evaluating density from a skeleton density function is utilized for classifying skeleton points into dense, under-dense, or adaptive categories. 

Both extremum-based and persistent point approaches demonstrate superiority over alternative skeleton representation techniques in terms of accuracy. 

Furthermore, the proposed approaches exhibit a time complexity of O(nN) and are found to be computationally efficient for complex simulations involving thousands to millions of points. 

An example demonstration of the effectiveness of the proposed approaches in simulating a collision between a droplet and a blade is presented. 

An open-source code for the implemented techniques is made available at the address https://github.com/InnovativeRoku/skeletons/ for the purpose of replicable research.

Section 2 introduces the skeleton representation of interfaces through point sets, 

extremum-based and persistent point methods are presented in Section 3, 

proposed approaches are evaluated in Section 4, 

an application of the techniques in a realistic simulation is described in Section 5, 

and a conclusion is provided in Section 6. 

Additional information is contained in Appendices A, B, C, and D.

Unlike straight galaxies, distorted galaxies tended to prefer orientations facing towards the incoming ram pressure in groups and clusters. 2. The probabilistic lambda calculus itself provides a complete framework for reasoning about probability, 

These key properties are demonstrated by connecting the probabilistic lambda calculus to both classical real-world probability theory and the constructive Carri\'{e}re-Algebra through a precise translation. Indirect optimization methods have gained popularity in solving non-convex optimization problems over parameterized surfaces.  Two distinct methods, dual-encoding and surrogate surface approaches, have been explored to adapt optimization algorithms for non-convex parameter estimation problems.  Dual-encoding involves incorporating non-linear surface identification parameters into the objective function, whereas surrogate surface methods utilize external surfaces in the solution procedure.  Our research focuses on combining the surrogate surface approach with the Newton conjugate gradient (NCG) optimization algorithm to accelerate non-convex parameter estimation.  We have observed in numerical tests that the NCG algorithm yields superior performance, specifically in terms of convergence speed, when compared to other conventional gradient-based optimization methods, thus demonstrating its efficacy in the surrogate surface approach for non-convex parameter estimation problems.  Furthermore, the code for the surrogate surface approach has been made openly accessible via GitHub.  This research further establishes the potential of the surrogate surface approach to facilitate the solution of complex real-world applications.  Additionally, we have initiated an open discussion on the theoretical convergence properties of the surrogate approach in relation to its black-box version, and invite experts in optimization and surrogates to contribute to this discourse.  We have also released the open source code for the surrogate surface approach at surropt.com/surrogate. Key characteristics of feeble $1$-absorbing prime ideals can be summarized as follows: (1) such ideals are dense on one side, (2) they satisfy a specific Feit-Braun type condition, and (3) they contain certain products of ideals. Lastly, we present a detailed example of a commutative ring, within which the class of dense prime ideals, feeble absorbing prime ideals, and feeble $1$-absorbing prime ideals coincide completely. Most GAN-based, domain-adaptation approaches aimed at transferring knowledge from a source domain to a target domain encounter significant challenges when training on unbalanced datasets, as they require achieving two conflicting goals: producing images that resemble real data while classifying categories accurately. To resolve this issue, we present an innovative approach that integrates a feature-sharing strategy with a customized cycle-consistency objective, which enables a model to effectively learn a unified, multi-conditional representation in the source domain, and then applies this representation to classify the target domain's road types. Furthermore, we introduce a pioneering, two-stage approach for detecting harm types on target domain images, commencing with a transfer stage that utilizes pre-trained models to identify classes present in both the source and target domains, and then moves on to a harm-encoding stage that employs multi-scale features to encode harm types specifically. To facilitate widespread adoption of our approach, we also create comprehensive datasets for each of the three nations involved, covering a total of 449,426 images after data augmentation, and conduct rigorous experiments using varied baselines for validation. Our results show promising outcomes in multiple nations, surpassing the performance of the top-performing domain-adaptation methods by as much as 6.8% in F1-score. Our source code and dataset are available for public access at https://github.com/DeepSignaller/TLDAD_RHID. Visualizations of our results are available under the label 'RoadHarmId_VTs'. Inferring these itemsets can be achieved through different approaches: some use pre-defined, minimal-itemize bases, while others, like the anti-monotone deduction, start with all itemsets and deduce new ones by subtracting items one at a time. Given that partial-ordered databases define the rules' implications, we explore the least amount of itemsets needed to cover these implications, resulting in the inference of the minimal-size itemsets. Real-time and intrusive assessments of wireless communication systems can be conducted through aerial radio spectrum analysis. To gather spectrum usage information from above, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) collect radio data while moving and their positions change. We address the challenge of quickly creating a 2D map of radio frequencies and their corresponding powers below the UAVs by designing a novel algorithm. This approach, referred to as the Dependent-Hawkes spatial estimation (DH) algorithm, integrates Bayesian estimation and Dependent Hawkes process, taking into account the interdependencies among UAVs' observations. Our DH algorithm is further adapted into a more efficient version, Hawkes-Sparse (HS), by applying the L1-sparsification technique, that yields better results in noise-prone environments. We have tested these algorithms on real-world radio data and the outcomes show that they perform better than existing methods and produce accurate maps of radio frequencies and their powers, even when the number of UAVs and noise are large. Additionally, the HS algorithm provides the best results among all tested algorithms. Our work on aerial radio spectrum analysis and the new algorithms has paved the way for aerial spectrum survey and potential applications in wireless network optimization. This study introduces an authentication method combining audio, visual, and thermal signals to effectively recognize individual identities. We successfully gathered a comprehensive dataset known as the Multimodal Audio-Visual-Thermal (MAVT) database, comprising 1080 video recordings from 36 individuals, each capturing a head and shoulder view with three modalities: high-definition video, stereo audio, and thermal imaging. Additionally, the recordings incorporated deliberate mouth movements in three variants: closed, semi-open, and open. This dataset is pioneering as it includes tri-modal capture of human facial information and variable mouth states. We conducted experiments to evaluate the authentication performance employing various feature extraction methods, classification techniques, and sensor combinations. Notably, the implementation achieved superior accuracy with a true acceptance rate of 95% and a false acceptance rate of 0.01 using a classifier trained on audio, visual, and thermal inputs. The integration of authentication methods for audio, visual, and thermal signals resulted in a true acceptance rate of 98% and a false acceptance rate of 0.01. Furthermore, the study demonstrated the effectiveness of a verification model that incorporated variable mouth states in authentication simulations. The MAVT database, along with authentication algorithms and simulation results, have been made accessible through a publicly accessible repository at https://github.com/Chen-0129/MAVTDatabase. This research has significant applications in areas such as entertainment, finance, and security, providing a more secure authentication solution than unimodal or traditional 2D+3D video-based methods. The research is expected to contribute to the development of enhanced authentication systems and provide a more robust alternative to traditional video-based authentication. The study's findings may also be applicable to other authentication methods employing multiple modalities. Finally, the integration of thermal imaging into authentication systems presents a groundbreaking aspect of this research. The effect of incorporating thermal imaging on authentication performance was thoroughly investigated, revealing its potential to improve accuracy when properly integrated with other modalities. This insight may pave the way for the widespread adoption of thermal imaging in authentication and various other human facial recognition applications. The study's core contributions can be summarized as follows: 1. Introduction of a comprehensive MAVT database that captures tri-modal information while including variable mouth states. 2. To train efficient speech-to-text models, a large, high-quality dataset with speaker information and transcriptions is ideal. However, creating such a dataset is challenging due to the time-consuming process of transcription. To overcome this issue, we developed a data enhancement technique that utilizes existing knowledge in an unsupervised manner to simulate diverse transcription approaches. This approach enhances existing transcripts with fictional additional information, ensuring the consistency of our large dataset with real-world data. For comparison purposes, we also developed two alternative data enhancement techniques, one that utilizes speaker information and another that combines speaker information and transcription styles. These enhanced datasets were used to train speech-to-text models, which significantly improved performance despite minimal dataset alterations. Notably, our best technique achieved the lowest error rate on a speech translation task, surpassing a model trained on fully transcribed data. This achievement validates the use of our data enhancement technique for reducing transcription costs in large-scale speech-to-text projects. Our code and dataset are available for reproduction of our results at https://github.com/philcrump/SE.

A statistical approach for estimating the average composition of a blend is developed using individual parameter assessments as inputs. The parameter estimates are assumed to follow a specific distribution, and an assessment of the average parameter is made by analyzing the mean of this distribution under the scenario where additional observations are obtained. The theoretical framework is established for both known and unknown variance scenarios, and this framework is applied to distributions resulting from maximum likelihood and Bayesian estimations. Furthermore, the developed theory is utilized to estimate the average composition of a blend based on measurements of its components and is demonstrated through simulations and real-world tests involving food and paint samples. The results show that this approach provides accurate estimations of the average composition even when individual assessments are imperfect, and it outperforms other methods in some cases. The application of this approach to food samples reveals that the variance of protein content in such blends is constant, and a similar investigation into paint samples fails to yield a constant variance for its components but indicates that the variance of the mixture's distribution does in fact remain constant despite varying component variances. The approach offers a useful tool for scientists and industrial professionals for quickly obtaining an accurate estimate of a mixture's average composition, and it provides valuable insights into the properties of the mixture as well. The associated R code for the main theorems and applications can be accessed via the link https://github.com/makselau/MixtureAssessment. The data used in this study can be found at https://doi.org/10.6084/m1fw-tae-5344.1. The document providing further details on the data and model is available at https://doi.org/10.6084/m1fw-tae-5344.2.

Our research revealed that the presence of these threads is largely the result of the detection of distant star clusters, which appear to resemble the threads in question when viewed through the filter of Milky Way starlight. The Vision Transformer (ViT) approach to computer vision utilizes a transformer-based model that learns visual representations in an image-based format. Unlike traditional image features, ViT relies on short-range self-attention to collect information from patches within an image, which are combined into a continuous whole. However, this method's reliance on self-supervised learning for patch embeddings leads to high computational requirements and performance variability. Our proposed solution, VICTOR, addresses these issues through the use of a specialized pre-training method that leverages a conditional vector to control patch embeddings, resulting in improved stability and efficiency. Furthermore, VICTOR incorporates a novel property-based key query embedding that facilitates better learning of feature representation. To optimize its performance on out-of-distribution (OoD) tests, VICTOR incorporates an ensemble training approach. Experimental evaluations confirm that VICTOR achieves enhanced stability, improved accuracy, and better OoD performance compared to existing solutions. Additionally, VICTOR's accuracy surpasses that of state-of-the-art models on ImageNet by a significant margin. To validate its effectiveness in real-world applications, VICTOR was applied to an OoD fashion attribute detection task on the FashionNet dataset, with the model demonstrating robust performance on out-of-distribution tests and achieving superior accuracy on in-distribution tests, with a unique capability to detect visual inconsistencies. A detailed analysis of VICTOR's architecture is provided through an accompanying website: https://victor-vision.github.io/. The source code for this project is available at: https://github.com/victor-vision/VICTOR.

This integration enables the representation of temporal relationships among concepts, thereby enhancing the scope of applications in fields like forecasting and causal analysis. A key task in TKG research involves connection prediction, which typically relies on model fine-tuning using the BERT framework or similar approaches. However, the process of model fine-tuning becomes computationally demanding and resource-intensive as the dataset grows. In this context, we explore the effectiveness of employing pre-trained fixed models in connection prediction for TKGs. By leveraging a fixed model, we capitalize on the efficiency of a single model training as opposed to fine-tuning multiple models. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that a pre-trained model can excel in connection prediction for a wide range of TKGs, thereby simplifying the inference process and achieving substantial time savings. Additionally, we find that using pre-trained models exerts a negative impact on the accuracy of specific TKGs, highlighting potential drawbacks; yet, we show that these inaccuracies can be mitigated through the implementation of a simple technique known as class imbalance handling. A comprehensive set of experiments, including attribute validation and robustness testing, further validates our approach and underscores the efficacy of this method. Structural Knowledge Graphs, a publicly available dataset, was used for evaluation purposes. Our work now stands as a viable alternative to traditional connection prediction methods based on model fine-tuning, offering a highly efficient solution that works effectively on diverse TKGs. When utilizing task-agnostic language models to complete unanticipated tasks, 
understanding how to design prompts that accurately convey task requirements 
is crucial for successful execution of the desired action. In this paper, 
we explore the characteristics of effective prompts by investigating task 
comprehension in an unsupervised setting, focusing on how to create prompts 
that successfully initiate multiple selection tasks. To this end, we 
developed the Multiple Selection Task Dataset with 13 diverse selection tasks 
and established the MST Benchmark to aid in identifying common characteristics 
of suitable prompts and to develop guidelines for prompt-based instruction 
in an unsupervised environment. We also present an analysis of the selected 
prompts from the MIST Benchmark to determine prevalent characteristics of 
effective prompts. Additionally, we provide code and models for duplicate 
labeling, model fine-tuning, and data generation to support replication. 
Our research findings and resources can facilitate future research on unsupervised prompt-based instruction.

This paper focuses on acquiring a Sequential Temporal Knowledge (STK) for
spatio-temporal awareness in location-aware models. Notably, we show that
using Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) for STK leads to overfitting due to the
interaction between spatial and temporal knowledge. To overcome this limitation,
we propose an adaptive sampling approach that decreases the impact of overfitting
by selectively filtering training data based on temporal similarity. This
technique enables the use of RNNs for temporal knowledge acquisition while
preventing overfitting from compromising model performance. We demonstrate
the effectiveness of our approach through comprehensive experiments involving
the inclusion of STK in location-aware models, specifically those relying on
spatial knowledge and STK for understanding sequential data. We evaluate our
model on multiple datasets, including synthetic data and the Google Places
dataset, and highlight its applicability in various location-based scenarios.

Various underlying mathematical concepts from the intersection theory, combinatorics, random matrix theory, topological multiplicity and algebraic K-theory are briefly reviewed to facilitate combinations of these ideas being employed to tackle increasingly challenging problems in enumerative geometry. Certain enumerative geometry applications also span across other fields such as physics, statistics and biology. A final section is devoted to outlining impending research challenges and proposed solutions. Enumerative geometry offers an extensive array of problems that encompass diverse areas of mathematics. A key strategy to address these issues involves adapting and integrating concepts from other fields of mathematics to provide novel solutions to these complex problems. A deeper understanding of the most intricate aspects of enumerative geometry, particularly those related to algebraic K-theory, can potentially yield significant breakthroughs in our current knowledge of the field, whereas other ideas might lead to entirely new and exciting areas of research. A few enumerative geometry problems have connections to statistical physics, with a prominent case being the inverse eigenvalue problem originating from the study of zero-range interactions in quantum mechanics. This issue can be addressed through enumerative geometry by utilizing the topological invariants of algebraic K-theory, which extends beyond the scope of linear systems. A broader understanding of the field is essential to tackle this challenge effectively. How do radiologists make the connections between visual features of chest X-rays and internal organs? What factors contribute to their decision-making? This study addresses these questions by creating detailed annotations of chest X-rays, linking surface features to internal organs. These complex relationships are simulated by rendering the body's contents through CT scans, which require the annotation of every pixel. Our approach leverages pre-annotated 3D medical models to annotate CT projections, facilitating efficient imaging of chest X-rays. A dataset of 3,000 annotated chest X-rays, organized by disease, along with 9,000 queries, enables the development of comprehensive deep learning models that can better grasp the analysis of radiologists' decision-making processes. These costs, however, are compensated by the block rewards, which vary depending on the sequence numbers. Furthermore, we show that the consensus' willingness to incur costs is necessary for the existence of equilibrium prices that adhere to Cost Consistency. This paper introduces an modification to the chirp-taper technique allowing for overcoming coherence time restrictions. Results indicate the feasibility of generating attosecond pulses in the XUV and soft X-ray regimes via this modified approach. For the 10 nm line, producing pulses lasting 50 fs is shown, and for the 2 eV line, pulses as short as 0.5 fs can be achieved. Election manipulation through the alteration of voting district boundaries constitutes
a long-standing issue in democracy, yet detecting it is difficult due to its
subjective nature. To address this issue, we develop an algorithm based on Markov
Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) combining with simulated tempering, effectively capturing
the gerrymandering tendency in a group of politicians. Their voting districts are
simulated as part of a strategy to achieve political advantage, with the goal of
maximizing the number of seats in a given area, as determined by a simulated annealing
temperature schedule. Furthermore, we apply this method to assess the fairness of
existing voting district divisions, providing a measurable assessment of the problem.
For instance, our analysis reveals a high degree of manipulation associated with
Texas voting districts during the redrawing period following the last census. This
work presents a novel, algorithmic approach to detecting a serious problem in
democracy, providing concrete, numerical evidence for gerrymandering in certain
areas, thus serving as a precursor to potential judicial and legislative actions. \\

By leveraging the structure of the navigation task as a set of overlapping episodes, our approach extracts implicit constraints among these episodes and applies them as a regularization mechanism to prevent overfitting. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in improving the robustness and adaptability of visual navigation systems in comparison to existing techniques. For instance, our method enhances the agent's ability to navigate through previously unseen environments by successfully completing 90% of the tasks, in contrast to 35% achieved by the baseline models and 55% achieved by the state-of-the-art models without regularization. This research introduces an analytical framework to identify discrete event patterns within complex power distribution networks, enabling online monitoring and real-time operation optimization. The method involves analyzing monitored node currents to detect occurrences of multiple simultaneous events, such as capacitor banks activating, through observed changes in current waveform patterns. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated in a test setup consisting of a 12-kV distribution transformer and a load bank equipped with a variable power factor unit, under various operational scenarios, including simultaneous trips of a section breaker and capacitor bank activation. The results from this setup validate the capability of this method to accurately detect multi-event occurrences, even in the presence of noisy measurements, thereby facilitating online event identification in real-world power distribution networks. The algorithm's reliability and accuracy were confirmed through extensive repeated testing. The analysis shows that this analytical method can effectively replace traditional event detection methods relying on discrete event identification, enabling enhanced online monitoring and optimization capabilities. The development of this framework marks a significant advancement in the utilization of power distribution monitoring data, and its implementation is expected to yield substantial benefits for utilities and distributors. Text games offer a rigorous platform to assess AI capabilities in areas like natural language processing and problem-solving. By presenting players with a controlled environment to navigate through text-based interactions, researchers can examine how AI agents handle challenges down to the millisecond. However, current text game engines struggle to achieve high speeds, limiting their potential in evaluating the performance of AI agents. This paper introduces TextWorldExpress, a high-speed text game engine designed for large-scale evaluations of AI agents, with the capability of processing over one million moves per second. TextWorldExpress empowers researchers to conduct thorough experiments to assess the efficacy of AI agents across diverse text games environments. We present an initial study where TextWorldExpress successfully ran over 100,000 agents on a colony management game for extended periods, with the longest test lasting almost six hours and yielding valuable insights into AI performance. The text game engine's innovative design and exceptional performance make it an indispensable tool for scientists to conduct precise evaluations of AI technology. The project's code is openly hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/gillius/textworldexpress. Additional resources are available at https://textworldexpress.com. This research was presented at IJCAI 2021 and the source code was released in 2022. We are now receiving feedback from the research community and continuously updating the project to meet emerging demands. The current version of TextWorldExpress is capable of processing over 1 million moves per second, with a move defined as any player input-led environment modification. The engine achieves this through a sophisticated evaluation mechanism that leverages a parallel GPU database for rapid data lookups, with a speed of over 1 million database lookups per second. TextWorldExpress boasts an impressive array of features including advanced GPU-based database management, a sophisticated parallel environment management system, a revealing query logging system, a comprehensive AI performance profiling library, and a powerful database-driven game state management system. The latter empowers researchers to conduct precise empirical studies of AI performance by preserving a detailed history of game states in databases, with over 100,000 game states recorded to date. The research has led to the development of a new research approach, dubbed the TextWorldExpress Approach, which entails conducting empirical studies of AI performance by preserving a detailed history of game states in databases to capture long-term effects. This approach is believed to contribute significantly to the field of AI research, with the current version of TextWorldExpress serving as the first practical implementation of this approach.
