To achieve successful object transfer between a robotic arm and another entity, such as a human, the trajectory of the object and the movements of the hand must be planned in harmony. This coordination requires considering multiple constraints, including the relative positions of the involved entities, the mobility range of the human, and the manipulability realm of the robotic hand. The manipulability realm, defined by the boundary of feasible joint values, needs to be taken into account when planning the object's trajectory to avoid violations. In addition to these constraints, the mapping between the arm-bound and world-bound coordinate systems must be considered, as their relationship changes constantly due to the movement of both entities. For accurate adjustment of the manipulability realm and alignment of these coordinate systems, we employ a modified Point Cloud ICP algorithm, which utilizes a surface-mapping Manifold ICPTable* that also estimates the arm-bound-to-world boundary**. The ICPTable* algorithm first identifies corresponding features in both point clouds, then adjusts the arm-bound point cloud to match the world-bound, all within a single step. The optimized ICPTable* algorithm leverages parallel convection to simulate human hand movements, allowing us to test its performance using real robotic hand poses. The resulting adjusted manipulability realm, obtained from ICPTable* simulations, can be applied to other tasks and used in real-time object transfer control. The code for this research will be publicly available. Experiments have confirmed the efficacy of the ICPTable* algorithm, which outperformed previous methods in adjusting the manipulability realm and aligning coordinate systems. The proposed approach therefore constitutes a valuable addition to state-of-the-art robotic hand planning strategies. To study Higgs boson pair production in the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ channel at the LHC using the matrix element technique, we examine how to efficiently reject Higgs boson events and accurately calculate Higgs boson pair signals. This study specifically focuses on final states with two leptons resulting from $\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*} \to \ell\nell$ decay. We implement this study within the C++ based CLEM framework, which provides the matrix element technique along with event selection and categorization tools. We investigate the performance of various event selection methods based on the Monte Carlo event sample of the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ process and tag efficiency predicted by the Standard Model for the $\textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ event tag. We determine the remaining background contributions from $\textrm{Q}\bar{\textrm{Q}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ and $\textrmon{\ell}\textron{q}\textron{q}\textrm{W}^{*}$ processes, along with the sensitivity to Higgs boson pair analysis in the $\textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ channel at the 14 TeV LHC with 300 fb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity. We find that after applying the matrix element technique, the $\textrm{HH}$ signal has a purity of 94\% with a total background of 0.32 fb and a signal-to-background ratio of 1:70. This study shows the effectiveness of the matrix element technique in enhancing the sensitivity of Higgs boson pair searches at the LHC. We have also found that despite the presence of additional final state particles from $\textrm{Q}\bar{\texrm{Q}}$ production, the matrix element technique remains capable of differentiating between Higgs boson pair signals and background processes.

The COVID-19 pandemic vaccination efforts have been hindered by an upsurge in anti-vaccination sentiments spread through misinformation. As the primary source of online information for many, social media platforms like Twitter, necessitate analysis to comprehend the diffusion of this misinformation and the resistance it encounters. We focus on distinguishing retweets that indicate acceptance or rejection of anti-vaccination tweets, particularly those concerning the COVID-19 vaccine. We introduced a new framework, referred to as the TwiDe, that can learn both the retweet intention and the response content by leveraging contextual information. This framework is versatile and can be applied to various online discussion platforms. Our experiments on a COVID-19 vaccine Twitter dataset found that the model could accurately classify the retweet intention in 60% of cases and predict the response content with a high degree of precision. Additionally, we found that approximately 4% of active users on Twitter are persistent disseminators of anti-vaccination misinformation, and that news media articles are often targeted by misinformation disseminators as a means of spread dissemination. The model's functionality and the obtained results can provide valuable insights to developers of online misinformation detection systems, as well as policymakers striving to combat misinformation. Furthermore, the model can aid in building a detection system that distinguishes between different types of online misinformation. As part of our dataset, we made available the code and the TwiDe model for public access to facilitate the replication of our results. We believe that this dataset can be utilized by the scientific community in various applications due to its versatility, and can potentially be applied to different domains, as evidenced by our success in using it to model an online discussion that is distinct from COVID-19, such as misinformation concerning law enforcement. Meanwhile, we are exploring methods to enhance the model's performance in predicting the response content, as well as expanding our research to comprise multiple social media platforms. An initial examination found that the model can achieve a high degree of accuracy in predicting the retweet intention on Instagram, and we intend to delve deeper into comprehending the diffusion of misinformation across different platforms. An extension of our research, referred to as the TwiDe2, was developed to model online discussions found in comments by leveraging user-specific information, as well as to delve into the differences and similarities between Discord and Twitter. The emergence of high-energy attosecond pulses opens a doorway to probing the atomic fast motion and its applications in coherent control of pulse patterns. Despite the potential, achieving pulses that can withstand ignition and retain coherence in the field, thus enabling simultaneous measurement and manipulation, remains an elusive goal. To overcome this challenge, we propose a new approach to generating isolated high-energy pulses via a laser-plasma interaction. By harnessing the spatial inhomogeneity of the plasma, we break the trade-off between pulse energy and coherence, yielding a robust pulse output. Our simulation reveals that the intra-pulse recurrence period can be accurately predicted, and the pulse energy is primarily governed by the laser intensity rather than the focus distance. Physics-informed neural networks have gained prominence as a forward modeling approach that combines flexibility with accuracy, yet, suffers from a scarcity of suitable training data, necessitating the development of creative sampling methods. Despite their effectiveness to some extent, existing data sampling techniques fail to exploit the inherent smoothness of the governing equations, leading to artificial noise insertion that compromises solution quality. In response, we introduce Residual Adaptive Node Creation for Grid-based models, a node creation technique for physics-informed neural networks that prioritizes residual reduction. By doing so, RANG decouples the sampling process from the solution grid, enabling dense, high-quality data creation without artificial correlations. Furthermore, RANG facilitates multi-dimensional data creation, supplemented by an energy-based data filtering method to combat noise. Through thorough experimentation, we demonstrate RANG's superiority over alternative sampling methods in a wide range of test cases. The source code for RANG is openly available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/krishna-shm/RANG. Deep learning techniques have shown remarkable potential in addressing person, image, and car recognition tasks. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are commonly used for these tasks, but they can be limited by their traditional rectangular Sliding Window Convolution (SWC), which may neglect orientation information. In contrast, orientation-inspired Convolutional Neural Networks (OCNNs) can capture orientation information, with variants of them being used for occlusion compensation in person recognition. However, the full potential of orientation information has not been fully explored until now. In this research, we introduce two new OCNN architectures: Strip OCNN (SOCNN) and Merge OCNN (MOCNN), which respectively capitalize on the advantages of horizontal and vertical regions, and combine them using a feature fusion technique. By doing so, we demonstrate that the full orientation information of an image can be leveraged. Moreover, we present two new extensions of SOCNN and MONCNN: Expandable Person Library (EPL) and Car Recognition (CR) modules, which can serve as a extensive person library or car database and facilitate effective car recognition. Moreover, we also introduce a Fused Orientation Convolution (FOC) layer for feature fusion. Experimental results show that SOCNN and MONCNN outperform SWC by significant margins on various person, image, and car recognition benchmarks. Meanwhile, EPL and CR modules offer superior performance and resource efficiency compared to conventional methods. Finally, FOC layer is found to be superior to arbitrary SWC in numerous experiments. These novel architectures and modules can be valuable resources for researchers and developers working on orientation-inspired CNNs and person, image, and car recognition. These findings contradict the existing existing data and show that carbon-12 fusion has not reached a complete high-energy astrophysical barrier. Our research also verifies that measured fusion cross-sections align with the calculated values near a barrier of around 340 keV. However, at lower energies, measured and calculated cross-sections diverge, indicating the presence of an anomalous behavior. This discrepancy is attributed to two-particle two-fragment channel cross-sections, which were previously underestimated and now accurately explained. Consequently, our research reveals that carbon-12 fusion crosses over to a new regime at lower energies, surpassing the usual astrophysical barrier. To resolve the long-standing issue of carbon-12 fusion cross-sections below a barrier of 340 keV, our research suggests that experimental measurements should be conducted over a broader energy range by utilizing the Trojan horse method. However, the effectiveness of standard DNNs is limited by their tendency to overweight peripheral nodes in the prediction process, leading to decreased performance in the presence of obstructed paths. This issue can be addressed through the use of the attention mechanism, which allows sub-channel weights to be dynamically adjusted based on channel conditions. This paper proposes an attention-enhanced DNN (A-DNN) approach for localization, which can prioritize crucial sub channels in the prediction process. The A-DNN design was evaluated and compared with a conventional DNN (C-DNN) in terms of its ability to learn diverse mapping patterns between CSI and location. Consequently, the A-DNN demonstrates superior robustness and generalization capability compared to the C-DNN. COPASI is a widely-used simulation and analysis tool for biochemical networks and their dynamics, but users were limited to local access to its features. To address this, a new extension was added to COPASI to enable web-based use, now available through ShinyCOPASI. This update makes it possible for larger networks to be analyzed within a browser, without relying on local execution or file uploads. Users can configure simulations and analyses through a range of options, including numerical output, plotting, and scenario management. To facilitate sharing and collaborative investigation, interactive views of models and their predicted outcomes are available online. ShinyCOPASI includes several predefined tools based on user feedback and can be expanded further with the help of custom extensions. The application is open-source, allowing developers to contribute their own modifications and improvements. ShinyCOPASI provides a useful resource for educational purposes and gives users hands-on experience working with COPASI, while also offering a flexible platform for integrating additional analytical software through web interfaces. The source code can be accessed on GitHub at https://github.com/copasi/shinyCOPASI. A live demo is available at https://shiny.copasi.org/. Please note that ShinyCOPASI requires significant local resources for large networks and extensive simulation periods, so it's recommended to first run a trial simulation through COPASI and refine models based on that experience before using ShinyCOPASI for more extended simulations. The primary target audience for ShinyCOPASI consists of students and instructors in biochemistry and systems biology, due to its educational features, although it can also be utilized by researchers and professionals for a broader range of tasks. With its web-enabled interface, ShinyCOPASI enables users to upload models from COPASI and run various analyses, including simulations, unit conservation analysis, equilibrium and steady-state analysis, parameter estimation, and sensitivity analysis. Users can customize display options, such as graphing, to visualize the outcomes and explore the results through interactive tools. To facilitate collaborative investigation, users can share models and results via URLs, enabling others to access and view the data without requiring local access to the software or additional files. The update extends the capabilities of COPASI, making it accessible to a broader range of users and providing a convenient, web-enabled interface for analyzing biochemical networks and their dynamics. The source code for ShinyCOPASI is available on GitHub at https://github.com/copasi/shinyCOPASI, and a live demo can be accessed at https://shiny.copasi.org/.

Nucleus-nucleus collisions provide a unique opportunity to explore how matter behaves under extreme conditions, at high energies and densities. Within the CERN LHC's energy range, xenon atoms are chosen for the experiments due to their relatively low atomic number. However, the resulting thermal model calculations show a significant need for re-expanding the coordinate space to accurately account for the observed particle production. In addition to the usual fireball model, our work includes re-expansion phases to better fit the data, with specific focus on pions, kaons, antiprotons, and $\phi$ mesons. A new parameter, related to the initial energy density, is introduced and shown to enhance model accuracy when applying the expanding fireball model to these xenon atom collisions. Furthermore, our work demonstrates the effectiveness of a re-expansion phase in simulating these nucleus-nucleus interactions and highlights the significance of considering the complex nature of matter under such extreme conditions, going beyond the conventional thermal model's expectations. A detailed tabulation of our model calculations is included, showing the dependence of model parameters on the re-expansion coordinate and its subsequent impact on the production of specified particles at varying energies and densities. These findings ultimately contribute to a deeper understanding of matter behavior in these exotic, quantum conditions, with potential future applications also spanning the realm of quantum physics, for instance in simulating the early universe's evolution. Finally, our work successfully addresses the long-standing challenge of producing the right amount of antiprotons through these xenon collisions, now accurately accounted for by the thermal model with re-expansion phase. A comparison with other experiments, such as those involving larger than average lead-lead collisions at 5.02 TeV, is also included to highlight the re-expansion phase's applicability at various energy densities. A brief exploration of the production of very heavy particles, such as J/$\psi$ mesons, is also included within this report to further refine the model and provide a more comprehensive understanding of matter behavior in these exotic conditions. A summary of our model's findings is included at the end in the form of a list for easy reference. Based on numerical results, it has been observed that various parton distribution functions continue to exhibit high sensitivity to the specific characteristics of the input PDF at momentum transfers beyond their respective matching scales. This prompts the need to reevaluate the way PDFs are defined and fitted, particularly as momentum transfers continue to increase. A novel approach is proposed to address this issue by strictly adhering to the definition of parton distribution functions within the DGLAP framework. This is achieved through the incorporation of a correction term, constrained by the DGLAP evolution equation, to account for any discrepancies arising from inputs outside the matching regime. The proposed correction term is designed such that it does not introduce any new free parameters, thereby enabling a more accurate representation of parton distribution functions at higher momentum transfers. Additionally, the concept of flavor symmetry is revisited and an increased level of precision is achieved in the resulting parton distribution functions. The proposed method is anticipated to yield improved results for various phenomenological applications. The impact of this approach on the determination of parton distribution functions using looser constraints is also explored, revealing the importance of strict adherence to defined parton distribution functions through the incorporation of correction terms beyond their respective matching scales. The code used in this analysis is publicly accessible and can be utilized for input PDFs spanning a range of different momentum transfers. The study presents a comprehensive comparison of the proposed method against alternative approaches, such as the interaction between PDFs at different momentum transfers. Notably, it demonstrates that notably different interactions between PDFs at momentum transfers $Q^2$ and $9Q^2$ can still yield essentially identical parton distribution functions at $Q^2$. The discovery of flavor asymmetry in u-quark and d-quark PDFs at increasingly high momentum transfers is highlighted, in line with previous findings. Furthermore, the study provides valuable insights into the behavior of gluon PDF at high momentum transfers, facilitated by the use of phenomenological PDFs that incorporate data from deep-inelastic scattering and lattice QCD. The analysis also explores the role of momentum-dependent flavor-splitting functions in parton distribution functions at high momentum transfers, and a detailed comparison is drawn between various sets of parton distribution functions, including MMRT, DGLAP, and NNPDF3.1. The study provides the first-ever estimation of the gluon polarization parameter at high momentum transfers, and suggests the need for further improvements, particularly at momentum transfers beyond 10 GeV^2. The study also delves into the application of parton distribution functions at high momentum

Using 3D printing technology, samples of Martian and lunar soil substitutes were created and subjected to various temperatures in a chamber simulator mimicking the atmosphere on the Moon and Mars. The building materials, resembling real lunar and Martian regoliths, were refined with 5% and 10% silica powder, and had a size of 10x10x10 mm. This paper marks a breakthrough in the field of universal diffusion research. Existing models of diffusion, including the fractional elliptic and parabolic equations, have numerous applications in modeling real-world phenomena. Conversely, these models sometimes yield unrealistic solution behaviors, such as unbounded solutions in the case of fractional diffusion. In response, this paper presents a novel approach to modifying the fractional Laplacian's operator ($\Delta^\frac{1}{2}$) and its powers, thereby introducing a modified fractional operator ($\Delta_p^\frac{1}{p}$) with $p\in (0,2]$. This new operator closes the gap between $p$-Laplace and fractional Laplace limits, providing a comprehensive model for diffusion. Additionally, the paper derives sufficient and necessary conditions for the existence of bounded solutions in the context of fractional heat equation problems. This research represents a first in this area, and the methods employed can be adapted for use in the development of new Caccioppi-Serrin theorems. Furthermore, the paper explores the equivalence between the generated semigroup's compactness and the $L^1$-compactness of the incompressible Navier-Stokes equation's solutions, thereby introducing a unique solution for the universal diffusion equation ($\Delta^\frac{1}{p}u=t^\frac{-q-1}{p}f(t,x,u)$) under specific condition parameters $q$ and $p$ with $p\in (0,2]$, and $q\in (0,2p]$.
The solutions to the universal diffusion equation are shown to be $t$-monotone for $p=1$, and sufficient and necessary conditions for $t$-monotone solutions are established for $p\neq 1$. This research also discusses the properties of modification operators and their counterparts in the context of $p$-harmonic functions, introducing new classes of function modifications and their applications in the field of fractional diffusion. Finally, the paper presents a wide range of examples illustrating diverse diffusion behavior, and explores the impact of variable exponents on the diffusion behavior of analytic functions. The research can be adapted for use in studying the properties of various physical systems, such as phase transitions and fluid flow, under variable exponent conditions. The paper concludes by outlining potential research directions in this area. The novel techniques and methods presented in this paper can be utilized in the development of new nonlocal operators and their applications in modeling incompressible fluid flow and phase transition phenomena. This research presents an innovative approach for generating synthetic speech at varied lengths using a non-statistical method, akin to WordPiece. We introduce a new model, called the Rake-Tagger, comprising two primary components: the Rake and the Tagger. The Rake leverages a median-based algorithm to dynamically determine word-unit divisions, while the Tagger models a posterior probability distribution based on hidden states. The Rake-Tagger combination is trained alongside a linear auto-encoder to optimize its performance. We evaluate the effectiveness of our model in synthesizing speech at various lengths and find that it achieves superior results compared to existing synthetic speech methods. Moreover, our model creates synthetic speech samples that are both phonetically and syntactically plausible when employed as a sequence tagging model. We consider the Rake-Tagger to be a versatile model that can be applied to a broad range of sequence generation tasks beyond speech synthesis. Our open-source code is publicly available for the convenience of fellow researchers. We anticipate that our model will pave the way for a deeper understanding of sequence generation algorithms rooted in non-statistical models, thus contributing to the advancement of synthetic speech synthesis. Furthermore, we envision that our approach will facilitate the induction of logical syntactic transformations in synthetic speech, thereby achieving a greater degree of control over the synthetic product. Ultimately, we aim to develop a mode that can generate synthetic speech samples that are both clinically nuanced and logically coherent. We hypothesize that our non-statistical model will play a pivotal role in achieving this goal. We test our hypothesis by presenting a case in point - a synthetic speech sample created through the application of logical transformations on the Rake-Tagger generated sequence. We acknowledge that our current model falls short in capturing the underlying logic, but we are confident that future enhancements to the model will enable the induction of logical syntactic transformations. We consider this an intrinsic aspect of our research and are eager to share our findings with the community, seeking feedback and guidance in this process. The R tool spHabitat is a package designed to implement habitat models for individual and multiple species, as well as an integrated model that considers the collective behavior of numerous species, taking into account the interactions within and between species within a bounded spatial area. The model assumes a dynamic system where species' populations adjust in response to changes in their habitats, which are shaped by the species' activities, such as foraging, migration, and lek behavior. The species' impacts on habitats are measured by the fraction of area affected during their activities and are weighted by their activity rates. Leveraging a vast library of spatial analysis tools, the spHabitat package encompasses a wide range of applications including: (i) single-species and multi-species spatial presence models that evaluate the influence of habitat and environmental factors on species' detection probabilities; (ii) spatial habitat models that analyze the relationship between habitat and species' abundance; and (iii) an integrated model that generalizes the previous approaches by simulating the dynamics of numerous species interacting with each other and their environment. The model derives from a general ecosystem dynamics model, where species' populations and habitats are in continuous evolution, although the detection probabilities and abundance analyses are typically treated as static conditions. The package follows the logic of the HABITAT/SPACE approach and is an evolution of previous works on single and multi-species spatial habitat models, integrated species-habitat models, and collective behavior models. The spHabitat package is distributed free via the CRAN repository under the terms of R License. The software described in this article is available at: \url{https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/spHabitat/index.html}. The current version of the software exceeds the version used in the tests, with the present version providing additional functionalities such as the capacity to model species' behavior, integrate lek behavior, simulate scenarios, and perform post-hoc analyses, among others. The package's documentation and tutorials provide in-depth guidance on the implementation of these novel features. The user manual is available at: \url{https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/spHabitat/vignettes/spHabitat.pdf} and tutorial at: \url{https://github.com/alexandra-munoz/spHabitat_tutorials}. The developer's GitHub page (\url{https://github.com/alexandra-munoz/spHabitat}) offers the software's source code, further information on the package, and a platform for users to share their experiences and suggestions. Due to a shortage of dermatologists and increasing skin cancer incidence, effective differential diagnosis methods are greatly needed. The Skincare initiative has provided a valuable resource for accomplishing this task by offering a free online dataset that includes over 100,000 dermatology images along with their diagnoses. A deep learning-based model, developed through an interdisciplinary collaboration between computer scientists and dermatologists, is presented in this technical report. It has undergone interaction with medical professionals via an intuitive user interface that facilitates input of unknown skin lesion images and diagnoses, allowing for a more comprehensive understanding of the complex differential diagnosis process in dermatology. A detailed explanation of the model's architecture, the approach taken to train and adapt it to dermatology, and the beneficial contributions of human expertise to the model are provided. Moreover, the advantages and limitations of the model are discussed, along with preliminary experiments that demonstrate its effectiveness in a differential diagnosis setting. By integrating the model with human expertise, it is shown that a highly proficient differential diagnosis can be achieved in dermatology through a collaborative effort between machine learning and professional input. It is hoped that this model will serve as a valuable tool for other fields and domains, paving the way for applications in clinical practices and decision-support systems in the future. Code and data are available at https://github.com/cdecephalo/Skincare.Official.Reports and https://github.com/cdecephalo/Skincare.Public.Reports. For technical contributions and details not included in the public report, please visit https://cdecephalo.github.io/Skincare.Official.Reports. Leveraging our experience with the Skincare initiative, our team developed a general, reusable framework for integrating machine learning with professional input that can be adapted to various domains, as explained in the associated technical contribution at https://cdecephalo.github.io/Skincare.Official.Reports. It is hoped that this framework will foster innovative applications of human-machine collaboration in the medical field and promote the development of decision-support systems in clinical practices. Moreover, the dermatology model presented in this study can serve as a valuable reference for achieving human-level performance in differential diagnosis through a collaborative effort between machine and human expertise in the complex domain of dermatology. It is anticipated that this model will contribute positively to decision-support systems in the future and promote the incorporation of professional input in decision-making processes. We introduced a stochastic autoencoder with a conditional model and noise-related regularization, designed to capture the time-dependent patterns in Type Ia Supernovae spectral data. The spectral sequences were analyzed using a noise-filled model, which can learn to ignore random noise and focus on the underlying temporal structures. The employment of the stochastic autoencoder showed promise in uncovering the inherent patterns within the data. We confirmed the effectiveness of our approach through multiple tests, including one where we demonstrated that the temporal dimension was indeed present in the data, as predicted by existing scientific knowledge. Furthermore, we found that our model was able to accurately generate temporal sequences similar to those found in the training dataset, and that it consistently outperformed a non-stochastic approach in sequence reconstruction tasks. The results of these tests validate our decision to utilize a stochastic autoencoder to capture the temporal patterns within Type Ia Supernovae spectral data. The application of our model may lead to the discovery of new temporal structures within the data, potentially paving the way for significant scientific breakthroughs. Understanding the spread of epidemics within networks, such as contact graphs, reveals patterns of disease transmission. However, assuming only pair-based interactions oversimplifies the complex human interactions seen in everyday life, neglecting the role of group meetings in disease spread. By transforming epidemics within hypergraphs into mean-field models of interacting particle systems, we explore the necessary and sufficient conditions for disease extinction and show that these conditions rely on the spectral properties of the hypergraph's adjacency matrix. This framework provides a promising approach to integrating group-based interactions into epidemic spread models, thus potentially yielding more accurate predictions of disease transmission. Furthermore, we derive the extinction conditions for specific types of hypergraphs, demonstrating that the critical transmission rates for these hypergraphs lie within a particular range on the spectrum of their adjacency matrices. By extending this methodology to more complex hypergraphs, we identify various group structures and transmission patterns, ultimately providing guidelines for policymakers to control disease spread within groups, such as schools, workplaces, and public transportation, by targeting high transmission rates. Computations involving the extinction threshold and spectral properties of hypergraphs could be facilitated through numerical methods, such as graph representation and approximation techniques. By bridging the gap between hypergraph models and real-world environments, this framework offers a valuable tool for applying graphical concepts to the analysis of epidemic spread within group-based settings. Lastly, we propose potential avenues for further research, such as integrating individual immunity and the dynamics of multiple disease outbreaks on hypergraphs. By pushing the boundaries of hypergraph-based epidemic modeling, this study contributes to the development of sophisticated models for disease transmission, thus advancing our understanding of epidemic spread within group-based settings. Additionally, we emphasize the versatility of our model, which can be adapted to interact with other mathematical frameworks, such as probabilistic models and optimization techniques, thus presenting a versatile approach for analyzing disease transmission. Lastly, we highlight the practical applications and potential research directions that this study has enabled.

Furthermore, the strain applied across the layers influences the pattern's shape, introducing non-linear influences that align with theoretical models of ferromagnetism in two-dimensional systems. Modifying the strain completely overturns the pattern, replacing the 120-degree shape with a antiferromagnetic configuration. The strain applied across the layers, as well as the magnetic field, introduce a chiral influence on the Rashba effect, distorting the 120-degree pattern and introducing an imbalance in the spin's orbital movement. Upon removal of the external influences, the system returns to a scenario resembling an intrinsic strain, also exhibiting a 120-degree pattern, although marginally deformed. By using a global simulation of a solar-type star, we discovered that when the rotation speed near the poles increases, the magnetic cycle is no longer observed. However, when the rotation speed near the poles decreases, the magnetic cycle reappears and the star becomes actively magnetic. Additionally, the star's energetic output in X-rays and other high-energy wavelengths increases. These findings suggest that a decline in polar rotation speed is essential for the development of a strong magnetic cycle in a star. Based on our research, we predict that stars with non-uniform rotation speeds, particularly those experiencing a decrease in polar rotation speeds, have a higher likelihood of exhibiting magnetic cycles. Furthermore, the appearance of magnetic cycles in these stars is sensitive to the rates of heat transfer and the generation of the magnetic field. If these processes slow down, the star becomes actively magnetic, while an enhancement of these processes prevents the star from entering the active phase. Our research also reveals that the star's activity levels during the magnetic cycle are influenced by the rotation speed at mid-latitudes, while the duration of the cycle is primarily determined by the rate of the rotation speed decline. Furthermore, we discovered that during the magnetic cycle, the star experiences rapid rotation speeds at low latitudes and slow rotation speeds at high latitudes. Finally, we found that at high latitudes, the star's magnetic field is primarily poloidal in shape, while at low latitudes, the magnetic field is primarily toroidal in shape. Conversely, the reverse is true at high rotation speeds, with the toroidal magnetic field being primarily found at high latitudes and the poloidal magnetic field being primarily found at low latitudes. This method can learn a common representation using contrastive divergence and applies well to classification tasks, but it has limitations in handling high-dimensional data and relies on ad-hoc techniques to incorporate additional inputs. To address these limitations, we have developed a new approach, the K-fan deep multimodal deep network, which can learn a shared representation for multiple data types with varying dimensions. This model uses a multi-layer architecture to capture complex features and can train using back-propagation for high-dimensional data. By employing a McMini model, developers can ensure that their code functions correctly according to the C11 specification by checking it against a set of established thread safety principles. McMini's reliability is realized through two primary components: (1) a thread model, which effectively replicates the behavior of multithreaded programs using a state machine, while facilitating the isolation of thread execution; and (2) a DPOR algorithm, which determines the order of thread activation, as well as identifies potential data race issues. Consider a general supercritical branching population where individual offspring are connected to their parents in a random manner, with the relationship between generations being relatively isolated. It's assumed that individuals can hold multiple genetic alleles at a single location, with one pair of alleles being inherited from each parent, whose values are taken from a shared distribution. The population's genetic allele prevalence is studied by analyzing a branching process that accounts for random genetic variation, resulting in a continuous probability distribution that fits the tau-prevalence distribution more accurately than previous Gaussian models. The resulting distribution has been mathematically derived and shown to converge consistently as the number of generations increases, with the convergence being unconditional. The findings of this study include the rates at which: (1) the probability of an allele reaching the population occurs over time, (2) the maximum and minimum number of occurrences of an allele deviate from their mean over time, and (3) the shape of a distribution deviates from Gaussianity over time. These rates were previously unknown and are now quantifiable due to the newly developed distribution. The applicability of these rates extends beyond genetic analysis to any general branching population where individual offspring are connected to their parents in a random manner, with the rates being easily computed and translated into an actionable metric known as the tau-efficiency, which measures how efficiently an allele achieves a desired number of occurrences above or below the mean. The tau-efficiency can be utilized in conservation management to develop an allele's trajectory and predict the success of a conservation effort. Finally, the accuracy of the continuously converging distribution was validated through numerical simulations in R, where the resulting precision was shown to be unconditional and highly precise (with a low MSE of 0.0006) for a population driven by a gamma distribution, with even higher precision expected for populations driven by distributions with larger parameters. The developed mathematical distribution therefore provides a useful model for general supercritical branching populations, enabling the estimation of the allele prevalence spectrum and offering insights into population dynamics, evolution, and conservation. The combinations of these findings can be employed in various applications, such as predicting population trends, evaluating the effectiveness of conservation strategies, and simulating the dynamics of beneficial and deleterious traits. The R code used in this study is publicly available at https://github.com/aminrafi/allele_prevalence. In addition to this repository, I also uploaded the numerical data and associated metadata to the Dataverse platform at https://dataverse.emory.edu/?syntax=user%2Faminrafi%2Fallele_preval

By leveraging attention mechanisms within the architecture, the system is able to identify and prioritize critical audio features in speech, thereby enhancing its ability to distinguish genuine from spoofed speech. Experimental results demonstrate that systems built using the Attention-based Activation Mechanism consistently achieve superior performance in spoofing detection tasks, thereby validating its practicality and effectiveness in real-world applications. This study employs terahertz near-field microscopy to analyze the local dielectric properties and microwave loss in superconducting quantum processing units. Utilizing a photoconductive switch modulated by 0.1 TS1 pulses, our technique offers sub-wire spacing resolution and directly measures the local E-field in nanometer-scale proximity to the surface. This close proximity enables detection of minor dielectric inhomogeneities and significant variations in loss tangent, facilitating the optimization of qubit design and fabrication. Our research involves examining a LPBm quantum processor at 9 THz, revealing how wire spacing influences loss and discovering a correlation between loss and dielectric loss in materials. These findings lead to the direction of future research on enhancing circuit performance by refining wire spacing in LPBm designs. This study employs a hybrid agent-based model to examine how novel investment approaches emerge and diffuse in a market. Introducing these new strategies is achieved through agents who modify their existing strategies by randomly altering key parameters. We investigate the impact of this modification method on agent strategy diversity and the performance of existing strategies. We find that introducing these new strategies reduces the long-term profitability of existing strategies. To mitigate this effect, we implement a search mechanism that allows agents to selectively adopt the most profitable strategies. This causes agents to favor exploring novel strategies only if they demonstrate significant improvement potential. As a result, the strategy diversity stabilizes and no longer suffers from the detrimental impact of introduced new strategies on established strategy profitability. Furthermore, the findings of this study align with the real-world phenomenon observed during the time of Jonathon Spence in the 16th century, where agents adopted new strategies more cautiously in the past. We relate this historical observation to the differences in the study's environment settings that influenced the results. We demonstrate that the success of a strategy, known as trend following, is contingent upon specific market conditions in the past, and this trend-specific performance does not translate to other environments; thereby making unrelated to novel investment approaches in general. This "trend-following fallacy" is shown to occur due to the common practice in the literature of presenting trend following as a novel approach, despite it being well-established, and thereby is an artifact of existing literature's biases, and not an inherent benefit, as the agents can achieve similar performance through other strategies in the given environment; and in another setting, the most profitable strategy is actually diversifying. Thermal excitation of magnons is a crucial issue in both magnonics and spintronics, with the former aiming to control magnons efficiently and the latter utilizing magnons for information transfer.  Magnon blockage by superconductor barriers is a well-documented phenomenon in the literature, with the underlying mechanism attributed to the spin-polarized exchange interaction they introduce.  However, this mechanism is insufficient to account for the experimental observations in this study.  An additional mechanism, namely the proximity-induced exchange interaction, must be considered to effectively gate the magnons, as evidenced by the research findings presented here.  An innovative device design featuring a YIG post situated between two superconductors is utilized to investigate the magnon blockade phenomenon.  Techniques such as finite-differentiation method and analytical fitting are employed to analyze the data, revealing that the device can function as either an effective filter or amplifier for magnons at applicable temperature conditions.  Importantly, the research also provides a method to eliminate systematic errors during the measurements and confirms that the exchange bias is the predominant mechanism governing the magnon blockade phenomenon.  Lastly, the researchers demonstrate that by adjusting the thickness of the superconductor, the magnon blockade can be adjusted within a broad range, specifically between weak and strong coupling regimes.  This breakthrough discovery opens up new avenues for further research in the field of quantum information technology by utilizing the unique properties of magnons.  Additionally, the research has potential applications in the development of novel magnonic devices such as magnon transistors.  The theoretical model proposed in this study can be applied to various materials beyond those used in this investigation and is expected to broaden the understanding of the magnon blockade phenomenon in ferromagnetic materials generally.  Furthermore, the researchers suggest that the technique could be adapted to detect the spin waves in other materials by incorporating superconductors, thus presenting new possibilities for the device's implementation.  Finally, the study presents a graph illustrating the relationship between the superconductor thickness and the corresponding magnon blockade factor for different YIG materials.  Utilizing the data from this graph, the researchers can accurately predict the outcome of the magnon blockade experiments conducted on other YIG materials within similar device configurations, thus offering a practical way to apply the research findings in real-world scenarios.  Additionally, the researchers point out several challenges that need to be addressed in order to achieve full-gain in the magnon transmission, specifically attributing it to the remaining magnon leakage beyond the superconductor barrier. The early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic saw major shifts in the media landscape, particularly regional news organizations that adapted to provide essential information to their audiences. This study analyzes data from the NewsData COVID project, which evaluated 57 regional news sources in the U.S., covering over 14,000 articles and 1,400 TV segments published between March 1, 2020, and December 31, 2021. Our research examines the relationships between COVID-related coverage, pandemic metrics, and audience engagement in 120 U.S. metropolitan areas. It's worth noting that while our sample size is substantial, it's comprised of metropolitan areas hosting regional news sources, limiting our scope to approximately one-third of the U.S. population. Our analysis reveals that regional news sources covered COVID at varying rates, with factors like population age and health statistics influencing coverage intensity. There's also evidence that news sources leaned towards negative framing, particularly in areas meeting COVID-related hospital capacity thresholds. Our findings suggest a connection between COVID-related coverage and pandemic outcomes, along with significant links between coverage and audience disengagement. These outcomes, however, varied according to region, with areas experiencing higher COVID fatalities linked to increased disengagement rates despite heightened COVID-related coverage. Our research offers a framework for exploring the complex interplay between news coverage and pandemic metrics, providing insights into the media's role in communicating crisis information to audiences and reflecting broader community dynamics. Ultimately, this study's insights can inform the development of theoretical and operational frameworks for predicting news coverage and simulating pandemic communication strategies. Counting is a fundamental ability that's essential in daily life, and understanding the cognitive processes involved is crucial for developing accurate models that mimic human behavior. We advance numerical knowledge through sequential learning, starting from basic units ("ones") that represent numbers. By modeling the inherent structure in this progression, we demonstrate how our model acknowledges the hierarchical, interconnected nature of numbers. By utilizing a recurrent neural network, we show that numerical knowledge can be retained even after learning individual digits, enhancing the model's performance in predicting the order of number sequences. Notably, our model exhibits a remarkable generalization of 4.5 to 5.0 in the last 10 sequence predictions of the CognIT test, and we successfully apply our model to the prediction of number sequences in everyday math problems. Finally, we provide evidence that our model integrates its knowledge about the magnitude of numbers, a key characteristic of the cognitive model it's based on, and demonstrates this integration through its performance on the CognIT test. By taking the inherent structure of the progression of counting into account, our model outperforms previous sequence-based models and accurately predicts the order of number sequences, surpassing even human performance after extensive training. Additionally, our model provides a new approach to understanding the underlying cognitive processes involved in counting. Although we primarily tested our model on the CognIT dataset, we also demonstrated its effectiveness in solving everyday math problems, highlighting its potential to facilitate math problem-solving for individuals with mathematical difficulties. By addressing the lack of a suitable artificial intelligence model that mimics the cognitive processes involved in counting, we develop a novel model that utilizes the inherent structure in the progression of counting and accurately predicts the order of number sequences, thereby facilitating math problem-solving. In doing so, we propose a new approach to understanding the underlying cognitive processes involved in counting. Furthermore, we utilize our model to analyze its knowledge about the magnitude of numbers, confirming that its magnitude awareness contributes significantly to its performance in the CognIT test. By retaining numerical knowledge through sequential learning, we show that our model can predict the order of number sequences with a generalization of 4.5 to 5.0 in the last 10 sequence predictions of the CognIT test. Additionally, our model performs accurately on everyday math problems, and we provide evidence of its magnitude awareness by analyzing its knowledge about the magnitude of numbers. In recent years, approximate membership queries have become increasingly common in various distributed systems. As a result, research has surged into filter data structures such as Bloom, Cuckoo, and Bloom-like filters to handle this demand efficiently. These filters, although widely used, suffer from drawbacks including larger sizes, longer initialization times, and inaccurate outcomes due to false positives. In contrast, hash-based xor filters have distinct advantages over these traditional filters in terms of accuracy, size, and setup time. The main contributions of this research are as follows: (1) a new xor filter construction method is proposed, (2) an efficient calculation method to determine the required hash function count for a given false positive rate is developed, (3) a numerical analysis to estimate the required hash function count is performed, (4) a comparison between the newly constructed xor filters and existing Bloom and Cuckoo filters is carried out through experiments, (5) an alternative to existing xor filters is provided by utilizing multiple elements per slot separated by xor operations. The results of the numerical analysis showed a divergence between the estimated and constructed values, which was then closed in the experimental section. The findings from the experiments revealed the newly constructed xor filters to be smaller in size, faster to set up, and more accurate in outcomes compared to the existing filters. Additionally, an upper bound was found for the existing Bloom and Cuckoo filters and it was shown to be worse than the newly constructed xor filters in all aspects. Furthermore, an efficient conversion method was proposed that can transform the existing Bloom and Cuckoo filters into a variant of xor filters with less false positives and a decreased size. The experiments also demonstrated the superiority of the newly constructed xor filters in terms of throughput and latency under three different scenarios, which further validates its advantages over the existing filters. Furthermore, a novel xor filter construction method that utilizes modulators instead of hash functions was explored and shown to provide a smaller size and faster setup time compared to the previously constructed xor filters. Lastly, an upper bound was found for the novel modulated xor filters and it was proven to be superior to the existing Bloom and Cuckoo filters in all aspects. The research laid the foundation for an efficient and accurate approximate membership query data structure by utilizing xor filters and modulators. Several future directions were also identified including the extension of the proposed modulated xor filters to support arbitrary false positive rates and accurate membership queries. A new approach to trend analysis is presented, one that utilizes data from market transactions throughout the trading day to forecast price movements. Instead of relying on historical price data, our method analyzes the correlation between future market forecasts and past transaction patterns, making predictions based on actual market behavior. We demonstrate how market trends can be extracted from transaction sequences, specifically the sequence of best-execution costs and shares sold, is capable of differentiating between upward and downward market movements. Furthermore, our approach reveals the underlying market dynamics by identifying various pattern types associated with future market directions. We maintain that the intrinsic value of our approach lies in providing in-depth market analysis for quantitative analysts, enabling them to make more accurate predictions and detect subtle market trends, thus ultimately contributing to superior investment decisions. We provide concrete evidence for our claims through a comprehensive case study involving four widely-traded S&P stocks, showing that our approach is both feasible and reliable. We offer a versatile trend-extraction technique, Net Trend Analysis (NETA), capable of detecting trends from diverse markets with minimal modifications. We present a trend-quality measure, Trend Strength Index (TSI), alongside an algorithm to assess the validity of future market forecasts, reducing the likelihood of inaccurate predictions and optimizing the use of our approach. NETA boasts a high accuracy rate in predicting upward or downward market movements and detects trends from real-world markets with ease, showcasing its numerous applications and versatility. We propose a trend-confirmation process, validating the accuracy of our approach by comparing our results with historical market data, and demonstrating the benefits of our approach over traditional financial time-series analysis methods. Ultimately, NETA facilitates trend analysis for financial quantitative analysts, contributing to superior investment decisions and adding value to financial analysis, while its low-cost and ease-of-use features make it an indispensable tool for professionals and individual investors alike. Moreover, we visualize our findings using various graphical tools, showing our approach to trend analysis in an intuitive manner. We make NETA available for public use through our publicly-available algorithm, enabling our results to be replicated and building on our work to facilitate similar research in the future. Our approach to trend analysis may be applied to other markets and financial instruments, expanding its use beyond our case study and adding new perspectives to the field of financial analysis. Furthermore, we recognize the contributions of our team members and research colleagues, facilitating the development and presentation of our approach, and expressing our gratitude for their support and expertise. Lastly, we recognize the broader research efforts building on our work, and their contributions to the development of financial analysis and market trend analysis.

We successfully trained an autonomous agent to navigate complex environments using only image gradients, overcoming the Sim2Real challenge. Our novel approach employed Gradients Assignation, a multi-agent reward system, and Gradients Induction, a specialized neural network. This innovative method bypassed the need for pixel-wise feature extraction, demonstrating exceptional navigation skills in both simulated and real-world scenarios. Our work extends the application of Gradients Assignation, facilitating the transfer of learned tasks through the transformation of reward structures. As a result, we enabled an automatic task assignment feature, empowering our agent to learn a diverse range of tasks independently. Furthermore, Gradients Induction was designed to focus on inducing gradients, which significantly improved the navigation quality in real-world environments. Our study examines the influence of several optical flow components and evaluates the robustness of our agent when encountering obstacles and perturbations. Our method has minimal computational requirements, allowing our agent to achieve high speeds of 15 frames per second on a GPU, and demonstrating remarkable generalization capabilities across various tasks. Our code is publicly available on GitHub, undergoing continuous development at GitHub.com/AArturoA/BGNAV. Our study aims to bridge the Sim2Real gap and facilitates the easy assignment of tasks to navigate complex environments autonomously. Moreover, we seek to enable autonomous agents to navigate effectively in real-world scenarios by modeling reward structures from gradient exponents rather than explicit pixels. Our work has broad potential applications in various areas, such as induced gradient-based therapies and expert decision-making systems in various industry sectors. Moreover, our novel approach extends the application of Gradients Assignation, a multi-agent reward system, and empowers autonomous agents to navigate diverse environments by assigning task structures independently. Additionally, our method ensures that navigation is achieved independently of specific pixel representations, promoting a more robust and generalizable agent performance, which is essential for autonomous tasks in real-world environments. Our study examines the critical components of independent learning and generalization, showcasing the notable navigation quality and excessive caution exhibited by our method. Strong deepfakes are highly realistic and indistinguishable videos of people, created through various transformation techniques such as image editing software and AI-powered tools like DeepMotion, which utilize 3D mesh rendering to produce lifelike results. An experiment involved applying these techniques to existing videos of actors performing specific facial expressions without voice, resulting in novel videos of the same individuals making different expressions, as well as videos of people speaking with unfamiliar voices. This process revealed several difficulties in creating strong deepfakes, primarily the limited control over precise facial features and the tendency for faces to appear distorted. An analysis of 350 strong deepfake videos found that nearly all contained visible flaws such as jerky movements and distorted facial features, whereas actual deepfake cases were difficult to spot. A new dataset containing 720 strong deepfake videos was created for identification purposes, along with a winning entry in an competition held to improve detection of strong deepfakes, with an accuracy rate of 95% when testing on a validation set, and remarkably accurate across multiple versions of a model despite significant increases in testing difficulty. An alternative method also achieved high accuracy rates of 94% and 94.5% on the validation and test sets, which demonstrated robust results across multiple versions of a dataset, and specifically showed a high correlation of 0.96 between accuracy rates of a model and its corresponding version of a dataset in terms of image resolution. An alternative strong deepfake creation method was found to not only produce less visible flaws compared to a previously used technique called DeepMotion, who's advantage decreased from 88% to 46%, but also easily reproducible with minimal training requirements, and when identified, could potentially aid in uncovering the creators of malicious strong deepfakes by tracing the metadata of the used software. Furthermore, an alternative strong deepfake detection method was found to not only outperform previous approaches by achieving high accuracy rates of 94.5% and Acc+0.96 on two test sets, but also specifically showed a high correlation of 0.96 and 0.88 respectively in terms of F1-score and Acc+0.96 on two test sets, when testing on six versions of a dataset, and demonstrated robust results when employed on multiple related tasks including detecting for real deepfakes, checking whether a video contains specific individuals, and extracting up to 238 facial features from video clips. The presence of a liquid envelope, especially if it contains water, is a necessary requirement for creating a habitable Earth-sized planet. Detecting such an envelope around small, nearby stars is extremely difficult in infrared thermal measurements but can be identifiable through visible light changes during the process of a planet passing in front of its host star (a transit event). Researchers have proposed a new method to determine if a liquid envelope, specifically containing water, surrounds a certain category of planets (those with masses between that of Earth and Neptune) by measuring how much water is present in the envelope during a transit event. This method relies on the distinct ways in which water and other gases behave under different temperatures, a phenomenon that's visible in spectroscopy data. We provide an alternative framework for understanding how water behaves in a planet's envelope, one that's based on the chemical equilibrium between water and other substances. This approach can result in multiple solutions that explain the same observed phenomena, and we propose future observations, including those enabled by the James Webb Space Telescope, to distinguish between these possibilities. This new framework highlights the need to reconsider how scientists interpret observational data from a planetary science perspective, and encourages flexibility in the interpretation of data as understanding the field evolves. Moreover, our study demonstrates the feasibility of testing compositional models of a planet's interior through transit spectroscopy, a technique with the potential to reveal crucial information about a planet's basic composition, such as the presence of an outer solid layer and a liquid envelope. If these models prove valid, they could provide crucial insights into a planet's formation and evolution, and could serve as a crucial tool in the search for a terrestrial planet with a habitable environment. As such, this study serves as a guide for researchers seeking to understand the composition of exoplanets through various methods and observational campaigns. We estimate that with data from the James Webb Space Telescope at a signal-to-noise ratio of 100, we can distinguish between an envelope composed mostly of H2O and H2O mixed with other volatile substances, and between the latter two scenarios. A necessary condition for determining whether an exoplanet has a liquid envelope is observing a transmission spectrum with high sensitivity to wavelengths below 1.5 $\mu m$ at a signal-to-noise ratio of more than 100. We also show that future observations of the telluric CH4 and CO2 could help distinguish between an envelope composed mostly of H2O and one containing other volatile substances. Inspired by brain's efficient information processing, neuromorphic computing aims to develop novel artificial neural networks. This work investigates whether spiking neural networks can effectively learn to replicate complex input patterns that resemble biological brain activity. To achieve this, we utilize a novel output encoding method, merging binary neural network weights with ternary input values, resulting in binary output neurons. This novel approach enables robust performance on typical machine learning tasks, such as the MNIST dataset, while also facilitating a substantial increase in network size, mimicking the diverse interactions present in biological neural networks. Moreover, we demonstrate that the learned spiking neural networks can efficiently process input data through the incorporation of temporal synchrony signals among neurons, mimicking biological temporal summation. The resulting networks exhibit a striking resemblance to biological brain activity, as observed through electrocorticography recordings, and can potentially be applied in prosthesis development for brain-stimulating therapy. Thorough experimental evaluations validate the novel output encoding method and the effectiveness of spiking neural networks in mimicking biological neural mechanisms. This paper reports on the findings from the 2022 Out-of-Lexicon Word Sense Disambiguation competition, where participants faced a novel 14-gram contextualization challenge. Due to limited participation, comprehensive results from task two (handling unseeded sense pairs) are reported, and we anticipate exploring this aspect further in future competitions. In addition, we reflect on the challenges and potential solutions for tackling the out-of-lexicon problem, considering the current advancements in BERT and other transformer-based models that prioritize frequency over semantic accuracy. It is observed that while these models excel in many areas, they often struggle with clear semantic interpretations in word sense disambiguation tasks. To address this issue, we emphasize the importance of incorporating additional contextual information and leveraging data-driven approaches to improve performance. Furthermore, we acknowledge the constraints of conventional evaluation metrics, which may overlook the effectiveness of certain models, and advocate for the incorporation of more diverse evaluation techniques in subsequent iterations of the competition. Finally, we outline our plans for the next edition of the competition, including enhanced datasets, a broader task spectrum, and improved evaluation methods to provide participants with clearer pre-existing solutions and evaluation criteria. Leveraging the out-of-lexicon approach, we demonstrate a flexible means of incorporating contextualization that can provide valuable insights for both automatic word sense disambiguation and more general natural language understanding. Moreover, this approach can serve as an accessible resource for developing practical applications in areas such as text classification, sentiment analysis, and machine translation, provided that a suitable threshold of lexical coverage is met. To further empower participants and foster cross-pollination of methods, we make available our implemented code, including BERT-based models and exhaustive search models, through an open-source repository on GitHub. This repository includes a comprehensive collection of datasets, including BERT-based and non-BERT-based resources, to facilitate research and development in out-of-lexicon word sense disambiguation. Moreover, we provide participants with a range of configurable hyperparameters and model implementations to aid in the exploration of complementary approaches to address this challenging task. Finally, we report the winning paper from the best paper track of the competition, which focuses on evaluating the performance of various neural network architectures in out-of-lexicon word sense disambiguation. A specific type of chaos expansions can effectively analyze differential equations with uncertain factors by approximating random solutions to such equations, however, verifying the accuracy of these expansions poses a significant challenge. To address this issue, we developed a post-processing method that allows researchers to evaluate the correctness of generalized polynomial chaos expansions in a particular context. This method involves comparing approximate solutions to exact solutions in a designated region, thereby determining the precision of the approximation. By utilizing this method, we were able to provide precise bounds for the errors in approximating random solutions to differential equations, which represents a primary contribution of this study. To illustrate the effectiveness of this approach, we applied it to the study of a Newtonian ball collision, where the outcome was found to be distinct from a previously proposed theoretical model. In contrast to previous work, our analysis reveals that the solution to this problem does not converge uniformly across all dimensions. Rather, we demonstrate the precision of the approximation through the application of our post-processing method, which yields a detailed estimate of the error. Furthermore, our approach reveals that the solution to this problem exhibits singularities in certain high-dimensional scenarios, which were not previously documented in the existing literature. This study represents a pioneering effort to verify the accuracy of generalized polynomial chaos expansions, which holds broad-ranging applications across a variety of fields. By utilizing our post-processing method, researchers can gain a more comprehensive understanding of the precision of approximations derived from generalized polynomial chaos expansions, which includes the derivation of precise error bounds for a range of applications. To facilitate the dissemination of this research, we have released an open-source software package that enables the reproduction of our results, as well as a flexible framework for the implementation of our approach in a diverse array of applications. This software package includes a range of useful tools, including an efficient Monte Carlo method for the evaluation of integrals, which can be applied to the analysis of the precision of approximations in a variety of contexts. Additionally, our approach includes a flexible framework for the representation of complex objects, which can be utilized to study the precision of approximations in a range of applications, including but not limited to Newtonian ball collisions. We anticipate that our research will contribute positively to a range of applications by fostering greater communication and collaboration across a variety of fields, which includes but is not limited to applied mathematics and computer science. Furthermore, our approach holds the potential to inspire further research into the precision of approximations in a range of applications, which we have made publicly accessible through our open-source software package. Alterations in sequential data, such as changes in motion patterns or sound frequencies, can be difficult to detect, especially when hidden within noisy data. In cases where every measurement contains valuable information, identifying these alterations becomes a challenging task. Our approach, called Adaptive Partially-Observed Alteration Identification (APOAI), not only detects changes but also isolates the exact time and sequence of alteration occurrence. To achieve this, APOAI relies on a non-parametric estimation of uncertainty levels in data and compares them to a threshold, determined by an optimized margin of safety. As a variation of APOAI, APOAI-E (Early Warning) helps prevent alterations to occur in the future. Our method is robust, efficient, and effective, as demonstrated by its successful application to real-world datasets of human gait and instrument sounds. Additionally, APOAI-E enables early interventions to prevent potential problems. Our source code is publicly available at a GitHub repository. Furthermore, to facilitate the use of APOAI in other fields, we provide publicly accessible datasets of alteration-embedded signals, captured through a custom-built laboratory setup. These datasets can be accessed at a publicly available web interface. Our work integrates APOAI and offers comprehensive integration guides, as well as a step-by-step tutorial on detecting alterations in a given video. APOAI has numerous practical applications and can be employed in various domains to detect alterations in sequential data, such as monitoring systems to detect failures, audio systems to detect noise or changes in voice, as well as medical equipment to detect patients' recovery or deterioration. We developed a new approach to understanding dwarf galaxies based on their chemical composition and the history of star formation within them. This methodology leverages detailed analysis of chemical data from various elements within galaxies, enabling accurate comparisons with simulations of galaxy evolution. Specifically, we utilized chemical abundance predictions from the numerical simulation ARcheon, applying a machine learning tool to identify the ideal input format that yielded the most accurate matching between simulation and observation. Our analysis focused on two key aspects: the distribution of chemical abundances and the timing of star formation. Regarding chemical abundances, the distribution of metals in dwarf galaxies can be accurately represented by a single parameter, which reflects both the overall metal content and the rate of chemical enrichment. This finding aligns with predictions from simulations, indicating that chemical evolution can be effectively described using parameter space of two variables. Furthermore, we observed a correlation between the average age of stars and the metal content in dwarf galaxies, which can be explained through the mechanism of gas inflow followed by star formation. Specifically, regions with lower metal content tend to have older star populations, which contradicts the standard model suggesting a linear relationship between metal content and star age. Additionally, we analyzed the mass of gas available for star formation in dwarf galaxies, which can be effectively modeled using a dependent relationship on stellar mass. Specifically, the available gas mass decreases steadily with increasing stellar mass, which holds true even at very low stellar masses. Lastly, we noted that although dwarf galaxies generally follow generally uniform evolutionary paths, there are notable exceptions. Specifically, some dwarf galaxies exhibit unique characteristics despite sharing similar properties with others. Furthermore, certain regions within galaxies can be accurately matched to others despite differences in their initial conditions, which suggests that their respective evolutionary paths may have converged. The current study serves as a foundation for a broader research goal, which aims to understand galaxy evolution through detailed analysis of chemical composition, star formation history, and other key astronomical indicators. Furthermore, the methodology developed here can be applied not only to dwarf galaxies but also to various other cosmic objects, which possess abundant chemical data. Ultimately, this research can be further developed into an inverse modeling framework, which utilizes chemical data to constrain simulations of galaxy evolution, thereby providing a mutually beneficial collaboration between observations and simulations. This will enable us to accurately match the outcomes of galaxy evolution simulations with real-world observations, which in turn can be used to make precise predictions about the future galaxy evolution. Given a profinite group G, an action spectrum can be defined, which is a collection of homotopy invariants, effectively classifying parabolic subgroups of G. These invariants exhibit crucial properties, including homotopy invariance, completeness, and the ability to distinguish between non-equivalent parabolic subgroups. Furthermore, the invariants can be extended to groupoids and linear algebraic groups, providing a clearer understanding of the invariants in these contexts. Additionally, the invariants of a subgroup or groupoid H, given that it satisfies specific solvability conditions, can be computed effectively by identifying a maximal set of subgroups or groupoids that are both closed and open in G. Such a strategy has significant applications in the study of moduli of curves, abstract groups, and Galois groups, and it offers potential avenues for research in these fields. The invariants also possess an iterative or'stratified' structure, which could be exploited to gain further insights into the nature of these invariants and their potential uses. The concepts and results presented here, involving action spectra and groupoids, are original ideas, whereas the application of these ideas to linear algebraic groups is an investigation of existing research, as proposed by J. A recent surge in the use of Artificial Intelligence has led to a high demand for labeled data, which is typically obtained through expensive annotation services. For visually rich data sets such as documents, visually-grounded transformation techniques can partially replace the need for full annotation, reducing the costs associated with labeling. However, such approaches are not suitable for data sets such as documents, because they often rely on visually intrinsic transformation models that assume a high level of visual understanding in the target format. As this approach requires extensive training on the target format, it can be impractical and expensive to train on rare formats such as historical documents.  This paper proposes a new, more flexible approach called Semi-Visual Mapping which can be applied to a wider range of data sets including those with low visual quality.  A comprehensive comparison of our approach with existing methods on visually rich data sets reveals that Semi-Visual Mapping delivers superior results, confirming its potential as a cost-effective solution for extracting data from diverse visual sources such as images and documents.  The proposed framework, named DeepDoc, based on Semi-Visual Mapping, outperformed existing competition by a significant margin, achieving near-perfect accuracy of 98.4\% on extracting data from digitized documents, exceeding the best competing method by over 10\% in accuracy.
