Deep, wide, and complex Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are increasingly being employed, leading to a significant rise in their computational and memory requirements. To address these issues, CNNs are being optimized through pruning, which leads to a more efficient and manageable model, but may also affect their accuracy. The problem arises when training such a model, as most pruning methods focus on improving inference efficiency but fail to account for the complexities of training a wide and deep model after pruning. A notable exception is the approach of continuing training the pruned model, but this approach often requires the replacement of original sub-layers in order to accommodate the pruned weights, resulting in a loss of control over the optimal structure of the original model. ClickTrain is an innovative training system that addresses these issues by preserving the original model structure during the training process of the pruned model, effectively eliminating any discrepancies between the original and pruned models. The system achieves this through a series of refined and detailed transformations of the original sub-layers, including the creation of proxy sub-layers, proxy weights, and proxy non-linearities, in order to effectively utilize the original model structure during training. ClickTrain offers a versatile approach that is compatible with various pruning methods and can be applied to a range of models, as evidenced by its superior performance in achieving high accuracy on the ImageNet dataset when applied to the pruned ResNet and MobileNet models. The system's code is openly available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/jdabbagh93/ClickTrain. The repository includes the code for ClickTrain as well as a range of useful tools and APIs to support the implementation of ClickTrain at the API level. The 2017 observation of a binary neutron star merger by LIGO and Virgo spurs research on identifying gravitational waves generated by neutron star-black hole collisions, presenting opportunities and challenges for classification algorithms. Prior studies on neutron star binary mergers' signal identification and classification serve as a baseline, but faced difficulties in distinguishing signals from noise, highlighting the need for improved detection techniques. Emerging deep learning methods, capable of learning complex patterns from data, offer promising solutions. A team recently used deep learning to identify and classify gravitational waves produced by neutron star-black hole collisions, based on simulated signals, and achieved an 99% accuracy in distinguishing true signals from background noise using a convolutional neural network. By incorporating a sequence of gravitational wave templates, they enhanced the classification accuracy to 70% for neutron star-black hole collisions, comparable to 80% for black hole binary mergers. This achievement lays a foundation for employing deep learning in multi-messenger astronomy's pursuit of a comprehensive understanding of neutron star-black hole collisions' physical phenomena. Furthermore, with deep learning-trained models, scientists can explore novel applications such as rapid alert systems for electromagnetic counterparts during actual gravitational wave detections. These deep learning models also exhibit contractual behavior, enabling estimation of signals that have been distorted by noise. Although contracting transformations accurately represent the effects of noise on gravitational wave templates, they are insufficient in accurately modeling neutron star-black hole collisions, due to the numerous unknown aspects of these events. Consequently, while deep learning-trained models can accurately identify and classify actual gravitational waves, their applicability to pure binary neutron star mergers remains limited. Nevertheless, with an understanding of the uncertainties surrounding neutron star-black hole collisions, deep learning can contribute to improved electromagnetic counterpart triggers from gravitational wave data. This study's results illustrate the potential for deep learning to enhance our knowledge of neutron star-black hole collisions, refining our understanding of these binary mergers and the phenomena observed during the event GW190410. Additionally, with deep learning-trained models, researchers can analyze the characteristics of individual gravitational waves, such as the binary's mass and spin at the moment of collision, enabling new areas of study. A notable instance is the analysis of GW190410, where deep learning correctly identified the event as a neutron star-black hole collision, and accurately predicted the binary's mass and spin within a specific range, in line with the estimated uncertainties from LIGO and Virgo's detection. This research introduces a groundbreaking approach to recognizing handwritten mathematical expressions by leveraging a pre-trained language model. Unlike traditional methods that depend on visual features, we've achieved remarkable results by utilizing a data-driven method, achieving a remarkable character error rate of 33.67% on the Math dataset after fine-tuning. Notably, our strategy surpasses the previous best performance, a character error rate of 35.19%, achieved through a complex rule-based method, exemplifying the efficacy of pre-trained language models in capturing semantic mathematical meanings. Furthermore, we've developed an innovative offline ground truth creation technique and offline recognition method, facilitating the use of modern speech-to-text technologies in a pencil-and-paper learning environment. Our findings reveal that, after fine-tuning, a pre-trained model can accurately recognize mathematical expressions even when ground truth data differs due to writing styles, achieving a character error rate of 33.67%. Additionally, we've analyzed the most challenging recognition tasks and identified positions where errors typically occur. The relationship between recognition errors and proximity to these challenging positions demonstrates the influence of location on recognition performance. These breakthroughs open the door to employing pre-trained language models in offline mathematical expression recognition, thereby enabling a broader range of applications in computer vision. We investigate supersymmetric quantum systems through the lens of morphism bundles in algebraic geometry. Our analysis reveals a connection between superselection sectors, which arise from extended cohomology classes in moduli spaces of morphism bundles, and Borel-Moore homology classes of moduli spaces. This relationship enables us to decompose superselection sectors into manageable components called topological solitons, which are effectively zero-dimensional supersymmetric quantum systems. Additionally, by considering the functorial nature of cohomology classes, we demonstrate how superselection sectors are aggregated through tensor products. Furthermore, our framework allows for a general formal expansion of sheaf cohomology classes as superselection sectors, which can be applied to diverse contexts including supersymmetric quantum mechanics and quantum field theories. Finally, supersymmetric quantum mechanics is exemplified through the study of linear systems in optics, encompassing the two-photon scenario, and our theoretical expansions are explicitly calculated in this specific case. Our work provides a unified algebraic geometric approach to supersymmetric quantum systems, extending the reach of algebraic geometric methods to the broad domain of superselection sectors. Moreover, our analysis opens up avenues for employing algebraic geometric tools in the unique examination of supersymmetric quantum dynamics. One such tool is the moduli space itself, which emerges as an indispensable resource for understanding superselection sectors. Our framework also unveils previously unseen connections between distinct fields, notably supersymmetric quantum mechanics and sheaf cohomology, whose links might be of independent interest to experts in these fields. Lastly, our study culminates by addressing open questions at the intersection of supersymmetric quantum mechanics and algebraic geometry, thereby paving the way for further research and development. Our work can also be seen as an extension of our previous published work, notably arXiv:2102.02169, and arXiv:2010.06594, where the fundamental ideas were first explored. Our research does, however, include novel contributions that are grounded in an in-depth case study of linear systems in optics. Our study reveals how the geometric structure of moduli spaces of morphism bundles, which may appear abstract, is actually manifested in the concrete, real-world context of linear systems in optics. Our analysis enables the translation of geometric concepts into the practical, physical language of linear systems, thereby establishing a direct link between supersymmetric quantum mechanics and the tangible world of linear systems. Our work therefore holds the potential for either initiating or supplementing research in supersymmetric quantum mechanics, depending on the level of detail one chooses to employ

Our primary goal is to explore how interactions behave in large, intricate networks where multiple factors coexist and influence each other. We develop a mathematical framework to analyze these interactions one by one, analyzing their patterns and relationships across different variables. This framework enables us to identify interactions that consistently emerge and vary reliably, as opposed to those that are fragile and alter frequently. To apply this approach, we create a simplified model of a network consisting of interconnected components, allowing us to analyze the process of interactions through stability analysis. Our findings demonstrate that variability in interactions is intricately connected to the stability of the entire network, affecting how interactions change over time. This new approach opens up possibilities for further investigation into the intricacies of interactions within complex systems. To showcase the applicability of our method, we apply it to the study of microbial ecosystems, examining how interactions with the environment influence the variability of interactions within those ecosystems. Our analysis reveals that the variability of these interactions declines as the interactions with the environment become more intense, and we propose an explanation for this phenomenon based on the original framework. Ultimately, we conclude that the underlying structure of the environment contributes to the patterns of variability in interactions, and we suggest a direction for future research to uncover the direct effect of the environment on these interactions. This study lays the groundwork for a deeper understanding of the intricacies of interactions within complex systems, and the resulting knowledge could be utilized to make predictive models of periods of stability separated by intervals of turbulence, as observed in microbial ecosystems and potentially other intricate networks. Furthermore, this research offers a novel approach to analyzing and interpreting the variability of interactions, and we expect this variation to be a universal characteristic of interactions in intricate systems. Lastly, we observe that this interaction process is akin to the mechanism by which molecules eliminate unnecessary information, effectively eliminating 'noise' from their surroundings to maintain order. In essence, the variability of interactions is a test of the system's tolerance for disorder before it reaches a critical threshold and the system collapses. We suggest that this tolerance for disorder could be harnessed as a form of storage or energy within microbial ecosystems and other intricate networks, where the disorder is tapped into and exploited for the benefit of the system. This concept presents a new perspective on the interplay between stability and variability, and we intend to pursue this idea in a future study. require advanced planning and execution strategies due to shifting ground patterns
at multiple layers. In comparison to two-dimensional navigation systems, three-dimensional
structures present increased complexity with obstacles, gaps, and changes in terrain
heights that must be accounted for. To overcome these challenges, this research aims to
develop an algorithm for navigating through any three-dimensional environment.
Currently, the team using sonar sensors to detect obstacles in real-time faces limitations
of slow processing speeds in the ground robot system, hindering immediate decision-
making abilities. To resolve this issue, we are incorporating a stratified navigation controller
already developed by the team into a faster ground robot system equipped with sonar
sensors for immediate obstacle detection and avoidance. The newly integrated system
will enable the ground robot to navigate through any environment in real-time by leveraging
the fast processing capabilities provided by the fusion of data from real-time sonar sensors. 
In particular, we address the challenge of fast ground robot navigation in any three-dimensional
environment by integrating real-time sonar sensors with the existing controller: Stratified
Navigation Controller. To evaluate the effectiveness of our real-time sonar integration,
several laboratory tests were conducted in diverse ground patterns. The results show a
significant improvement in processing times, enabling the ground robot to navigate through
any three-dimensional environment in real-time. The code for this project has been openly
shared at the following link: https://github.com/robotics-ai/real-time-sonar-integration. 
This research will contribute to the field of autonomous navigation by providing an efficient
solution for navigating through any three-dimensional environment in controllable and
uncontrollable environments. Additionally, the team's approach to integrating real-time sonar

obstacle detection and real-time navigation capabilities. To expand on these findings, multiple
applications are presented, such as navigating through fields with growing crops and
forest paths with understory vegetation. The integration of real-time sonar sensors can further

A new type of superconductivity resulting from multiple electron interactions is studied, specifically in a system featuring flat energy bands created by a strong magnetic field near the surface of a topological insulator.  In this unique flat band superconductivity, multiple electrons can interact with each other directly, contrasting with traditional superconductors that rely on electron interactions with lattice vibrations.  We find that under specific conditions, the interaction among multiple electrons stabilizes a novel superconducting phase, characterized by an increased number of coherence lengths in comparison to traditional superconductors.  Furthermore, we observe that this superconducting phase exhibits multiple gap functions that vary in size, with all gaps closing collectively as the superconducting phase transitions to the insulating phase at a critical threshold of interaction strength.  Notably, this superconducting mechanism may also occur in other systems featuring flat energy bands.  Therefore, we propose an experimental design using ultra-low-temperature scanning tunneling microscopy to investigate this superconducting mechanism in a platinum film.  Such an investigation has the potential to validate our theoretical predictions of multiple-body superconductivity.  Additionally, we speculate that this superconducting mechanism could serve as a starting point for understanding and potentially replicating the superconducting properties of the high-temperature superconducting material, doped cesium cobaltate.  Specifically, we recognize similarities between the magnetic field-induced flat energy bands in topological insulators and the flat energy bands present in doped cesium cobaltate, suggesting that the multiple-body superconductivity we studied could also be a contributing factor to the superconducting properties of doped cesium cobaltate.  Therefore, further research into this effect in doped cesium cobaltate is warranted to fully elucidate its role in the material's high-temperature superconductivity.  Finally, we acknowledge that this superconducting mechanism may also be a component of another candidate for high-temperature superconductivity, hole-doped iridium arsenide, due to the presence of multiple electron interactions and flat energy bands, potentially resulting in superconductivity, although we note that a detailed theoretical investigation of this system is required to confirm the relevance of multiple-body superconductivity.  Therefore, further research is needed to fully understand the superconducting mechanism in hole-doped iridium arsenide.  Conversely, we propose that scanning tunneling spectroscopy could serve as an experimental method to investigate and confirm the role of multiple-body superconductivity in iridium arsenide as well

This research examines various clustering techniques suitable for dimensional data representing the presence or absence of molecular characteristics across different samples. Unlike traditional data, such representations yield distances and similarities that are inherently non-metric, necessitating the adaptation of existing clustering methods or the development of new approaches. Alternatively, transforming non-metric data into a metric format, such as ultrametric or tree-like structure, is another possibility. The author compares and contrasts different clustering methods, highlighting their strengths and weaknesses in a theoretical context. Notably, some of these clustering methods were initially applied to the analysis of microbiome data but have never been directly compared on a dataset specifically designed to illustrate the challenges posed by dimensional data. The evaluation involves a comprehensive analysis of various clustering techniques, including traditional hierarchical clustering, k-means, MCLUST, SLink, SHINE, CLADO, ADPClust, and a novel hierarchical approach developed through an online application. The results suggest that each method has inherent advantages and disadvantages, and a thorough understanding of the underlying principles is essential to make informed decisions about data analysis. The author recommends a combination of graphical and statistical tools to aid in the diagnosis and effective use of these clustering methods. The success of the state-based hierarchical approach in capturing the true classes suggests that this type of clustering method is particularly suitable for dimensional data, and the availability of R code for this method may encourage its adoption. The effectiveness of CLADO and ADPClust in classifying the data also indicates that distance-based clustering methods can be adapted to handle dimensional data, and further developments in this area may yield valuable approaches for dimensional data representation. The author proposes three general directions for future research: the exploration of adaptive clustering techniques, the application of dimensional data to the analysis of single-cell transcriptomics data, and the extension of the hierarchical clustering method to accommodate multi-dimensional data. Furthermore, the author acknowledges readers for their valuable comments and suggestions, and seizes the opportunity to incorporate these comments into the existing text, particularly in the sections regarding the applications of dimensional data and single-cell transcriptomics. The author also clarifies the role of SHINE and SLink, and provides an updated version of the hierarchical clustering method, CLADO, and ADPClust, alongside a comprehensive guide to running these algorithms on a test dataset. The author also shares a long-standing hypothesis on dimensional data, and its connection to the applications of spectral graph decomposition and deep learning in data analysis. In recent years, salient item identification (SII) has garnered significant focus within the research community due to its numerous practical applications in daily life. SII can be viewed as a distinct variant of the salient object segmentation task, where the primary goal is to identify individually isolated objects of distinct saliency. Existing approaches to SII are found to be inadequate, as they fail to effectively tackle novel challenge scenarios involving small, opaque, partially visible, or uniquely textured salient objects. To address these limitations, a novel framework called IntegratedSII (I-SII) is proposed, designed to capture salient objects across both RGB and RGB-D domains through a unified approach. I-SII leverages a dual-cohesive-masking strategy, integrating two distinct masking methods to enhance object isolation and reduce background interference. An experimental evaluation of I-SII is conducted on large datasets, revealing significant performance enhancements over state-of-the-art approaches in terms of both numerical metrics and visual fidelity. Furthermore, comprehensive ablation studies confirm the isolability and robustness of the proposed method, demonstrating its versatility on a range of challenging challenge scenarios. Finally, qualitative comparisons with state-of-the-art techniques in terms of identified salient items reveal I-SII's superiority in accurately detecting salient objects across a diverse range of real-world images. The proposed I-SII framework is found to be effective in salient item identification tasks, outperforming existing approaches and providing a positive contribution to the field. The code and generated results are publicly available for testing and validation at the URL provided in the paper.

A figure in a square grid is considered a palindrome if it reads the same from top to bottom and a mirror image if it reflects symmetry along its diagonal. For each ratio, we examine the limit as the grid size (n) becomes very large, comparing the number of palindromic figures to the number of mirror-image palindromic figures, both with and without central squares, to understand the magnitude of the latter in relation to the former (originally investigated by Chisholm in 2020). Our research extends Chisholm's findings by exploring these ratios for both 2x2 and indefinitely large squares (n x n) while analyzing the computational challenges involved. Additionally, we investigate the distribution of the symmetry group for each type of figure, expressing the count of each type using lattice point intersections in terms of these groups, which enables us to compute the desired ratios for 1x1 and 2x2 squares exactly. To estimate the limit for indefinitely large squares, we approximate the mirror-symmetric figures as rectangles, showing that this approximation converges to the actual ratio as n becomes very large (e.g. n>=100) and verifying a conjecture by Chisholm in the process. Our method also reveals a surprising connection between the proposed ratios and the well-known 'hole in the square' problem, which links the number of valid configurations to the absence of a hole (a filled square) in a grid. Finally, we generalize our results to higher-dimensional spaces, though the computations become increasingly complex and less feasible to complete manually. As such, we outline the approach for completing the investigation in higher dimensions using computer-assisted methods. To demonstrate the efficiency of our technique, we use Mathematica to generate the necessary code and showcase its output for 3x3 and 4x4 squares, which can be modified to apply to any n x n square grid. As such, our research not only verifies an earlier conjecture but also extends and generalizes the investigated problem while also highlighting potential areas for further exploration.

Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively employed in both engineering and medical fields for imaging purposes. However, CT data susceptible to various forms of noise necessitates pre-processing to enhance quality. Additionally, certain industrial applications require the removal of high-frequency vibrations resulting from the scanning process. Our research focuses on enhancing low-quality CT data, with a novel approach tailored to diverse applications. We introduce a statistical noise model that upscaler data sampling, with a corresponding regularization term ensuring smooth data. Moreover, our framework accommodates polyenergetic CT data, a common phenomenon in medical CT scans caused by energy-dependent attenuation. By formulating the attenuation behavior as a first-order partial differential equation (PDE), we propose a novel variational model. Our statistical noise model and PDE attenuation formulation can be combined to effectively remove high-frequency vibrations. Our experimental results, featuring both simulated and real-world data, demonstrate the success of our proposed method in achieving noise reduction, sensor noise suppression, and polyenergetic correction. Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with limited resources remains a complex challenge due to the scarcity of labeled data, extensive character sets, and font variations. Although recent approaches have shown promise, they often require sophisticated and rarely available class balance information, making the problem even more difficult. To overcome this limitation, a new method has been proposed, allowing for the generation of useful training data from unlabelled documents through an automatic analysis of their structures. By processing a document as a whole rather than individual lines or words, the algorithm identifies repeated patterns, potentially representing frequently occurring words, which are then used to enhance the accuracy of HTR models. Preliminary experiments on a real-world dataset indicate that the method can effectively improve performance, particularly in the presence of large class imbalances. Furthermore, the method exhibits adaptable performance across various dataset sizes and can produce consistent results regardless of the algorithm used to create the structured data. The code for the method is available on GitHub at: https://github.com/SebastianHesse/SingleShotStructuring. The dataset used for evaluation can be accessed through the following link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.3725330. Evaluation results suggest that a model trained on unstructured data performs worse compared to one trained using the proposed method, especially in the presence of imbalanced classes. While the performance may not improve at the level of balanced data, the method demonstrates a more consistent and robust performance across various dataset sizes. The best performance is achieved when combining the proposed method with a balanced dataset, indicating that the value of the method lies in its ability to enhance models that are already trained on balanced datasets, allowing for more efficient training times and improved accuracy. The most notable enhancement in performance is observed in the frequency-based evaluation metric, indicating that the method is more effective for character recognition tasks rather than word recognition tasks. An analysis of the generated data structures has been conducted, revealing that the method effectively identifies lines and words across various datasets, also confirming that the algorithm can tolerate varying levels of noise in the data without adversely affecting its performance. The efficacy of the method has been confirmed through a comprehensive comparison with alternative approaches, also validating the distribution of generated data to be more uniform compared to unstructured data training methods. The proposed method has been confirmed to be competitive with other data structuring algorithms while also outperforming models that receive balanced training data, also allowing for a notable reduction in the required dataset size for training models to achieve similar performance levels. Focusing on the isomers $^{226}$Ra and $^{243}$Am, our analysis combined theoretical results with experimental findings to gain deeper insights into nuclear architecture. Specifically, we examined the isomers' energy differences, decay modes, and structural characteristics within a $^{132}$Sn core. Our calculations successfully merged the principles of the Hartree-Fock and HFB methods with the MCSCF approach based on small basis sets. These merged results not only validated the isomer's stability but also accurately predicted the energy differences and decay modes, thereby confirming a positive quadratic mass dependence for $f_2$ and a zero slope for $f_4$ in the Am isomer decay. Furthermore, our analysis highlighted the significance of incorporating higher-order drift phases in nuclear wave functions to achieve convergence. Our method of merging theoretical approaches can serve as a modular tool for analyzing complex nuclear structures and designing experiments. Additionally, our study has important implications for nuclear reactor physics and decay heat estimation in long-lived and beta-decaying nuclei. Our research paves the way for merging computational techniques to study light nuclear clusters and, more broadly, their hadronic counterparts. Lastly, our analysis underscores the interconnectedness of theoretical tools in nuclear physics and showcases their seamless integration to attain a higher level of understanding in analyzing nuclear structures, decay modes, and particle radiation phenomena. To enhance our understanding, we recommended conducting more Monte Carlo simulations grounded in variational approaches and performing extensive decay heat estimates. These proposed actions are likely to yield valuable insights into nuclear architecture and facilitate decay heat estimates in long-lived beta-decaying nuclei. To achieve this, we would utilize the full range of variational approaches and perform precise decay heat estimates, thereby refining our understanding of nuclear structures and decay modes in the analyzed isomers and other heavy nuclei. High-performance computing on GPUs heavily relies on efficient memory management to achieve optimal performance. Despite the availability of automatic memory management in programming languages, unnecessary memory allocations can impede GPU performance, leading to over-subscription and decreased efficiency. To refine the memory usage of GPU applications, a novel dynamic memory allocator called DynaSOAr has been developed, featuring an innovative scheme that conquers memory allocation hurdles on GPUs. DynaSOAr employs an optimized policy to maximize memory efficiency through optimized memory access, outperforming current state-of-the-art allocators and achieving up to a 5.8 times speedup in allocation operations over a benchmark test. To further enhance the overall quality of the resulting application, DynaSOAr includes a forward-compression feature that minimizes memory waste, resulting in improved memory usage and simplified memory management, ultimately leading to a substantial 3.2 times speedup in some GPU applications. To facilitate its inclusion in existing GPU applications, DynaSOAr allocates memory in a device-agnostic manner, allowing it to be easily integrated into widely-used programming frameworks and ensuring a high level of stability and compatibility. Furthermore, DynaSOAr is a completely automatic memory allocator, eliminating the need for developers to modify the code of existing applications for its utilization. To showcase the superiority of DynaSOAr, a set of comprehensive benchmark experiments were performed, revealing that memory management represents a significant performance bottleneck in some practical GPU applications, but whose solution leads to a considerable performance improvement through the use of DynaSOAr. This comprehensive material is made available to the public under a flexible licensing model to foster the inclusion of DynaSOAr in a large number of existing GPU applications. A specific challenge arises from the degradation of semiconductor sensors in magnetic fields, particularly concerning strain and temperature, which hampers accuracy. Investigating the longitudinal vibration of a cylindrical shell as a semiconductor sensor substitute, this study focuses on the effects of internal pressure and surface heating. Utilizing the finite element method, the authors analyzed a simplified model of a particle detector coil, subjected it to various loads, and mapped its mechanical behavior. Comparing the results to existing literature on monocrystalline silicon, the investigation concludes with a exploration of a possible probe to test the detector's structural stability. Ultimately, this research aims to enhance understanding of detector accuracy and reliability under real-world conditions.

In applications requiring high reliability, certain classes of probability distribution over complex events must be guaranteed to contain credible versions of a target distribution, rather than merely resembling them. The notion of credal reliability controls the likelihood of invalidating a Bayesian network's confidence in predicting certain conditions, given uncertain evidence. While existing techniques can analyze the reliability of simple probabilistic models, their computational efficiency deteriorates as complexity increases. Although approximate methods for credal reliability analysis are available, they may not always guarantee an error margin of less than one percent. To improve on this, we introduce a more robust approach to assessing credal reliability in the form of probabilistic bounds. By introducing adjustable looseness factors to structural constraint analysis, we develop a more precise method for evaluating the reliability of convolved probability distributions, at a manageable computational cost. The resulting framework provides a flexible strategy for refining the precision of reliability approximations, at the expense of increased computation time. The proposed method offers a useful strategy for confirming the reliability of Bayesian network predictions in practical applications. The approach can be applied to a wide range of probabilistic models by selecting a suitable level of looseness, at the cost of potentially less precise results, rather than relying solely on time-efficient, but less reliable approximations. The method's efficiency and effectiveness are illustrated through numerical examples. The source code for this research is available at https://github.com/jase-clarkson/CredalReliability. A generalized quadrangle (GQ) is a geometry where two distinct points determine a line. A set of points in a GQ is called a neighbor-transitive code if it includes all points that lie on the lines shared by a given set of vertices. We are investigating the neighbor-transitive codes in GQs that consist entirely of rational points. A particular class of these codes includes the elements of a rational hyperbolic plane. This research also delves into the partial hyperbolic planes found in GQs and the linear codes that correspond to them. A partial hyperbolic plane in a GQ is similar to a hyperbolic plane but may be comprised of fewer pairs of distinct points. We have successfully identified all the neighbor-transitive codes in the GQs that correspond to the linear and linearized Arrangements A4 and A3 respectively. The Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) at the heart of the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) is an intriguing region that is both mass-rich and velocity-displaced.  This study delves into the construction of a novel two-dimensional spectrum analysis technique to determine the mass distribution pattern in the CMZ's plane, based on the established two-dimensional velocity field map.  To achieve this, we develop a new approach for identifying equivalent features in two-dimensional spectra and employ a calibration method that utilizes a Gaussian function to measure the amplitude of each feature.  By applying this technique to a map generated from molecular line velocity data, we obtain a clear, high-resolution visual representation of the CMZ's mass arrangement.  This new method enhances our understanding of the CMZ's structure and helps to clarify the pattern of mass displacement within the region.  Furthermore, we calculate the average mass density of the CMZ, with the results suggesting that the region holds approximately 6.5% of the LMC's total molecular gas mass, though this estimate may vary depending on the assumed expansion velocity and total cloud mass.  This research provides valuable insights for further investigations of the CMZ's dynamics and helps to build a more comprehensive understanding of the region's morphology and evolution.  It is also an essential contribution that can be applied more broadly to the analysis of similar astrophysical structures in the far future.

To unlock the full potential of fourth generation light sources, it's crucial to develop highly sensitive and sensitive enough detection systems that can effectively use the intense flux provided by these sources. To accomplish this, we've created an advanced electron group rate framework for achieving ultra-high resolution XANES (X-ray Absorption Near-Edge Spectroscopy). Our approach combines elements of traditional rate-based models, probabilistic methods, and Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulations to model the behavior of electrons during the absorption process. Our model employs discrete electron groups with specific characteristics and a probability distribution for electron transitions. Our results demonstrate that this model can produce high-resolution spectra from data streams containing intense flux, surpassing the capabilities of conventional integration and detection methods. To validate our model, we've applied it to simulate data from the N K-edge absorption of nitrogen gas and compared the resulting spectrum to the reference spectrum provided by the X-ray absorption fine structure (XAFS) standard database. Our analysis shows that our model can produce high-quality spectra with lower noise at much lower count rates, achieving a signal-to-noise ratio that is ten times better than conventional methods at a 100 times higher count rate. Our work on this rate framework represents a significant breakthrough in detecting and analyzing data in the presence of intense flux, and we believe it has the potential to greatly enhance the analysis of experimental data obtained from fourth generation light sources and similar facilities. Additionally, we acknowledge the access to light sources provided by National Synchrotron Light Source II, Brookhaven National Laboratory, and Diamond Light Source that assisted in our research. Our method identifies and connects a subset of the network's vertices, establishing a constant ratio between distances within the resulting structure, while also allowing efficient computation using local information. To generalize this concept, we develop a new class of distributed algorithms for spanning trees and trees that approximate short paths in the network. Furthermore, we propose a distributed algorithm for creating a spanner on the Internet, specifically utilizing a heuristic that combines local information with query data from network devices to rapidly identify a substantial vertex subset. Our results will be further integrated into a practical system, demonstrating the effectiveness of these concepts in real-world Internet applications. To demonstrate the efficacy of these concepts in real-world Internet applications, we showcase a working implementation of the algorithm in a network of billions of IP addresses, showcasing both its accuracy and efficiency under query limitations. To achieve this, we developed novel distributed spanner construction algorithms for various network topologies, yielding improvements over five prior approaches in terms of vertex approximation ratio, efficiency, and applicability to diverse topologies. Finally, we present a new query-efficient algorithm for the distributed minimum spanning tree problem, yielding an improvement over the previous best known approach by a factor of $\ln n$ and facilitating tree construction from linear network information, evaluating the potential impact when applied to the Internet. improving device classification accuracy. By accurately classifying devices, users can 
identify gadgets that draw excessive power, preventing wastage of energy in the future.

synergizes expense monitoring and feature selection techniques to enhance IoT device 
classification efficiency. By minimizing redundant features, EFS minimizes computation 
costs, allowing users to achieve better classification results with lower overhead.

reducing computational expenses compared to existing methods. As such, EFS offers a 
viable solution for companies selling IoT devices to monitor their clients' energy usage

purchase decision. This experiment also proves the feasibility of online, real-time device 
monitoring to aid classification and waste energy detection for various IoT devices on

loss and save resources by detecting inactive or idle devices to select the right devices

The study provides a comprehensive look at these logics through the lens of algebraic and relational semantics, citing relevant results from the existing literature and presenting new results in addition to some notable extensions. In unsupervised bilingual learning, various techniques have been developed to learn a word translation dictionary without manually labeling a training set. This paper explores a novel approach that utilizes an unaligned training corpus to establish a dictionary between two languages on a single machine, with no external bilingual resources except for a comprehensive web dictionary. Additionally, it introduces a simplified word embedding learning method and a 'find-the-matching-needle-in-a-haystack' strategy to enhance translation accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods, outperforming existing techniques in most cases. A detailed analysis is provided to elucidate the significance of each component. All source code is freely accessible at https://github.com/aleju/unsupervised_bilingual_learning.

We suggest a distorted resolvent method to build Nash equilibria in extensive games. Our approach involves taking the distorted resolvent of the mixed strategy stationarity condition, a concept similar to Fédonné's idea of taking the resolvent of a matrix. This new method can be efficiently computed using linear complementarity problems, and it enables us to obtain rigorous analytical approximations of Nash equilibria by varying a parameter under strict condition. To showcase the effectiveness of our proposal, we apply it to two notable economic problems: oligopolistic competition in a particular market space and a repeated game scenario, and we further establish and explain the limitations of our approach via numerical examples and a detailed numerical analysis. One key finding indicates that under certain conditions, solutions obtained through our method converge to the true Nash equilibrium as the parameter approaches a specific value within the interval (0,1). Additionally, while solutions may diverge as the parameter reaches either extreme of the interval, we observe through numerical examples that some Nash equilibrium properties can still be discerned or at least some form of extensive game solution that adheres to certain criteria can be identified. Achieving single-pixel images in various quantum imaging techniques is a major goal, particularly for sensing applications at a fundamental level. Two main methods, interaction-free measurement and entanglement-based approaches, have been developed to this end. Yet, both methods have significant drawbacks in real-world applications due to requirements of either visible, direction-specific photons or shared states between pixels. These limitations make the techniques impractical for single-pixel quantum visualization, notably when dealing with rare events and low illumination conditions. Here's a different approach. We introduce a novel scheme for single-pixel quantum visualization that utilizes unseen photons exclusively. By leveraging the properties of neural networks, our method enables single-pixel imaging even in the absence of measurable photons. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by achieving high-contrast ratios in both direct and indirect detection settings. Furthermore, we successfully apply the scheme to its first practical use case – imaging beyond current CMOS detector limitations – with promising results. The novel technique enables single-pixel imaging from the detection of photons below current technological limits and paves the way for sensing rare events and transitioning to the quantum regime. It also boasts enhanced resilience to various forms of noise, thus demonstrating an alternative solution for single-pixel quantum visualization. We visualize the project outline, data processing pipeline, and the connection between our approach and the band-limited nature of light, showcasing its potential for single-pixel quantum sensing, over conventional pixelated sensors. We validate the image quality by analyzing its resolution, contrast ratio, and the process of single-pixel image generation, along with demonstrating the sensitivity to 930 nm wavelength – a quantum regime well beyond the current camera limitations. Finally, we verify the image by checking its accuracy and demonstrating its functionality in the "single-pixel and seeing single photons" regime, thereby successfully completing the first quantum visualization of an unseen photon and opening up new avenues for single-pixel in situ quantum sensing applications. This research may be applied to various fields such as computational physics, cryogenic imaging, single-photon astronomy, and quantum medicine, among others, by employing only the techniques and hardware currently available to us. The flow of complex liquids with surfactants is heavily influenced by various mechanisms, a phenomenon that has been extensively researched for decades. Despite significant advancements, a recent study reveals that surface tension plays a crucial role in the flow of liquid foams, especially at high velocities. This is remarkable, considering surfactants are known to mitigate surface tension. To explain these findings, the researchers developed a model incorporating roughness of the glass walls of the cell used in rheology experiments. When the surfaces of the cells are smooth, surfactants dominate the flow. However, at higher velocities and with rough surfaces, the impact of surface tension becomes predominant. This new understanding of foam flow challenges existing theories and may lead to more accurate predictions in this field. Additionally, the researchers observed the creation of persistent channels during flow, a phenomenon further investigated using X-ray microtomography. These channels, resulting from the interaction of surface tension and roughness, pose significant implications for the flow of liquid foams. The study not only offers insights into this unique flow but also connects it to broader phenomena, such as dry friction, and may help develop a universal model for this field. Lastly, the researchers observed that rough surfaces can lead to foams exhibiting elastic as well as plastic behavior, a discovery that expands the understanding of foam dynamics. This research may enable new applications of liquid foams and contribute to a deeper understanding of their behavior. The study was published in a journal with high impact in the field of physical research and is authored by a team of researchers from the CNRS, University of Lyon, and University of Montpellier. The experiment was conducted at the European Synchrotron Radiation Source in France, yielding novel results and insights into the underlying mechanisms of liquid foam flow. Recent research has revealed that Transformer encodings can function as robust visual features in the absence of supervision. However, these unsupervised methods generally fall short of supervised representations in terms of accuracy. To address this, we propose a universal framework that seamlessly integrates Transformers with self-supervised contrastive learning, and leverages auxiliary tasks to enhance representation quality. Our approach, called Transformer in Transfer, utilizes a multi-head Transformer architecture to generate features suitable for a variety of learning strategies. By incorporating three straightforward modifications - using a shared multi-layer perceptron for map projection, adding a stop gradient technique, and employing an momentum encoder - we boost the performance of the contrastive loss and establish a new state-of-the-art outcome. Furthermore, our experiment demonstrates that incorporating downstream task-specific fine-tuning and a range of trait development methods such as distillation, re-ranking, and gradient alignment can significantly enhance the accuracy of our traits. These methods, integrated into our framework, achieve a record 73.0% top-1 accuracy on the ImageNet validation set, and offer a range of flexible options for developing and fine-tuning traits on specific downstream tasks. Additionally, our traits exhibit exceptional transferability on various benchmark datasets, and demonstrate a range of innovative applications in benchmark tasks. The proposed approach, code, and datasets are publicly available at https://www.robots.ox.ac.uk/~vgg/research/transformer-in-transfer.

A novel method called unsupervised information-hiding steganography (UIS) is introduced, allowing a sender and receiver to exchange information while keeping the steeganalyzer uncertain about its presence. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach delivers exceptional performance in stegananomaly tasks. Our approach is the first to tackle both blurring of human subjects and the background motion in images simultaneously. To achieve this, we introduce an innovative architecture that comprises two modules: a dynamic module which learns the optimal filter for a clear image, and a pseudo-blur generator that mimics real-blurring effects typically found in actual captured images. By incorporating both modules, we can accurately remove motion-induced blur from both the subject and the background. Our technique's reliance on pseudo-blur estimates enables the learning of a filter optimal for deblurring, as opposed to relying on conventional sharp pre-estimates. Our experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms existing techniques in image deblurring. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/asharathp/ESHRN. Our dataset of blurred images is also available at https://asharathp.github.io/ESHRN/Dataset.html. Its creation was facilitated by collaboration with actual shop-owners who provided blurred images thereby simulating real-blurring effects. Notably, this is the first time a $5$-colorful graph with high degree has been shown to include a pentuple; a $4$-colorful graph with a pentuple would contradict known results by Hoory and Musha. The approaches developed here can potentially be adapted to examine approximability in other eigenvalue problems. Recent advancements in neural dependency parsing have shown considerable success,
notably through the application of contextualized representations. Despite achieving
subpar results on low-resource languages, our research aims to enhance contextualized
models for dependency analysis via self-learning methods that leverage resourceless
data. We propose a novel, contextualized-dependent self-learning approach that
synergistically integrates supervised and self-supervised learning techniques.
This approach features a unique dependency-aware masking strategy for contextualized
word representations, aiming to mimic the dependency structure in the masked token's
neighborhood. By doing so, the model exploits masked token prediction to learn
dependency relationships. We also establish a mapping between the dependency trees
and the hidden representations of the models, which enables the models to generate
fake cross-sentential dependencies in the self-supervised learning phase.
Through the combination of the two strategies, our contextualized-dependent self-learning
model outperforms the existing state-of-the-art methods on four languages with
limited resources, and also shows comparable results on high-resource languages.
Furthermore, our approach has the advantage of requiring no annotated dependencies
and no need for resource-intensive phrase alignment techniques. The source code of our
model can be accessed at https://github.com/cdswc/DepSSLC.

This research explores the concept of circular and nontransitive likelihoods in relation to voting systems, specifically examining cases where such likelihoods lead to cyclical and anti-transitive rankings of options. We provide a detailed analysis of symmetric circular likelihoods, establishing a fundamental result that their maximum likelihood estimates are uniquely defined. Our research contributes to the extension of existing voting system design methodologies through the utilization of likelihoods, offering a potentially valuable approach for future studies in this field. A key feature of JIT compilers is the ability to dynamically configure the runtime environment, allowing for efficient memory usage by allocating resources on demand.  However, this approach can lead to performance instability due to the overhead of runtime allocations, and is often mitigated by the relatively small startup costs of traditional JIT compilers, which can launch with default runtime configurations and defer optimization until runtime.  This paper explores an alternative strategy in which compile-time optimizations yield single, optimized runtime images, and observes a corresponding correlation between compile-time overhead and improved runtime performance in benchmark testing.  By examining the extent to which benchmark code is amenable to optimization, we seek to understand whether such overhead can be justified in order to attain later performance gains.  While some benchmarks reveal a clear pattern of increased performance in proportion to compile-time costs, others demonstrate over-specialization leading to diminished performance, and in still others, the relationship between compile-time costs and runtime performance is found non-significant at a 95% confidence level.  Notably, it is observed that the costs of producing an optimized runtime image can be substantial, and in some cases, far exceeding the relative differences between the initial and final compile times, and amounting to tens of milliseconds in some cases, and even up to 250ms in others.  These findings encourage the development of more effective heuristics for guiding the specialization of runtime setup, and suggest the utility of statistical analysis in identifying optimal points of balance between compile-time costs and runtime performance.  Furthermore, it is observed that some benchmarks reveal a consistent pattern of improved performance in proportion to compile-time costs, and encourage the continued investigation into the hypothesis that JIT compilation can yield better runtime performance than naive approaches.  Although some benchmarks are found to yield no significant correlation between compile-time costs and runtime performance, these findings are seen as not disconfirming the hypothesis, and instead reveal a need for the development of more robust benchmark suites that can further validate the JIT compilation approach.  To this end, a strategy is proposed for selecting benchmark tests that can help to further establish the relationship between compile-time costs and runtime performance, and it is observed that the resulting extended benchmark suite yields a consistent pattern of improved performance in proportion to compile-time costs.  Finally, it is noted that the investigation into the costs of producing an optimized runtime image can yield valuable insights in their own right, and encourage the continued development of more effective heuristics for guiding the specialization of runtime setup, and suggest the utility of statistical analysis in identifying optimal points of balance between compile-time costs and runtime

The Active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Particle (AOUP) is a stochastic particle motion model that integrates both autonomous propulsion and thermal movement. Propulsion force magnitude and timescales auto-regulate in response to an attractance towards a target location, leading to complex behavior such as ergodicity breakdown and multiple motion patterns around the target. We developed an analytical method for determining the mean speed and efficiency of AOUP dynamics over a wide range of parameters. Our results show that an optimal propulsion force exists to achieve the highest speed in a given time, and that a varied motion pattern near the target may be more efficient than a direct, straight course. We observed that labor, or idle time during the slow phase near the target, affects the particle's overall efficiency, with higher labor leading to increased efficiency in certain parameter ranges. We analyzed the behavior of AOUP in both two and three-dimensional spaces, confirming the existence of an optimal propulsion force in both environments, but revealing a difference in their respective labor-dependent efficiency patterns. Additionally, we derived a condition for determining the most efficient AOUP motion in a d-dimensional space, up to a d value of 4. Our study of AOUP dynamics contributes to our understanding of the active movement of microbial swimmers and their behavior in various environmental contexts. Furthermore, the observed motion patterns and the target-attractance mechanism have parallels in human locomotion, making this research relevant to broader fields of study. We discussed potential applications and implications of these findings for biological motion analysis and potential technological applications of active particle models. Moreover, we commented on potential future research directions in this field, emphasizing the need for numerical simulations to validate the results of our analytical approach in diverse environments, and the potential for active particle models to facilitate new methods in computational physics. By combining theoretical analysis with numerical simulations, researchers can gain new insights into the behavior of active particles and the unique phenomena associated with their autonomous movement. Furthermore, the active particle models hold promise for solving intricate movement problems in biology and technology, where environmental and propulsive timescales interact and affect the trajectory of the moving objects. Additionally, these particle models can contribute to the development of novel algorithms for computational physics that account for autonomous movement in simulations, leading to innovative insights in biological motion and potentially transformative technologies for autonomous vehicles. We noted that numerical simulations, beyond the scope of this analytical study, are required to thoroughly investigate active particle behavior in various environments and to develop computational methods capable of effectively modeling autonomous movement, which could lead to new methods and tools in computational physics and biology. To reduce the expense of creating NLP models for less studied languages, researchers are exploring model transfer across language boundaries. We focus on undertaking a cross-lingual transfer without relying on parallel text data, instead utilizing a diverse range of tasks such as sentiment analysis and name tagging. Our key contribution is the creation of a task representation scheme called TaskDep, enabling the conveyance of task information to a model through a compact, visual representation. TaskDep effectively transmits task-specific details and promotes coherent, task-relevant feature learning across languages. We thoroughly evaluated its effectiveness through comprehensive cross-lingual transfer experiments involving multiple tasks, revealing that TaskDep outperforms control groups and existing cross-lingual pre-training objectives by a significant margin. Importantly, our findings indicate that TaskDep achieves high levels of performance on the target language without receiving any target-language data, highlighting its immense value in cross-lingual transfer scenarios. To facilitate further research, we have released TaskDep along with accompanying code and data repositories for easy access. In complex environments with limited computational resources, training multiple tasks at once using reinforcement learning can be challenging due to the potential for large environmental setup costs. Moreover, the benefit of learning multiple tasks simultaneously is only realized once all tasks are completed, making it an inefficient use of resources in the early stages of training. To address these issues, we present a new approach that allows for the training of multiple tasks in a modular system without the high setup costs and lacks of efficiency in the early stages of training. By breaking down a single large task into multiple smaller tasks, our modular reinforcement learning framework implements a micro-services architecture to balance training multiple tasks simultaneously with the ability to switch between them quickly. Additionally, we introduce a new control mechanism that allows existing tasks to continue execution while new tasks are being trained without interruption. Our experiments, conducted on three different environments with different computational characteristics, demonstrate that our modular approach leads to more efficient training and significant performance gains compared to model-driven multi-task reinforcement training frameworks. Furthermore, our modular approach exhibits comparable results to the top-performing non-linear reinforcement learning methods across different environments. Our code is publicly available for reproduction of the results at https://github.com/yaseen-ahmed/modular-multi-task-reinforcement-learning. Additionally, the results of the experiments can be replicated by running the script 'run_experiment.sh' in the same repository.

Clifford analysis employs the Dirac operator to evaluate partial differential equations on R^n or more complex settings.  We investigate functions u(x) that satisfy the Dirac equation in n-dimensional space u(x) = 0, and our main argument demonstrates that if u is not identically zero, it will have at least three distinct singular points, or else it will be identically zero.  This proof relies on a constructed complex that links u to a non-zero homogeneous function v on the unit sphere S^m-1, and then expresses u via V v, where V represents the gradient operator on R^n.  Consequently, our result implies that the function v can then be analyzed using standard harmonic function principles to show it has at least three singular points.  This proof actually reveals more information - each zero of u will be a non-degenerate singular point.  We also discuss applications of this theorem within Clifford analysis to functions defined in R^n+1 or more complex spaces, and examine the connections between these results and established three-sphere theorems in complex analysis. We investigate complex systems where components interact in a predictable, rule-based manner, resulting in the development of heterochaos - a phenomenon where system disorder initially increases and then decreases over time. Despite its relevance to many fields, heterochaos has not been extensively studied. In this research, we apply the Dyck framework to analyze two prototypical systems: the Hake's thermodynamic system and the Pyragas control system. By utilizing the Dyck framework, we identify periodic, binary, and ternary patterns that correlate with measures of system disorder. These patterns, referred to as "J" and "U" patterns, comprise an essential part of the study. Building upon previous work, we demonstrate that these patterns are inherently linked to the (1+X)th Dyck language and establish the collapsibility of entropy approachability as a fundamental property of the (G,X) Pyragas complex system. Additionally, we expand the Dyck framework by linking it to the concept of entropy, thereby providing a more comprehensive understanding of system disorder. This study not only sheds light on heterochaos but also offers a unified approach to analyzing and modeling complex interactions between order and disorder. Moreover, we believe that our discovery of collapsible entropy approachability will have far-reaching implications, extending beyond the systems examined here to potentially encompass problems like language modeling and data compression. Ultimately, this work lays a foundation for a new direction in nonlinear dynamics research, encompassing a wider range of fields, where the interplay between predictable components and system disorder is explored.

This paper introduces a new generative framework called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet), an autoregressive raw waveform model, to mitigate its computational and memory limitations. We develop QPNet by integrating the Autoregressive IEEE Features model, which incorporates pitch-sensitive dilated convolution neural network (CNN) into WaveNet (WN). We evaluate QPNet on three low-latency tasks, including TDA, pitch tracking, and singer-independent song melody extraction (SIMEM), comparing it to WN and IEEE. The experiments demonstrate that QPNet achieves comparable or superior performance to WN and IEEE features models on these tasks while reducing the computational complexity and memory requirements by a significant margin (approximately 30x and 10x, respectively). Furthermore, QPNet outperforms IEEE on TDA with an overall accuracy of 82.96%, surpassing IEEE with an accuracy of 79.19%. Additionally, QPNet shows greater resilience to adversarial attacks than WN and IEEE, making it a more robust autoregressive generative framework for audio processing. The code for QPNet is available on GitHub at: https://github.com/aurora86/Quasi-Periodic-WaveNet.

Unstructured user feedback yields an overwhelmingly vast user-rating matrix, making key aspects of preference indistinguishable - the individualized nature of each user's taste, the regional concentration of highly rated items, and the subjective objectivity of ratings. These complexities pose significant challenges to traditional CF methods in uncovering user preferences and producing accurate predictions. Our proposed bicluster CF approach addresses these issues by seamlessly integrating individualized user preferences, regionalized item groups, and a uniform rating scale. A novel algorithm is presented that: (1) employs a bicluster model encompassing the intricacies of user preferences and highly recommended items; (2) uses biclustering and entity disambiguation to segregate overlapping user preferences and highly rated item clusters on an item-rating matrix; (3) assigns a uniform scale to user ratings within each bicluster by determining a cohesive group profile, thereby eliminating subjective rating variations and leveraging regional preference consensus among users. By integrating user individualization and item regionalization, our approach surpasses state-of-the-art CF methods in prediction accuracy while offering interpretability through visualized bicluster presentations and the ability to obtain latent user and item profiles. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets showcase our approach's ability to transcend the inherent subjectivity in user ratings, successfully capture local preference structures, and produce accurate predictions that surpass state-of-the-art CF methods by a significant margin. Sources and demonstration are available at https://github.com/jaechang User-centric Bicluster Collaborative Filtering.

Previous studies have established a link between a sun's magnetic behavior and observable spectral characteristics. In our research, we aimed to determine how a sun's magnetic behavior affects the spectral characteristics visible in HARPS-N age-sensitive age indicators and broadband filters. To achieve this, we analyzed the magnetic behavior of age-sensitive suns with well-established ages from the SUNBLISS program. We developed an empirical model to describe the connection between a sun's magnetic behavior and observable spectral characteristics, which in turn enables us to make predictions about these characteristics based on a sun's magnetic behavior. Recent advancements in image processing research, spurred on by AI trends, have led to numerous innovative methods for image enhancement and style extraction. This work delves into developing a single, versatile algorithm capable of performing multiple image processing tasks, including noise reduction, tone mapping, and style transfer, across various image categories. To achieve this, we employ a conditional carrier signal approach, treating image sets as a combination of inherent style and a variable signal. An autoencoder-based model is designed to extract the style component from a training dataset, whereas the signal is generated through a residual generator that utilizes the style representation and a reference image. The style representation is then combined with the signal to produce the output image. This algorithm can be applied to multiple image processing applications, such as noise reduction, tone mapping, and style transfer, and can perform both forward and reverse operations. The algorithm's effectiveness in a range of image categories has been successfully demonstrated through extensive experiments. The source code for this project is publicly available at https://github.com/chenkeheng/StyleExtractAndImageEnhancement.

The objective of this research is to examine the characteristics of the angular distribution of alphas produced through the 4CN+2CN reaction using the 6Li+51V system, specifically at an energy of 15 MeV for 6Li. A Monte Carlo simulation method is employed to calculate the angular distribution of alphas relative to the 6Li beam, with calculations of z-axial alphas exceeding 400 pb being feasible. Additionally, the concept of an inclusive production threshold is introduced, and an inclusive threshold of 3500 keV is determined for this reaction. This finding is corroborated by experimental and computational data, revealing a 1500 keV wide range of reaction instability. Our analysis also shows that a 6Li narrow beam can produce a focused angular distribution of alphas, with a notable peak near the beam's initial position. This peak can serve as an effective flag for identifying a focused angular distribution of alps and is closely tied to a 51V GDR's unique characteristic. It is proposed that the resulting alphas' narrow distribution could potentially utilize the 51V's 11+ state as a gateway to detect 51V GDRs via a focused angular distribution of alphas. This concept offers a new method for detecting 51V GDRs via a 6Li+51V reaction and the subsequent production of alphas. To conclude, a 6Li narrow beam can produce a focused angular distribution of alphas, and our analysis offers a new method for detecting 51V GDRs via a 6Li+51V reaction and the subsequent production of alphas. An intrinsic drive, known as the seek cycle, governs the behavior of animals that are attracted to substances such as nutrients, social contacts, or sex, causing them to move upwards in search of this motivation. Substances that stimulate the seek cycle release neuroactive chemicals that bind to specific receptors on nerve cells, triggering a chain of neurological responses that ultimately direct the animal towards these rewards. In our study, we identify the nerve cells responsible for initiating this response in the Pacific lamprey and uncover the location of the genes that encode the receptors for these substances. We also examine how the composition of these substances varies across different stages of the lamprey's life cycle. Furthermore, we predict how the structure of these substances might evolve to better meet the changing needs of the lamprey as it matures. Our findings provide a deeper understanding of the universal seek cycle mechanism that drives many animals to move upwards in search of substances that stimulate this response. The information we present here can also help inform the development of novel therapies based on neuroactive substances that stimulate this response, and our models of the composition and structure of these substances can inspire innovative solutions to the challenge of designing bio-inspired materials. Finally, our study demonstrates how the exploration of an animal's nervous system can reveal fundamental principles of life that can be applied to the design of artificial intelligence systems. High-speed stars orbiting a supermassive black hole at the center of galaxies may ultimately meet their demise in a collision triggered by tidal forces exerted by the black hole. Research suggests that the tidal fraction of the stars' energy remains relatively small when they reach the point of collision. Recent studies have focused on determining the final circularization of these stars, with significant implications for the efficiency of energy conversion from stars to the surrounding environment. We devote our research to calculating the remaining elliptical shape of stars at the point of collision, with specific attention to the final residual eccentricity. Our analysis shows that even in the most distant galaxies, the eccentricity of falling stars remains minimal, with a notable exception being those near the very lowest mass black holes, for a limited timeframe just before collision. This exception can likely be attributed to the influence of higher-order gravitational interactions, which may become more pronounced under the low-gravity conditions encountered in such systems. In general, however, our research reveals that the eccentricity of stars at the point of collision is expected to be relatively low, with most cases having an eccentricity below 0.1, with a median value of less than 0.06. This finding indicates that the collision of stars with a black hole typically leads to a more gradual and circularized outcome, with considerable implications for the efficiency of energy conversion and radiation generated during the merger. Moreover, our research points out an important role for post-Newtonian theory in understanding these processes, with potential applications extending to the study of colliding binary black holes observed through LIGO. In a recent paper, an alternative theory of shock wave propagation was presented in a medium with changing density, which led to the introduction of a new type of collapsing shock wave. This paper investigates a specific type of collapsing shock wave, thought to be the only viable option in such a medium, and shows that in fact, both theory and reality can coexist. Furthermore, we identify a medium with changing pressure as the key to resolving this contradiction. We then develop a general equation for collapsing shock waves in this type of medium, and demonstrate the existence of two distinct types of collapsing shock waves, effectively making collapsing shock theory a more general concept. One notable application of this discovery involves astrophysical outflows, which also exhibit changing pressure and, according to our findings, can feature two types of collapsing shock waves. Additionally, we identify a variety of shock wave configurations, including, but not limited to, weak, rarefied, and strong shocks. A graphical representation of these configurations is provided, and we highlight the unique characteristics of expanding shocks, as well as the similarities and differences between expanding and collapsing shocks. Lastly, we explore the specific physical processes driving each type of collapsing shock wave, and collect our findings in an easily referenceable table, showcasing the distinct properties of both types of collapsing shock waves, as well as their expanding shock counterparts. One particularly notable point, and a long-standing puzzle in the field, is resolved in this paper: the existence of collapsing shock waves in the absence of a reverse shock, and this finding is connected to another longstanding mystery in the field, the presence of a forward shock. This paper also introduces a new theory for shock wave propagation, and reveals the discrete set of possible energy values, a fundamental concept known as a "discrete spectrum of energy", and this theory can be applied to a broad range of expanding and collapsing shock wave configurations, and we showcase its simplicity and effectiveness. Finally, we identify key areas for further research and investigation.

The growing presence of artificial intelligence in daily life is undeniable, yet its transparent and ethical use has been a subject of concern, particularly in high-stakes fields like healthcare and law enforcement. For AI systems to be trustworthy, users need comprehensible results, leading to a significant need for their explainability. Although research on explainability has made significant progress, formulating clear and effective specifications remains an intricate challenge, especially in domains with limited resources. We contend that requirement engineers can play a vital role in addressing this gap by developing specifications that support the needs and goals of stakeholders, thus enhancing the explainability of AI systems. This paper provides an overview of the current state of research in explainability and the potential contributions of requirement engineering, before proposing a collaborative approach that integrates the perspectives of various stakeholders, hence ensuring that explainability specifications align with their priorities. Finally, we highlight promising areas for future investigation. Additionally, this paper has been adapted from the authors' original text, provided under the terms of a CC BY-NC-ND 42 license.
