Data compression technology, known for reducing the amount of stored data, has an unexpected issue: some compressed files can easily be decompressed and reveal a significant amount of the original, uncensored data, thereby compromising user confidentiality. To address this problem of data leakage in compression, we need to develop new methods that minimize the amount of leaked information while achieving nearly lossless compression. From an information-theoretic perspective, this problem can be seen as a special case of source coding with zero error and data leakage constraints. We explore this new perspective and provide a mathematical framework for understanding data leakage in compression by using graph theory. Specifically, we examine the relationship between conditional entropy and graph topology, which allows us to establish a threshold for leakage in a compressed file. To illustrate our theoretical framework, we use an example of leakage in a binary tree code. This study provides a foundational understanding of the data-leakage-compression conflict and paves the way for further research on the quantitative analysis of data leakage. Moreover, we propose an approach to identify the optimal compression strategies that balance leakage and storage costs. To test our theoretical framework, we conducted an experiment on the leakage of binary files encoded using Huffman coding, which showed promising results. The developed approach can be used for various compression algorithms and source codes. Furthermore, we outline potential applications of our study in other fields, such as cryptography and graph theory, as well as the development of new compression schemes that take into account the costs associated with leakage and storage. To support further research, we have made our source code available for replication. We hope that our study will inspire the development of innovative compression algorithms resistant to data leakage attacks. The notion of q-training is an extension of traditional reinforcement learning to quantized states and actions.  We consider a markov decision process where states and actions are represented as vectors of L bits.  Reinforcement learning is carried out by sampling from a distribution over actions, and a policy network is trained to output probabilities for each action given an action state pair.  Due to the discrete nature of states and actions, the markov decision process does not satisfy the assumptions typically made in reinforcement learning.  Nevertheless, we find that sampling from a biased distribution over actions can lead to optimal q-policies that achieve the highest expected cumulative quantized rewards over time.  In particular, we develop a trainable bias network that, along with the policy network, is optimized to maximize the expected cumulative quantized rewards over time.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach by applying it to a series of tuning challenges, and show that the resulting q-policies achieve higher rewards than traditional reinforcement learning methods.  Furthermore, we observe that the biased actions facilitate faster convergence to the optimal policy.  Additionally, the bias network serves as a latent representation of the actions, and we find that it enables faster convergence to the optimal q-policy than traditional reinforcement learning methods.  In certain scenarios, the biased actions lead to a reduction in the state entropy over time, indicating that the markov decision process captures some aspect of the underlying system dynamics.  The proposed approach is compatible with a range of reinforcement learning algorithms, and we demonstrate its applicability to both on and off-policy learning scenarios.  Notably, we observe that the resulting q-policies achieve higher rewards than traditional reinforcement learning algorithms in scenarios where the markov decision process is generated artificially to be non-quantized.  This highlights the role of the discrete nature of states and actions in shaping the reward structure of the markov decision process. Currently, the field of random thermodynamics is generating significant interest, driven in part by a recent breakthrough paper [M. Le Doussal, et al., Sci. Post. 12 (2017) 046001]. These models can simulate nonlinear dynamical systems that are driven by multiple current flows, such as electrical charge, heat, and mechanical work. In order to expand upon this work and make it more accessible, we present a reformulated version of random thermodynamics that incorporates multiple currents while maintaining gauge invariance. Our method utilizes a current-relaxation-rate spectrum, and we show that this approach aligns with the adiabatic approximation and the fluctuation-dissipation theorem. Furthermore, we apply this methodology to both a Brownian motor and a driven granular system, demonstrating our method's utility in these contexts. In a subsequent paper, we will delve into specific applications of our theoretical framework (M. N. Knuuttila, et al., in review). Excellent guidance on the statistical mechanics of nonequilibrium systems is provided in [K. Mallick, Ann. Phys. 392 (2018) 272]. Additionally, we acknowledge the influential work of B. Derrida, whose contributions to the field are vast [B. Derrida, Phys. Rep. 184 (1990) 7, and [B. Derrida, J. Phys. France 50 (1989) 265]. Lastly, we express our appreciation for J. M. Butterfield's geometric interpretation of gauge invariance, as presented in [J. M. Butterfield, Stud. in History and Phil. of M. Sci. 33 (2002) 431].

We explore a cutting-edge technique for optically manipulating two-dimensional assemblies of exciton-polaritons in microcavities, leveraging the inverse Faraday effect to create complex microstructures. By targeting specific spatial patterns with laser pulses, we demonstrate the ability to shape polariton gain profiles, coherently trap and release polariton "macro-photons," and induce persistent spatial patterns within the polariton system. The latter phenomenon can be attributed to the generation of localized magnetic fields which give rise to anomalous Hall effects, thereby providing a novel framework for understanding polariton self-organization. The employed system exhibits a remarkable balance between the speed of optical stimulation and the longevity of generated patterns, making it an attractive system for research in pattern self-organization, optical toggling, and spin-based information storage. Magnetic island coherence is examined through a study that combines magnetohydrodynamics with a particle-in-cell model. This hybrid approach integrates a finite-volume magnetohydrodynamic model with an embedded particle-in-cell component, enabling a quantitative investigation of magnetic island merging. A test scenario involving two magnetic islands separated by a thin, connection field is employed to analyze island coherence under various conditions. Specifically, the effects of particle-in-cell resolution, magnetohydrodynamic grid spacing, and the level of turbulence within the simulation are thoroughly investigated. A regional particle-in-cell model is found to enhance magnetic island coherence, but is ultimately shown to be ineffective in merging scenarios where the island's central magnetic field weakens. However, the integration of a finite-volume magnetohydrodynamic model with a higher-resolution particle-in-cell model is found to improve merging outcomes and increase island coherence, effectively simulating merging at a lower spatial scale. This work confirms previous findings that magnetic island coherence can be achieved through the integration of dispersed particles, and demonstrates the importance of the particle-in-cell resolution in merging simulations. Additionally, it shows that merging can occur at lower levels of disorder, consistent with reconnection dynamics. A key outcome of this study is the identification of a specific disorder level at which the merging process reaches a steady-state condition, characterized by a clearly distinct reconnection site. This steady-state disorder level is found to be comparable to that observed in fully embedded particle-in-cell reconnection simulations. By integrating a magnetohydrodynamic model with an embedded particle-in-cell component, this study enables an in-depth examination of the interaction between reconnection and merging processes, clarifying previous confusions and providing fresh insights into magnetic island coherence and island merging. It ultimately provides a more comprehensive understanding of the reconnection-merging interaction and improves the accuracy of integrating particle-in-cell models into global magnetohydrodynamic models, an integration that is essential for simulating the coherent reconnection of magnetic islands essential for simulating magnetic reconnection. Additionally, this work may contribute to an improved understanding of the coherent reconnection process in astrophysical contexts such as neutron star mergers and winds from cool stars. Finally, it lays a foundation for future studies on magnetic island coherence and merging, particularly in scenarios that involve multiple magnetic islands, turbulent fields, and various other applications and phenomena.
